We further discuss representative applications and open challenges. The goal is to provide an accessible entry point to the field and to support continued progress toward reliable learning-based control in real-world systems. To support learning and practical exploration, we share implementations and illustrative examples along with our discussion, together with additional resources on our website: https://learning-based-control.github.io/tutorial/.

title: SAFTER: Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability for Robust Reinforcement Learning under Distribution Shift
abstract: Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.

title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.

title: Experimental Characterization of SMD Inductors for Cryogenic Power Conversion at 4 K
abstract: With the increasing complexity and scalability demands of cryogenic electronic systems, such as quantum computing platforms, conversion of power within the cryogenic environment has become a primary concern. Magnetic inductors are among the key components affecting converter performance, as their electrical and magnetic properties can change significantly at low temperatures. In this paper, five commercially available Vishay SMD power inductors are experimentally characterized down to 4 K: DC resistance is measured continuously during cooldown, while frequency-dependent AC inductance and resistance are measured up to 2 MHz at both room temperature and 4 K. The results show substantial DC resistance reductions of 25x-58x at 4 K, while the inductance degrades by only about 5-5.5%. Although cryogenic operation slightly increases the AC resistance (due to the intensified skin effect) and raises core losses, converter-level analysis shows an inductor-only efficiency improvement of approximately 5.3-6.9 percentage points at 1 A, and up to 22.8 points at 3 A. The measured frequency-dependent impedance of each inductor is imported into Cadence and a complete single-phase 24 V-to-1 V buck converter with GaN power devices is simulated at 1, 2, and 3 A at 4 K. The full-converter efficiency at 4 K is shown to improve by 3.0-5.2 percentage points at 1 A and by up to 22.5 points at 3 A for the AC-characterized devices. These findings indicate that commercially available off-the-shelf power inductors remain operationally viable under cryogenic conditions and can simultaneously increase inductor efficiency and reduce the overall power loss in cryogenic power conversion systems.

title: Funnel-Precompensated Disturbance Observer for Uncertain Minimum-Phase SISO Linear Systems of Arbitrary Relative Degree
abstract: Disturbance observers (DOBs) recover nominal behavior, but fast filters risk peaking. We propose a funnel-precompensated DOB for uncertain minimum-phase single-input single-output linear systems of known relative degree. A stable-factor residual yields a minimum-phase channel. At relative degree two, gain conditions require positive plant high-frequency gains and one positive common design gain; for higher degrees, the common-design result also uses a plant-gain interval and mismatch condition. Global boundedness, practical nominal-output recovery, and open-funnel initialization are established.

title: Spatial-Frequency Control Authority of Grid-Forming Inverters over Voltage Waveforms in Distribution Feeders
abstract: This paper develops a spatial-frequency framework to quantify the impact of distributed energy resources with grid-forming inverters (GFMs) on voltage waveforms at different locations along a feeder. An analytical authority function is formulated to characterize how controllability varies with both electrical distance from the point of common coupling (PCC) and frequency. It is shown that the GFM control authority generally decays with both distance and frequency, reflecting the limited ability of inverter actions to influence voltage waveforms at distant points. To better capture controllability near resonance, a relative dominance metric is introduced to compare the influence of inverter-induced and grid-induced voltages at a given location and frequency. These results highlight that waveform controllability is fundamentally a spatial-frequency phenomenon along the feeder. Simulation studies validate the analytical findings by demonstrating both the spatial decay of control effectiveness along the feeder and the frequency-dependent trends in control authority in a realistic electromagnetic transient setting. The proposed framework provides insights into the placement and coordination of GFMs to enable effective waveform-level voltage control across electrical distance along the feeder.

title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
abstract: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.

title: Hybrid PPO-Based Multi-Objective Optimization for UAV-mounted STAR-RIS with Energy Harvesting
abstract: This paper investigates a multi-objective optimiza tion framework for UAV-mounted reconfigurable intelligent sur face (STAR-RIS)-assisted Sixth Generation (6G)-enabled Internet of Things (IoT) systems. The considered framework jointly supports communication enhancement and radio-frequency (RF) energy harvesting (EH) through adaptive STAR-RIS transmission and reflection control. A weighted multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to jointly optimize the base station (BS) beamforming vectors, STAR-RIS transmission and reflection coefficients, RF power-splitting factor, and UAV trajectory under quality-of-service (QoS), power, and mobility constraints. Due to the strong coupling among the communications, EH, and UAV mobility variables, the resulting problem is highly non convex and difficult to solve using conventional optimization methods. To address this challenge, a hybrid proximal policy optimization (H-PPO) framework is proposed. The developed hybrid actor-critic architecture combines a categorical policy for discrete UAV movement decisions with Beta-distributed policies for continuous communication-control variables. In addition, a two-stage reward mechanism is introduced to enforce QoS feasibility while balancing system sum rate, energy efficiency, and harvested energy. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed H-PPO framework achieves faster convergence and more stable training behavior than proximal policy optimization (PPO) and twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) baselines. In particular, H-PPO achieves approximately 66% and 60% faster convergence than PPO and TD3, respectively, while maintaining more stable training behavior. Furthermore, the proposed framework effectively balances communication performance and EH under different QoS requirements, STAR RIS sizes, transmit power levels, and user densities.

title: Robust Procurement Planning for Community Choice Aggregators: Managing Market Price Uncertainty
abstract: Community Choice Aggregators (CCAs) play an important role in the energy transition by procuring renewable electricity for local communities while balancing affordability, resource adequacy, and clean-energy requirements. In California, these long-term procurement decisions are coordinated through integrated resource planning (IRP). However, conventional IRP frameworks typically represent wholesale electricity prices deterministically, even though price uncertainty can expose CCAs to substantial financial risk by affecting the cost of market imports and, particularly, the value of export opportunities. This paper develops a robust optimization framework for CCA resource procurement that hedges against uncertainty in wholesale import and export prices. We extend the open-source GenX capacity expansion model with a budgeted robust optimization formulation that protects procurement decisions against adverse price realizations while remaining computationally tractable for large-scale, multistage planning studies. Using data from a California CCA, we show that market price uncertainty can materially change optimal procurement strategies. Rather than aggressively expanding renewable capacity based on expected export revenues, robust portfolios reduce dependence on uncertain market revenues, leading to more conservative renewable investments and less reliance on market exports. We demonstrate that moderate uncertainty budgets provide most of the risk-reduction benefits of robust planning at limited additional cost, whereas higher robustness levels yield diminishing benefits as portfolio conservatism increases. These findings provide guidance for selecting uncertainty budgets in IRP studies and demonstrate how robust optimization can support affordable and resilient procurement decisions as CCAs contribute to the transition toward low-carbon electricity systems.

title: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go?
abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%.

title: A Comparative Study of LED Lighting Control Strategies for Energy-Efficient Greenhouse Operations
abstract: Greenhouse supplemental lighting is essential for meeting crop Daily Light Integral (DLI) requirement. However, conventional always-on and rule-based strategies are inherently energy-inefficient since they ignore future sunlight availability. This paper reports the results of deploying various supplemental lighting control strategies, namely, always-on, always-off, heuristic, optimal prediction-based, and two peak-shift variants, simultaneously in a single greenhouse at the Hampton Roads AREC of Virginia Tech, to ensure that every treatment experiences identical conditions. %The shared infrastructure is built on an MQTT-based IoT platform with Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density (PPFD) sensing and PWM-driven LED control; The prediction-based and peak-shift strategies optimize LED schedules using a Markov chain-based solar forecast. Experimental results over two replicates %(20~February--15~April~2026, 72~plants per treatment) show that the prediction-based strategy meets the desired DLI target at 65\% cost reduction relative to the always-on baseline while achieving the highest dry-mass yield among the proposed adaptive strategies. The heuristic strategy incurs only a 6\% cost premium over prediction-based control, offering a competitive forecast-free alternative. The peak-shift variants achieve the lowest active-strategy costs by shifting LED demand into off-peak tariff windows. A yield-per-dollar efficiency metric is finally introduced to jointly capture energy cost and crop output showing that the prediction-based strategy ranks highest at 18.976~g/\$, more than double the always-on value of 9.391~g/\$. These findings can provide greenhouse operators with an evidence-based framework for selecting a lighting control approach that balances energy cost, crop quality, and system complexity.

title: Attracting Rotations Obstruct Almost-Global Consensus on Spheres over Strongly Connected Graphs
abstract: We study discrete-time consensus on the Euclidean unit sphere, where weighted combinations of neighboring states are normalized to unit length. For symmetric weights on connected undirected graphs and ambient dimension $d\ge3$, earlier results establish instability of non-consensus fixed points under suitable weight conditions. For directed graphs on the unit circle, earlier results show that fixed points other than consensus and antipodal configurations occur only for a measure-zero set of weights. We show that these conclusions do not extend directly to general strongly connected directed graphs in higher dimensions. First, we construct full-rank non-consensus fixed points whose tangent eigenvalues all equal one, showing that strict linear instability need not hold. In a separate construction, for every $d\ge3$, we present a sparse strongly connected graph admitting full-rank fixed points on an open set of its permitted weights. Our main result establishes robust counterexamples to almost-global consensus: attracting rotating motions exist for $d=2$ with every $n\ge3$ and for $d=3$ with every $n\ge6$. These motions are locally asymptotically stable modulo common rotations and have asymptotic phase. They persist on open sets of strictly positive weight matrices. For each such matrix, an open set of initial configurations approaches neither consensus nor any fixed configuration. Thus the absence of full-rank non-consensus fixed points does not ensure almost-global convergence to consensus.

title: Distributed Platoon Control for Safe and Smooth Crossing at an Unsignalized Intersection-Part I: Stability Analysis
abstract: We propose a distributed platoon controller that guarantees safe and smooth crossing of multi-vehicle systems at an unsignalized intersection. To support the stability analysis, we consider a multi-vehicle platoon maneuvering along a closed path with a single unsignalized intersection. Unlike traditional bi-level decoupled designs on open paths, which primarily focus on intersection control while neglecting its coupling with platoon convergence, and thus hindering rigorous convergence analysis, the closed-path setting allows us to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the platoon. The local exponential convergence analysis of the switched closed-loop system, induced by repeated vehicle switching at the intersection, is presented. Under some mild conditions on the controller gains, we show that safe intersection crossing is ensured during the transient phase and smooth crossing is achieved in steady state, where all vehicles travel at a common constant speed while avoiding collisions at the intersection. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed distributed controller is demonstrated in a high-fidelity CARLA simulator using multiple commercial vehicle models.

title: Conformal Koopman Certificates for Nonlinear Multi-Agent Consensus on Time-Evolving Graphs
abstract: Robot fleets must often agree on a shared value before they act, over wireless networks that change as the robots move. Their supervisor needs a deadline: the number of communication rounds after which the fleet has agreed with a stated probability. Today it comes from simulation plus a safety margin, with an open probability of being met. We certify it. Our method, conformal Koopman certification, rests on one observation: averaged over the random network changes, the expected behaviour of the fleet evolves linearly, for any nonlinearity of the agents. The decay rate of this linear evolution gives the shape of the deadline. One remaining constant is calibrated from 200 short test runs by conformal prediction, a statistical method that turns any predictor into a guarantee that holds with a user-chosen probability. The certified deadline holds for every agreement tolerance at once and for any error in the estimated rate. The same linear model predicts the value the fleet will agree on and certifies how much corruption of the exchanged messages the collective decision absorbs. For 60 simulated robots the certified deadline was met in all 500 test runs against a 90\% target and exceeded the slowest run by 16\%. The classical worst-case bound exceeds that run by more than 160 orders of magnitude, a linearised deadline is missed in up to 26\% of runs, and direct conformal calibration costs 80 times more simulation per tolerance.

title: Norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.

title: Controllability Allocation Scores for Linear Infinite-Dimensional Systems
abstract: We define finite-time controllability allocation scores (CASs) as optimal solutions to two convex optimization problems that allocate a fixed actuation budget among prescribed input functions of linear infinite-dimensional continuum systems with selected target outputs. The objectives are expressed using controllability Gramians for the selected outputs and correspond to maximizing the volume of output changes reachable with unit control energy or minimizing the mean energy required for unit output changes. To compute these CASs, we discretize the system in space, construct the resulting Gramians, and solve the resulting allocation problems by a domain-aware projected gradient descent method. We study the behavior of CASs when the actuator-to-target responses of the spatially discretized systems converge to those of the continuum system as the mesh is refined. If the continuum system is target controllable, we show that the spatially discretized systems are also target controllable on sufficiently fine meshes and that the optimal values of the approximate problems converge to the optimal value for the continuum system. If the allocation problem for the continuum system has a unique CAS, we show that the CASs obtained from the spatially discretized problems converge to it. We also derive quantitative bounds on the errors between these CASs when the Gramian map for the continuum system distinguishes allocations. A two-dimensional advection-diffusion example illustrates how transport dynamics affect target controllability and CASs. Spatial refinement reveals apparent controllability caused by numerical diffusion and supports the theoretical convergence results.

title: From Market Signals to Maintenance Decisions: Grid-Informed Maintenance Optimization in Offshore Wind Farms
abstract: The reliable and cost-effective integration of large-scale offshore wind farms into power systems is largely influenced by maintenance operations. To date, power producers primarily rely on farm-level information (e.g., health signals, power generation, weather conditions) for maintenance planning of wind turbine fleets. We propose to consider additional grid-level information in maintenance operations, such as generation curtailment and market pricing. Periods of high generation curtailment or negative electricity pricing can be viewed as opportunities for preventive maintenance, since assets are fully or partially shut down due to grid-imposed constraints. We first analytically establish that access to market information has non-negative economic value for maintenance scheduling under a stylized setting, providing a theoretical foundation for treating market and grid information as a maintenance opportunity. We then formulate a grid-informed opportunistic maintenance scheduling model as a receding-horizon mixed integer linear program that jointly leverages both farm- and grid-level signals under realistic conditions to determine a maintenance plan for offshore wind turbines. Considering a 600-MW offshore wind farm in the United States, our proposed method reduces annual maintenance costs by up to 10%, while enhancing asset availability and resource utilization, relative to advanced maintenance models that solely rely on farm-level information.

title: Control of Isolated Four-Quadrant Single-Stage Three-/Single-Phase X-Rectifier for EV On-Board Chargers
abstract: The single-stage isolated eXtended-functionality rectifier (X-Rectifier) electric vehicle (EV) on-board charger (OBC) employs 650V GaN monolithic bidirectional power transistors (M-BDS) in the input stage, provides sinusoidal input currents and four-quadrant operation in three-phase and split/single phase grids without power derating, operates from asymmetrical three-phase mains, provides reactive power if needed, and supports extremely asymmetric phase loading in standalone vehicle-to-load (V2L) mode. This paper presents a new improved phase-modular control method for the X-Rectifier that enables tracking of arbitrary and independent phase current references regardless of the instantaneous grid voltage (i.e., enables four-quadrant operation). The method supports grid-tied (i.e., grid-to-vehicle, G2V, or vehicle-to grid, V2G) and grid-forming (i.e., V2L) operation. Further, aiming towards a practical realization of the X-Rectifier, the paper addresses implementation aspects of the M-BDS half-bridges, like commutation logic around the grid-voltage zero crossing, fault handling, and soft-switching behaviour. Finally, a realized 5.5 kVA hardware demonstrator of the X-Rectifier is used to validate the proposed control method experimentally for all operating modes, including grid-tied three- and single-phase four-quadrant operation (G2V, V2G, and full reactive power modes). Further, robust V2L operation is verified with real-world loads, i.e., in three-phase mode with asymmetrical loading of the phases including a woodworking power tool, and in single-phase mode with a high-power vacuum cleaner with high inrush current and hence momentary overload of the X-Rectifier demonstrator.

title: Temporal Difference Learning of Probabilistic Reach-Avoid Value Functions
abstract: Reach-avoid sets, defining the states from which a task can be completed while avoiding unsafe regions, are fundamental tools for deploying robots in environments subject to disturbances and uncertainty, as well as for runtime task-feasibility monitoring, allowing prediction of whether a state is safe and will lead to successful task completion. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability (HJR) and its recent neural extensions (e.g., Lipschitz Continuous Reachability Learning, DeepReach) treat disturbances adversarially, computing the reach-avoid set under worst-case disturbances from a bounded set. This guarantees safety but can yield overly conservative sets when disturbances are stochastic rather than adversarial, and additionally requires the disturbance set to be known or specified in advance. We propose Probabilistic reach-avoid Value Function (PVF), a self-supervised method, applicable to black-box systems, for computing reach-avoid sets as the states with a certain reach-avoid probability under stochastic, potentially unbounded disturbances. We evaluate our approach against HJR-based baselines on systems of increasing complexity, up to a Hopper locomotion task, and show that our probabilistic sets are less conservative and more accurate than adversarial HJR sets when disturbances are non-adversarial.

title: Observer-Based Control for Multi-Agent Systems under Communication-Task Graph Mismatch and Directed Switching Topologies
abstract: This paper addresses decentralized estimation and control of heterogeneous multi-agent systems communicating over directed switching topologies. The objective is to satisfy cooperative tasks that require coordination among agents according to a time-invariant task graph. To address the potential mismatch between the communication and task graphs, each agent is equipped with a k-hop Prescribed Performance State Observer (k-hop PPSO) to estimate the states of agents up to k communication hops away using only information exchanged with its 1-hop neighbors. A novel prescribed performance funnel construction is developed to account for the switching communication topology, and a sufficient lower bound on the dwell-time is derived to guarantee the prescribed performance specifications under topology variations. Further analysis shows that, if the desired control objective is achieved with exact knowledge of the required nonlocal states and the resulting closed-loop system is uniformly set-ISS with respect to the state estimation error, then replacing these states with their estimates guarantees convergence to a neighborhood of the desired set. The size of this neighborhood can be made arbitrarily small by appropriately selecting the observer performance bounds. A simulation study demonstrates task satisfaction under directed switching topologies.

title: Speculative Imbalance Positions by Non-Physical Traders: Impacts on Electricity System Balancing in Great Britain
abstract: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian modeling of agrivoltaic dairy-calves under missing information
abstract: Livestock 5.0 provides a framework to optimize animal welfare and productivity amidst escalating climate change and current pressures to sustainably increase production through limited expansion of agricultural lands, while equilibrating the food-water-energy nexus. Directly tackling the food-water-energy nexus, agrivoltaics emerges as a promising solution for dual-land use for food and renewable energy production. In this paper, we evaluated the effectiveness of agrivoltaics for dairy-calves in a commercial farm through a joint hierarchical Bayesian model, developed to account for non-linear and time-varying relationships, pedigree structure, and missing information. Uncertainty from missing information was propagated to the posterior estimates. While weight at birth and calf sex were not associated with serum Brix, we found that serum Brix was positively associated with colostrum Brix, which allowed to estimate the probabilities of the serum Brix quality (poor, fair, good, or excellent) given colostrum Brix. Poor serum Brix quality was positively associated with disease event rate, with similar rates for the other quality classes. Serum Brix quality was not associated with calf weight, indicating that farm management overcame the negative effects of low serum Brix quality. Previous number of diseases was positively associated with disease event rate, while weight at birth was negatively associated with disease event rate. Agrivoltaics were not associated with disease event rate, indicating that agrivoltaics can be implemented as a safe, dual-use system for increased calf comfort an welfare.

title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey offers a consolidated reference for researchers developing and evaluating RL solutions on specialized hardware.

title: Neural Closed-Loop Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Stability and Generalization Guarantees
abstract: Neural networks are expressive models of nonlinear dynamics, but identifying such systems from closed-loop data raises two difficulties: the feedback loop correlates inputs with measurement noise, biasing standard open-loop estimators, and the identified model must be stabilized by the data-collection controller, so that its closed-loop behavior matches the true plant's. We derive a complete parameterization of all nonlinear systems stabilized by a given controller, generalizing the classical dual-Youla parameterization to the nonlinear setting. Building on this characterization, we propose Internal Controller Identification (ICI), a computationally tractable framework for identifying potentially unstable systems while ensuring closed-loop stability by construction; in the linear case, our indirect method reduces to an open-loop identification problem, for which standard consistency results apply. The framework accommodates contextual information, letting a single certified model identify a family of systems, and supports a PAC-Bayesian training objective that, when data are scarce and prior knowledge is available, bounds the identified operator's expected prediction loss. Experiments show that ICI identifies open-loop unstable plants where uncertified baselines diverge, outperforms direct methods under weak excitation and feedback-correlated noise, generalizes zero-shot to environments unseen during training, and, with limited data, avoids the overfitting of empirical risk minimization while providing a non-vacuous generalization bound.

title: Explicit Convex Inner Approximation of TSO-DSO Flexibility Regions via Exact Second-order Cone Relaxation in Radial Networks
abstract: Accurate representations of the flexibility in distribution grids via tractable algorithms are essential for TSO-DSO coordination. However, flexibility region (FR) estimation based on nonlinear optimal power flow (OPF) generally lacks feasibility guarantees, while conventional convex relaxations may suffer from inexactness. This paper proposes a framework for constructing explicit inner approximations of active-reactive power FRs in radial networks based on the augmented relaxed OPF (AR-OPF). First, less-conservative sufficient conditions for the AR-OPF exactness are derived and extended to generalized objectives. Furthermore, an interior-feasibility analysis is established, guaranteeing that the entire region enclosed by the traced boundary is AC feasible under the proposed sufficient conditions. Building on these theoretical results, two adaptive algorithms are developed to construct explicit inner approximations and numerically convex representations of FRs. Numerical evaluations on different benchmark networks demonstrate consistently small relaxation residuals and high flexibility area retention in most cases, showing that the proposed methods provide a grounded approach to construct operationally admissible FRs for TSO-DSO coordination.

title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.

title: Adaptive Traversal Tubes for Posture-Aware Navigation of Bipedal Humanoids
abstract: Bipedal humanoids can change their effective footprint by adjusting body yaw, enabling both narrow-passage traversal and socially aware yielding. This paper presents a posture-aware navigation framework centered on \emph{Adaptive Traversal Tubes} (ATT), \emph{Interval Velocity--Heading} (IVH) control, and a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior. ATT represents a behavior-feasible corridor width field along a reference path, unifying geometric clearance and social comfort into a continuous signal. IVH maps this width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and omnidirectional velocity commands. A velocity-conditioned AMP policy, trained with GVHMR-retargeted frontal/sidestep motions and coupled \((v_x,v_y)\) tracking rewards, is designed to improve transition stability over a generic locomotion controller while remaining interchangeable with the default onboard policy. This preprint presents the full method; a planned evaluation protocol on a Unitree G1 is outlined, with quantitative results to follow. Demo videos of MuJoCo simulation and real-robot deployment are available at: github.com/lborogzj997/Humanoid-Navigation-in-Crowds-and-Narrow-Spaces.

title: Minimum-Energy Control for Stochastic Linear Systems: A Data-Driven Approach with Finite-Sample Guarantees
abstract: The open-loop minimum-energy control (MEC) problem asks for control inputs that minimize the control energy while ensuring the terminal state reaches a desired value. In this paper, we study the open-loop MEC problem for stochastic linear time-invariant systems. We consider a variety of stochastic constraints that enforce the terminal error to be small, and show that Stochastic MEC (SMEC) problem can be formulated as a QCQP. We obtain the optimal solution for SMEC and show that it generalizes the well-known Deterministic MEC problem by introducing novel stochastic variants of controllability and Gramian matrices. When the system dynamics is unknown, we obtain a direct data-driven solution to the SMEC problem using maximum-likelihood estimation and conformal calibration approaches. Finally, we quantify the sub-optimality and constraint violation of our data-driven solutions via finite-sample high-probability upper bounds, and highlight their dependence on the number of experiments, system dimension, and noise-to-signal ratio. We present numerical simulations to validate the theoretical results.

title: Sensitivity-Orthogonal Residual Learning for Adaptive Sideslip and Cornering Stiffness Estimation
abstract: Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers sideslip error by 12.7% to 22.0%. In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter's nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip error slightly above the uncorrected filter's.

title: Multiplexed Label-Free Cytokine Sensing Using a 128x128 CMOS ISFET Array with Flexdym Microfluidic Partitioning
abstract: Cytokine-mediated inflammation disorders such as sepsis and cytokine release syndrome demand bedside multiplex panels that resolve pro- and anti-inflammatory dynamics in minutes, yet label-free FET cytokine sensors remain limited to few devices, single analytes, and PDMS packaging that sorbs small molecules and leaches oligomers. We present a CMOS platform pairing a 128 x 128 ion-sensitive field-effect transistor (ISFET) array (SkyWater 130 nm, SiN gate) with a FlexDym 4 x 1 micro-well overlay that partitions the membrane into four chemically independent regions (approximately 2,176 pixels each, square-root-of-N averaging). Two wells carry capture antibodies (anti-IL-6, anti-IL-10), one is a non-specific reference, and one tests specificity; the transduced signal is defined as the differential current relative to the reference signal (Delta I_D(W_n) - Delta I_D(W_3)). Single-analyte dose-response measurements spanning 100 fM to 10 nM successfully resolve both IL-6 and IL-10 above the non-specific detection floor, including at healthy-serum baseline concentrations. The array shows a per-pixel pH sensitivity of 1.13 microamperes per pH unit (CV approximately 14%). Across two chips, device-to-device variation is dominated by transconductance spread (g_m CV approximately 62%); a one-time per-device g_m calibration reduces analyte-measurement variance to approximately 16%. We further validate the surface functionalization, characterize device-to-device variation, and demonstrate the FlexDym integration workflow. Simultaneous multiplexed cytokine measurements resolve IL-6 (W1) and IL-10 (W2) against the chemistry-only reference (W3). At the same time, cross-specificity characterization is assessed by applying IL-6 to an anti-IL-10 well (W4), establishing a scalable label-free ISFET architecture for multiplexed cytokine sensing.

title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.

title: Design and Control of a Multimodal Legged-Aerial Robot Through Separate Control Contraction Metrics
abstract: The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot. The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM). We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP). This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations. We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations.

title: DeGroot Dynamics on Multiplex Networks with Directed and Acyclic Interlayer Connectivities
abstract: In models of opinion dynamics, researchers typically examine how an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced by the opinions of their neighbors in a network. However, people's opinions on a topic are also influenced by their opinions and their neighbors' opinions on related topics. In an election, for example, the opinions of a voter on a variety of issues inform their opinions of electoral candidates. To consider the influence between people's opinions on multiple distinct topics, we study a multiplex extension of the traditional DeGroot consensus model. In our multiplex DeGroot model, different network layers represent distinct topics and directed interlayer edges (which are not allowed to form cycles) encode relationships between distinct topics. In our model, an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced both by the opinions of their neighbors on that topic and by their own opinions on related topics. We prove under mild conditions that our multiplex DeGroot model converges to a limit state. We also prove that strong connectedness in ``source layers'' (which represent fundamental beliefs) eventually yields a consensus opinion in each layer. In particular, we show that consensus on source layers can lead to consensus on other layers even when those layers otherwise would be polarized. By numerically simulating our multiplex DeGroot model on a two-layer network, we examine the effects on opinion dynamics of (1) different network structures and (2) different types of initial opinion data.

title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.

title: Dynamic Line Ratings Counteract Transmission Investment Needs Driven by Climate Change
abstract: Rising temperatures due to climate change will reduce power system transmission capacity. This reduction will interact with an ongoing shift from static to time-varying transmission rating standards. Previous research has yet to disentangle the effects of changing rating standards and climates on investment decisions. We quantify transmission investment needs for the Western U.S. power system (WECC) through mid-century under climate change and three rating standards: static ratings (SLR), ambient-adjusted ratings (AAR), and dynamic line ratings (DLR). By embedding alternative rating standards and high-resolution future weather data into a generation and transmission expansion model, PyPSA-USA, we find WECC will lose 1-3% of its transmission capacity across potential future climates under static ratings by mid-century, necessitating a 1-5% increase in transmission investment. Adoption of AAR or DLR eliminates most (81-99%) of the adaptation-driven transmission capacity needs, and further reduces aggregate transmission investments (by up to 31%). Additionally, we demonstrate that planning with time-varying ratings does not increase investment variability for individual lines under climate uncertainty relative to planning with static ratings. Our results emphasize the value and practicality of considering alternative rating standards in climate adaptation planning.

title: Controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable and not recursively enumerable
abstract: Sontag conjectured in 1988 that global controllability of polynomial control systems with rational coefficients is undecidable, but that the controllable systems form a recursively enumerable set. We prove the first part of the conjecture and disprove the second. For every homogeneous polynomial vector field $F$ of odd degree with rational coefficients, we construct an explicit polynomial control system $Σ_F$, with one more state than $F$, that is globally controllable if and only if the origin is \emph{not} globally asymptotically stable for $\dot x=F(x)$. By a recent result, the homogeneous polynomial vector fields with a globally asymptotically stable origin form a set that is recursively enumerable but not decidable. Consequently, global controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable, and the controllable polynomial systems are not recursively enumerable. The same conclusions hold for systems of the form $\dotξ=f(ξ)+Bu$ with a polynomial drift and a constant input matrix.

title: Data Center Oscillation Isolation and Grid Support: Fundamental Limits and Source-Selective Control
abstract: The grid integration of large data centers poses a growing power-system stability challenge. Rapidly varying computing demand can induce oscillations, while the facilities must provide a prescribed response to grid disturbances. Existing controls address load fluctuations and grid support but do not establish their jointly achievable performance. This paper derives fundamental limits and develops a source-selective controller for simultaneous oscillation isolation and grid support. A coupled closed-loop model gives a condition for distinguishing disturbance sources and reveals a direct isolation-support conflict under grid-import-power feedback alone; additional electrical measurements can remove this pointwise conflict but leave a conditional cross-frequency sensitivity limit. Guided by these limits, we design a local residual-feedback storage controller through convex frequency-domain optimization with stability, isolation, and grid-response constraints across operating points. Tests on a single-generator interconnection and a modified nine-bus network show stronger oscillation isolation than equal-order optimized comparators while meeting the prescribed grid response across operating points.

title: Exact model reduction by Lie symmetry groups
abstract: We develop a model-reduction technique based on Lie group theory for general engineering models described by a system of algebraic, ordinary, and/or partial differential equations with an arbitrary number of inputs, outputs, and constant parameters. The proposed method reduces the parameter space of these models without changing their external behavior, that is, their input-output maps. We apply this method to phase-field models used for high-fidelity simulations in electrochemistry to accelerate the analysis and design of metal-ion batteries.

title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

title: System Identification for Nonlinear Stochastic State-Space Models Using Ensemble Kalman Inversion with Application to Lithium-Ion Batteries
abstract: Nonlinear state-space system identification has attracted decades of interest, yet remains challenging because of the interplay among unknown parameters, nonlinear dynamics, and latent state variables. Its difficulty increases dramatically when the state and parameter dimensions increase. To address this challenge, we develop an ensemble Kalman inversion (EnKI)-based approach. This approach leverages EnKI to perform maximum a posteriori parameter estimation through successive local Gaussian approximations, enabling an iterative and incremental search for unknown parameters. The search combines Monte Carlo sampling with Kalman-type updates to evolve an ensemble of parameter samples, thereby offering empirical stability and the ability to handle strongly nonlinear models. The EnKI search is coupled with state estimation conditioned on the latest parameter estimates. This enables parameter identification along with latent state recovery. To improve scalability for large datasets, we further develop a cascaded EnKI (CasEnKI) method, which assimilates subdatasets sequentially to accelerate computation. We validate the proposed methods using a lithium-ion battery model with ten state variables and 18 unknown parameters. Simulation results show that the EnKI approach offers high identification accuracy and empirical stability in parameter search. Further, experimental results illustrate the computational efficiency and scalability of the CasEnKI method for large battery datasets.

title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

title: Motion Planning with Temporal Logic Precedence Specifications in Dynamic Environments via Spacetime Augmented Graphs of Convex Sets
abstract: We extend the augmented graph of convex sets GCS framework for motion planning with temporal logic precedence specifications to dynamic environments in which obstacles, keys, and doors undergo piecewise-linear translation and/or dilation over time. The main insight is that piecewise-linear motion of polytopic sets in R^d lifts exactly to a static polytopic partition of spacetime R^d X R_>=0. We show that the main result from the static case carries over to spacetime essentially without modification: a shortest path in the spacetime augmented GCS provides an exact optimal solution to the motion planning problem with precedence specifications. Moreover, the layered subgraph lattice that encodes signal temporal logic (STL) precedence specifications retains precise correspondence with the Bellman--Held--Karp (BHK) algorithm, and the full library of restricted but expressive STL specifications generalizes to the dynamic setting. Further, the framework allows time-gated keys and doors, collectible or passable only within a temporal window. The geometric side of the framework requires two modifications: a causality constraint (the time coordinate of a trajectory must be non-decreasing) and a spacetime speed constraint (bounded physical velocity), both of which are convex in the Bézier control points.

title: Convex Inner Approximations for Safe AC Dispatch With Device Dynamics
abstract: Safe AC dispatch requires both feasible operating points and enough ramping capability to reach the next target. This paper constructs convex inner approximations that connect nonlinear network feasibility, constrained device response, and dispatch-interval tracking. A fixed-point certificate enforces AC operating limits under bounded load uncertainty. Componentwise response envelopes convert heterogeneous device dynamics into affine conditions on measured states and power references. A command governor then combines these conditions with available ramping capability and a hard terminal-error bound. It selects an admissible target through a minimum-deviation objective and holds the corresponding reference while reserved fast regulation remains active. The resulting quadratic program optimizes controllable references and auxiliary variables. Tests on the IEEE 39- and 118-bus systems include 96 single-target executions and 64 transitions in continuous dispatch sequences at five- and fifteen-minute intervals. All 160 transitions satisfy the AC constraints, independent balancing-generator capability checks, and the prescribed regulation-adjusted terminal accuracy. Complete admission-cycle medians are 3.45 and 8.79 ms. A connected synthetic system with 3,200 buses and 1,000 generating units extends the computational assessment to 999 independent references, with a median cycle time of \LargeMedian{} s. The construction provides a tractable link between available ramping capability and safe, timely execution of AC dispatch.

title: Decentralized Stability Certificates for Interoperability in Power-Electronics-Dominated Power Systems
abstract: The rapid integration of power electronics converters has fundamentally altered the power grid's dynamic landscape, making modularity of operation and interoperability of heterogeneous devices two critical hurdles for power system reliability. In control language, these challenges can be paraphrased as decentralized certificates on the input/output behavior of every device, assured by local control, so that stability and guaranteed performance of the interconnected system emerge. For the power system application, such certificates should eventually be part of the rule book, the so-called grid code, and thus be generic and minimally restrictive for the control architecture of each device. Classical system-theoretic angles of attack to these questions go back to dissipativity concepts, which have historically been co-developed in automatic control, circuit theory, and power systems. Since standard dissipativity (e.g., passivity or small gain) criteria fall short in terms of conservatism, a range of more flexible and advanced tools have been developed to assure less conservative decentralized certificates guaranteeing stability under interconnection as well as dynamic performance following a disturbance. In this article, we review a range of methods that have been put forward to tackle these questions, compare and validate them, and point towards practically relevant research gaps which are amenable to control-theoretic approaches. Moreover, we provide a tutorial exposition of practically relevant power systems/electronics issues accessible to control engineers.

title: PhyPro-FM: A Physics and Prompt-Guided Graph Foundation Model for Contingency Analysis
abstract: The continuous evolution of next-generation power systems, characterized by the high penetration of renewable energy resources and dynamic topology variations, poses formidable challenges to traditional N-1/N-2 contingency analysis in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. While deep learning-based methods offer accelerated inference, existing studies predominantly treat contingency analysis as a pure regression problem, often overlooking the physical essence of grid operation and engineering requirements of real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a physics and prompt-guided graph foundation model (PhyPro-FM) for generalizable and engineering-viable contingency analysis. The proposed architecture integrates graph neural networks with a learnable global query mechanism and, notably, introduces a prompt-guided learning paradigm. By leveraging historical snapshots as few-shot prompts, the model dynamically captures correlations between target and historical operating conditions, significantly enhancing generalization capabilities under unseen topologies. Furthermore, we design a physics-informed training mechanism that prioritizes branch power flow errors over nodal voltage errors, aligning the optimization objective with critical grid security constraints. To ensure engineering applicability, a physics-informed inference mechanism is also developed, incorporating a residual-based correction module and a specialized post-processing strategy for singular branches to circumvent numerical instability. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PhyPro-FM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and generalization, validating its superior physical consistency and robustness for practical engineering applications.

title: Beyond Observability: Sharp Sample Bounds for Minimax State Reconstruction
abstract: We study how many output samples match the worst-case state reconstruction error obtainable from a continuous history under bounded measurement noise. For observable scalar-output linear time-varying systems with $n$ states, $n$ samples suffice for exact reconstruction, whereas at most $n^2$ attain the continuous-history minimax error in the $\ell_\infty$ norm. An explicit construction proves sharpness even for real-analytic systems. For time-invariant systems, strict total positivity yields one $n$-sample schedule optimal for every state coordinate; endpoint-observed tridiagonal cooperative chains satisfy this conclusion in physical coordinates. Interior sensing behaves differently: an explicit three-state family requires four samples despite positivity and distinct real eigenvalues. The strict three-state gap persists under small stabilizing damping. A nilpotent four-state example and an interval proof for a six-state mechanical system give gaps. The results identify how temporal sampling and the prescribed state-error geometry determine the measurements required for minimax reconstruction. Time-domain experiments illustrate the resulting estimation bounds.

title: Reassessing Clean Power 2030 Pathway Using Real Time Records
abstract: The National Energy System Operator (NESO) Clean Power 2030 advice to the government, accepted as United Kingdom (UK) government policy in December 2024, outlines a rapid increase in wind and solar generation capacities with the associated infrastructure by 2030, with the objective of reducing carbon dioxide emissions from the UK electricity system to 5.2 million tons per annum. Our previous paper used real-time records from 2017 to analyze Clean Power 2030 proposal. This paper extends the previous assessment, using real time records of 2017, 2018 and 2019 to test the resilience of the UK energy system under more diverse weather patterns. Two different modelling methods predict that the 2030 carbon dioxide emissions will be five times greater than Clean Power 2030 prediction. Furthermore, the projections show that, due to increased curtailment, only about half of NESO proposed increases in wind and solar capacities will be economically justified. NESO also advised the government that 35GW of unabated gas-fired generation would maintain security of supply, whereas our models suggest that at least 42 GW will be required during winter wind lulls. Recent events, such as grid stability problems in 2026, also discussed in the paper, validate our estimated and suggest the risk of blackouts in the UK is increasing.

title: Optimizing Airport Electric Ground Support Fleets with Digital-Twin-Guided Predictive Control
abstract: Electrifying airport ground operations is a key step toward reducing aviation-related emissions, but it makes task assignment and charging coordination strongly coupled in real time. This paper develops a digital twin of airport ground handling operations for electric ground-support vehicles (EGSVs), combining an agent-based model of airport operations with live flight-schedule updates and vehicle-energy dynamics. On this platform, we compare three control strategies for EGSV dispatching and charging: a rule-based heuristic, a rolling-horizon model predictive controller (MPC), and a Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) controller. The controllers are evaluated on three representative Schiphol Airport operating days and for multiple fleet sizes. The results show a clear trade-off between delays and energy use. Across all tested scenarios, MCTS yields the lowest average flight delay, with a pooled delay of 4.09 min, improving on the heuristic and MPC controllers by 64.7\% and 31.5\%, but at an increased energy consumption of 1\% and 0.3\%, respectively.The MPC and MCTS controllers coordinate charging more effectively throughout the day and reduce the peak charging infrastructure required by 6.0 and 4.7 charger units, respectively. Additionally, we find more vehicles can result in lower overall energy consumption and lower charging infrastructure requirements for all controllers. These findings highlight the value of digital twins not only as offline design evaluation tools, but also as practical environments for real-time control policies in electrified airport operations.

title: Fast Reassessment of Prolonged Electricity Shortages under Shared Fuel Interruptions
abstract: When several generators share a fuel supply, one interruption can disable them together and cause electricity shortages lasting days. Such interruptions can be made less frequent, for example by weatherizing gas supply, or shorter, for example by on-site backup fuel. Yet traditional resource adequacy indices, expected unserved energy and loss-of-load hours, fail to distinguish such measures whenever they remove the same expected time without fuel, because for interruptions independent of system conditions these indices depend on the interruptions only through this time. Their difference is revealed by prolonged-shortage exposure, the expected annual hours in shortages of at least a given duration, whose exact chronological calculation must be repeated for every interruption scenario. To reduce this cost, a fast reassessment method with guaranteed accuracy is proposed. Network calculations are performed once and condensed into a restoration response, the additional prolonged-shortage hours caused by one interruption of each duration, from which any scenario is evaluated as a weighted sum without new simulation. An hour-by-hour error bound determines whether this evaluation is accurate enough, and exact dynamic programming is applied otherwise, so that every result lies within a requested tolerance of the exact value on the same Monte Carlo samples. On the Reliability Test System of the Grid Modernization Laboratory Consortium, most evaluations were accepted, fully accepted scenarios typically ran more than 200 times faster than exact calculation, and total computation time decreased in every workload. Measures against fuel interruptions can thus be screened quickly and accurately by their effect on prolonged shortages.

title: Who Breathes the Detour? A Coupled Traffic-Emission-Dispersion-Exposure Pipeline
abstract: Road traffic is among the largest sources of health-damaging air pollution in inhabited areas. Direct measurement of resident exposure at the scale of an entire corridor remains costly, and existing simulation approaches often target either high-fidelity local snapshots or regional averages, leaving the corridor scale underserved. We present a coupled, end-to-end pipeline that links four stages: (i) microscopic traffic simulation with SUMO, (ii) per-vehicle emissions from the HBEFA4 model, (iii) deterministic three-dimensional Eulerian diffusion solved with an implicit finite-difference scheme on a geometric vertical grid, and (iv) resident-level exposure expressed as an air quality index over a synthetic population. The design deliberately trades the fidelity of full CFD dispersion for a workflow that runs end-to-end for the residential areas of several settlements on a single laptop, and the complete implementation is released open source. We showcase the pipeline at the example of the Swiss Gotthard transit corridor, covering the residential areas of six villages, two days, four scenarios, and three pollutants, to enable assessment of congestion mitigation measures. Code & Material: https://github.com/cedriczeiter/zeiter_coupled_pipeline.

title: Every minute counts: Wind farm power control during imbalance settlement using distributional soft actor-critic
abstract: Wind farms can provide flexibility by curtailing their output during periods of excess generation in the power grid. This can be done through implicit balancing, where the power setpoints of the farm are adapted to anticipate the imbalance price. By doing so, the wind farm helps reduce the resulting system imbalance while also lowering its own costs. However, implicit balancing is challenging since the imbalance prices are unknown in advance and hard to predict. Furthermore, the control strategy of the wind farm can affect the imbalance price formation. To address both challenges, we develop a control policy with 1-minute setpoints using distributional soft actor-critic. Evaluated on real data of the Belgian grid and an offshore wind farm, we show that our method outperforms a price threshold controller, often used in industry, by 88% and performs on par with soft actor-critic. Furthermore, unlike soft actor-critic, our approach can learn a risk-averse policy by optimizing a risk measure, such as conditional value at risk. The risk-averse policy was found to better account for its own impact on the price, showing a reduction in overshoots, while achieving a similar degree of imbalance cost savings. Last, we find that using 1-minute instead of 15-minute setpoints further reduces imbalance costs for all evaluated control policies.

title: Timing Skew Estimation of Time-Interleaved ADC based on Inter-Channel Correlations without Computing Derivative of Input Signal
abstract: Time-interleaved analog-to-digital converters (TI-ADCs) enable multi-gigasample-per-second throughput in high-speed applications, but sub-picosecond timing skews among interleaved channels introduce large spectral artifacts that degrade dynamic performance. To continuously track parametric drifts without interrupting normal operation, background calibration is required. However, extracting timing skews under unknown inputs is challenging, and many existing correlation-based methods rely on resource-heavy derivative filters that restrict input bandwidth. This article proposes a novel background timing-skew estimation technique for two-channel TI-ADCs that overcomes these limitations. Closed-form timing-skew expressions are derived using: (a) adjacent-channel cross-correlation combined with single-channel auto-correlation for sinusoidal inputs, and (b) adjacent-channel cross-correlation for Wide-Sense Stationary (WSS) inputs, specifically bandpass-filtered wideband noise and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexed (OFDM) signals. The derived analytical models are validated through comprehensive simulations, offering an efficient framework for real-time background calibration in high-speed data converters.

title: The Exact Boundary of Linear Optimality in Witsenhausen's Counterexample
abstract: Witsenhausen's counterexample has resisted a closed form solution for decades. However, it has remained unknown whether a mathematically tractable representation exists or not. In this paper, we solve this open problem, showing that the optimal policies are either linear or not tame and characterizing the exact regions where the two properties hold. Moreover, in the linear optimal region, we give an essentially unique closed form solution for the optimal policy, and show that no optimal first-stage policy is definable in any $o$-minimal expansion of the ordered real field in the nonlinear optimal region.

title: Adaptive Long-range UAV Flight Planning using Monte Carlo Search Trees
abstract: Long-range fixed-wing UAV missions require energy-efficient, dynamically feasible trajectories that can adapt online to evolving wind and airspace constraints. We present a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based framework that addresses this challenge by formulating mission planning as a finite-horizon Markov decision process incorporating aircraft kinematics, onboard energy dynamics, forecast wind fields, terrain, and time-varying no-fly zones.
