Immune dysregulation was quantified using IDDA v2.1; HCT-CI and PARI were also calculated. 2-year overall survival (OS) was 79%, and event-free survival was 59%. Higher IDDA v2.1 scores were associated with inferior OS in univariate analysis (HR: 2.23 per five-point increase, P = 0.043) and remained associated in an exploratory multivariable model (HR: 2.76, P = 0.041). Harrell's C-statistic for OS was 0.722 for IDDA v2.1, 0.661 for HCT-CI, and 0.772 for PARI. Exploratory quadrant analyses suggested that IDDA v2.1 provides complementary information, identifying patients classified as lower risk by comorbidity indices who nonetheless had adverse outcomes. These findings support IDDA v2.1 as an adjunct pretransplant risk stratification tool in pediatric IEI.

title: Open-label extension study of leniolisib in activated PI3Kδ syndrome: Long-term efficacy and safety.
abstract: Activated phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta syndrome (APDS) is an inborn error of immunity characterized by immune deficiency and dysregulation. Leniolisib is a selective phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta inhibitor approved to treat APDS in patients ≥12 years old. We report final results from a single-arm, open-label extension study in 37 patients with APDS (NCT02859727). Median leniolisib exposure was 4.3 years (range, 1.2-7.0 years). Adverse events (AE) were reported in 34 patients; 87% were grade 1. Serious AEs, reported in 10 patients, were deemed unrelated to leniolisib. Two patients discontinued treatment due to AEs: cardiac arrest and Hodgkin's lymphoma. There were significant reductions in annual infection (P = 0.0005) and respiratory infection (P = 0.0017) rates per year of treatment. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IRT) use significantly decreased per year of treatment (P = 0.0095). Clinically meaningful improvements in general health scores from the 36-Item Short Form Survey were observed. Overall, long-term use of leniolisib was generally well tolerated, and infections and IRT use reduced over time.

title: Employing Protein Language Models to Predict TCR-Peptide-MHC Binding: A Comprehensive Methods Guide.
abstract: Predicting the binding specificity between T-cell receptors (TCRs) and peptide-major histocompatibility complexes (pMHCs) represents one of the most challenging problems in computational immunology. Accurate prediction of these interactions is essential for advancing immunotherapy development, neoantigen vaccine design, and understanding adaptive immune responses. This chapter provides a comprehensive methodological guide to computational approaches for TCR-pMHC binding prediction, with particular emphasis on protein language model-based methods that have transformed the field since 2022. We describe the theoretical foundations, input requirements, output specifications, and practical implementation details for major prediction tools, including TCR-ESM, NetTCR-2.2, ERGO-II, pMTnet, ATM-TCR, and emerging approaches utilizing ESM-2, tcrLM, and graph neural networks. Additionally, we provide detailed protocols for data preparation, model execution, and result interpretation, along with essential notes addressing common challenges and best practices for method selection based on specific research objectives.

title: Adaptive MR-guided whole-pelvic SBRT with or without focal intraprostatic lesion boost for high-risk localized prostate Cancer: Adverse events and longitudinal quality-of-life outcomes.
abstract: PURPOSE: Evidence remains limited for combining elective pelvic nodal SBRT, online MR-guided adaptation, and simultaneous integrated boost (SIB) to intraprostatic lesion (IPL) in high-risk localized prostate cancer. We evaluated adverse events (AEs), quality-of-life (QOL), adaptive workflow, and longitudinal clinical outcomes after adaptive MR-guided whole-pelvic SBRT with or without SIB. METHODS: Consecutive PSMA-PET-staged patients treated on a prospective institutional protocol were analyzed. Treatment comprised 5-fraction MR-guided SBRT: 40 Gy to prostate, 33.5-35 Gy to proximal seminal vesicles, 25 Gy to elective pelvic lymphatics, and, when treated, 42.5 Gy to the IPL. Spacer use was clinician-selected. AEs were graded using CTCAE v5.0, and EPIC-50 outcomes were analyzed longitudinally. RESULTS: Seventy-seven patients were treated (median follow-up, 37.7 months); 40 (51.9%) received SIB and 34 (44.2%) received a spacer. Acute grade ≥2 (G2+) GU AE occurred in 5/76 (6.6%), with no acute G2+ GI events. Late G2+ GU and GI AEs occurred in 5/72 (6.9%) and 7/72 (9.7%), respectively. SIB was not associated with more grade ≥2 AEs. Spacer use was associated with fewer late G2+ GI AE (0/30 vs. 7/42; CONCLUSIONS: Adaptive MR-guided whole-pelvic SBRT with optional SIB demonstrated favorable medium-term tolerability. These findings support the feasibility of integrating pelvic nodal SBRT, online adaptation, and focal boosting, and suggest that spacers may mitigate bowel morbidity. Prospective validation is warranted.

title: Development and validation of a cumulative risk model and assessment tool for radiation-induced hypothyroidism in head and neck cancer: a multicentre study.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Radiation-induced hypothyroidism (RIHT) is a common late toxicity after head and neck radiotherapy. We aimed to develop and externally validate a multimodal Cox model for patient-specific cumulative RIHT risk assessment. MATERIALS & METHODS: This retrospective multicentre study included 1407 patients across four cohorts. The model was developed in the training cohort and externally validated in three independent cohorts. Candidate predictors included CT radiomics, dosiomics, dose-volume histogram parameters, and clinical variables. A multimodal Cox model was developed and used to estimate cumulative risks across time horizons. Temporal risk groups were derived from predicted 3- and 7-year risks. RESULTS: A total of 1407 patients (mean age, 55.4 ± 13.8 years; 1027 men) were evaluated and RIHT occurred in 694 (49.3%). The final model integrated three CT radiomics features, four dosiomics features, mean thyroid dose, age and N stage. It achieved C-index/overall AUC values of 0.714/0.765 in the development cohort and 0.725/0.800, 0.680/0.754, and 0.627/0.690 in the three external validation cohorts. Four temporal risk groups had RIHT event rates of 21.7%, 46.1%, 58.3%, and 71.8%, with significant differences in RIHT-free survival (log-rank CONCLUSION: The externally validated multimodal Cox model provided time-resolved, patient-specific RIHT risk estimates and temporal risk stratification using routinely available radiotherapy-planning data.

title: The Lipid Paradox in Chronic Liver Disease: Integrative Evidence From Intrahepatic Transcriptomics and Population-based Cohorts.
abstract: BACKGROUND/AIMS: Chronic liver disease (CLD) is associated with major metabolic disturbances. Although an elevated atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) reflects cardiometabolic risk, progressive liver dysfunction may instead be accompanied by lipid depletion, suggesting a "lipid paradox." We aimed to investigate its intrahepatic transcriptomic basis, systemic manifestations, and clinical implications using an integrative molecular-to-population approach. METHODS: Intrahepatic transcriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes associated with chronic hepatitis B progression, and hub genes were screened by machine learning. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2015-2018 data were used to examine the association between the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) and AIP using survey-weighted models and mediation analyses. Data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) were used to model 4-yr AIP trajectories and explore associations with cardiometabolic outcomes and all-cause mortality. RESULTS: Transcriptomics identified nine immune-fibrotic hub genes; functional enrichment showed immune activation and matrix remodeling with suppressed lipid metabolism. In NHANES, higher fibrosis risk was independently associated with lower AIP, with mediation more consistent with metabolic depletion than inflammation and independent of the age term in FIB-4. In CHARLS, individuals with liver disease showed an attenuated AIP trajectory; within this subgroup, lower AIP was associated with a higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome, with an exploratory adverse survival signal. CONCLUSION: Across transcriptomic, cross-sectional, and longitudinal analyses, reduced AIP in CLD may reflect metabolic and nutritional vulnerability rather than cardiometabolic protection, warranting further evaluation as an indicator for risk stratification.

title: Peri-urethral calcifications as a potential biomarker for acute genitourinary toxicity following prostate stereotactic body radiotherapy.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Peri-urethral calcifications (PUCs) are readily identifiable on planning computed tomography (CT) and may reflect chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and reduced peri-urethral tissue compliance. We evaluated whether baseline PUCs are associated with acute genitourinary (GU) toxicity following prostate stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT). METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 60 consecutive patients with localized prostate adenocarcinoma treated with definitive SBRT between June 2023 and February 2026. PUCs were assessed on non-contrast planning CT using predefined criteria by blinded observers. The primary endpoint was acute grade ≥ 2 GU toxicity occurring during treatment or within 90 days, graded according to CTCAE v5. Associations with toxicity were evaluated using logistic regression, with Firth penalized regression used for multivariable analysis. RESULTS: PUCs were identified in 17 patients (28.3%). Interobserver agreement was high (93.3%; Cohen's κ = 0.84). Overall, 21 patients (35%) developed acute grade ≥ 2 GU toxicity, including three (5%) with grade ≥ 3 toxicity. Acute grade ≥ 2 GU toxicity occurred significantly more frequently in patients with PUCs than in those without PUCs (64.7% vs 23.3%; OR 6.05, 95% CI 1.78-20.51; CONCLUSION: PUCs on routine planning CT were independently associated with acute grade ≥ 2 GU toxicity after prostate SBRT. If externally validated, PUC assessment may provide a simple, cost-neutral imaging biomarker for pretreatment urinary toxicity risk stratification.

title: Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Trigeminal Neuralgia: A Comparison of Proximal and Distal Isocenter Outcomes.
abstract: PURPOSE: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a chronic neuropathic pain condition affecting the trigeminal nerve, with an incidence of approximately 4 to 5 per 100,000 persons annually, increasing to 20 per 100,000 after age 60 years, and a female-to-male ratio of approximately 3:2. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) delivered by Gamma Knife or linear accelerators is a noninvasive alternative to surgical approaches for medically refractory cases. Although SRS for TN is commonly performed, consensus regarding optimal anatomic targeting remains lacking, with the 2 most common targets being the dorsal root entry zone (proximal) and the retrogasserian zone (distal). This study aimed to evaluate treatment outcomes in patients with TN treated with SRS based on proximal versus distal isocenter target locations. METHODS AND MATERIALS: This multicenter retrospective analysis included patients treated for TN between 2017 and 2021 with Gamma Knife or linear accelerator-based SRS who were followed for at least 1 year. All patients received 85 Gy prescribed to the isocenter, located in either the dorsal root entry zone (proximal) or the retrogasserian zone (distal). Patient-reported pain relief was recorded as complete, partial, or absent. Duration of pain relief and medication de-escalation were also assessed. Outcomes were compared using the log-rank test and Cox proportional hazards analysis. RESULTS: Eighty-six patients were included: 54 of 86 (63%) treated with proximal targeting (median age, 63 years; 72% women) and 32 of 86 (37%) with distal targeting (median age, 66 years; 71% women). Overall pain relief rates were 74% (proximal) and 90% (distal), although complete pain relief rates were 46% (proximal) and 31% (distal) ( CONCLUSIONS: Both proximal and distal targeting approaches achieve high response rates for TN. Distal targeting may be associated with higher rates of any pain improvement, whereas proximal targeting may be associated with higher rates of complete pain relief and complete medication discontinuation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant further investigation of efficacy and safety differences between these 2 approaches.

title: Human Intravital Microscopy.
abstract: Human intravital microscopy (HIVM) permits the real-time investigation of tumor vessels in vivo. Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility and clinical utility of this technique to characterize tumor-associated vessels in real time. While the importance of tumor vessels in cancer progression and resistance to anticancer therapies has largely been studied using animal models, HIVM has recently provided insight into the significant role of tumor vessels as a barrier to cancer treatment delivery and a potential biomarker for worse outcomes. In this chapter, the devices and methods to implement HIVM are presented. Techniques in postimaging acquisition, pathologic correlative, and statistical analyses to investigate HIVM tumor vessel characteristics with cancer-specific outcomes are also described. Lastly, the future potential applications of HIVM are discussed.

title: Comprehensive Approach to Heterogenous Tumor Cell Dynamics Analysis for Intravital Microscopy.
abstract: Intravital microscopy (IVM) enables observation of single-cell behaviors in live animal models, allowing detailed analysis of cancer cell dynamics within native 3D environments. However, comprehensively analyzing the extensive and complex data generated by IVM requires robust tools that exceed conventional approaches. This chapter presents a protocol for profiling heterogeneous cancer cell behavior within IVM movies, facilitating the study of cellular movement patterns and their associations with microenvironmental cues. The protocol allows researchers to systematically quantify single-cell (morpho)dynamics, providing unbiased analysis of cellular heterogeneity without requiring advanced computational expertise. The framework is adaptable to various tumor and non-tumor models, supporting insights into processes such as invasion, migration, and spatial relationships with distinct cell types, offering an accessible approach to studying heterogeneous cell behavior within its microenvironment.

title: Ex Vivo Models to Study the Interaction of Immune Cells and Cancer Cells Under Therapy.
abstract: Recent developments in cancer therapeutics have focused on modulating the immune component of the tumor microenvironment in order to activate antitumoral effector functions and induce cytotoxic immune responses. To further advance the design of treatment strategies, it is essential to understand what factors within the tumor microenvironment limit therapeutic efficacy and immune responses. Intravital imaging is a pioneering technology that has been utilized to study these processes in an intact environment, successfully highlighting the importance of cancer cell-immune cell interactions such as cancer cell killing caused by longitudinal and repeated interactions with immune cells. Despite the clear advantages that intravital imaging provides, its low throughput limits the variety of drugs, genetically altered parameters, and cell-cell interactions that can be studied. In other fields, a complementary approach has been to turn to ex vivo models, which offer greater throughput and simpler experimental protocols. Here, we describe the setup of an ex vivo technique to study dynamic interactions within an intact environment. This chapter will, in detail, 1) demonstrate strategies to generate fluorescently tagged cancer and immune cells using genetic as well as dye-based approaches; 2) present a method for how to best generate lung metastasis for ex vivo imaging; 3) describe the protocol to generate precision cut lung metastasis slices; and 4) detail how to prepare them for multiphoton or confocal microscopy. This protocol can be utilized for following the effect of therapeutics on tumor growth within the lung microenvironment ex vivo and on the interaction of cancer cells with immune cells. Ex vivo lung slices are an excellent model to 1) prepare the design of follow-on intravital imaging experiments (e.g., determine appropriate fluorophores, drug concentrations, or cell types to label), 2) study immune and cancer cell interactions in a complete environment, 3) select promising drugs from a pool of targets, and 4) select the best timing for intravital imaging experiments.

title: Combining Intravital Microscopy and Transcriptomic Analysis to Study Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: In recent years, multiphoton intravital microscopy has become a powerful tool that reveals cellular and molecular features of cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis in numerous cancer mouse models. In this chapter, we describe a method that combines intravital microscopy and RNA-seq to acquire molecular information on well-defined tumor lesions generated in a carcinogen model of tongue squamous cell carcinoma. Here, cancer lesions are first imaged longitudinally by intravital microscopy, and then precisely excised using a branding approach. The tumor epithelium is isolated, and the RNA is extracted and subjected to next-generation sequencing. This method enables the analysis of the transcriptome of tumor lesions with high precision during their progression.

title: Assessment of Metastatic Dissemination in Mouse Breast Carcinoma Models Using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
abstract: Metastatic dissemination remains the principal cause of cancer-related mortality, yet methodologies capable of directly assessing the dissemination process in vivo remain limited. Tumor Microenvironment of Metastasis (TMEM) doorways are specialized intravasation sites that facilitate cancer cell entry into the circulation and represent validated predictors of metastatic recurrence in breast cancer. We previously developed the TMEM Doorway Activity-MRI (TDAM) assay, a magnetic resonance imaging-based approach that detects TMEM doorway-associated vascular opening (TAVO) events and provides a noninvasive estimate of cancer cell dissemination risk. Here, we describe detailed protocols for implementing the TDAM assay in preclinical mouse models of breast cancer, including spontaneous transgenic tumors, syngeneic transplant models, and patient-derived xenografts. The methodology covers tumor transplantation procedures, MRI acquisition, contrast-enhanced dynamic imaging, first-pass permeability mapping, and computational TDAM calculation. This protocol provides investigators with a standardized framework for evaluating metastatic dissemination, monitoring therapeutic interventions, and advancing the development of imaging biomarkers capable of informing metastatic risk and treatment response.

title: Multimodal Imaging of Cancer by Combined Magnetic Resonance and Two-Photon Intravital Imaging.
abstract: Recent advances in single-cell technologies have allowed us to gain increasing insights into the mechanisms underlying tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. In combination with static approaches to study cancer, intravital multi-photon microscopy has significantly contributed to a better understanding of the crosstalk between tumor cells and their microenvironment. To further advance the live imaging of cancer, we have developed a multimodal longitudinal imaging strategy that allows multi-photon microscopy and magnetic resonance imaging in the same animal [1, 2]. In this chapter, we describe the surgical and imaging methods that enable studying the dynamic aspects of cancer at a micro- and macroscopical scale.

title: Employing High-Resolution Microscopy to Identify Dormant Disseminated Tumor Cells in the Brain.
abstract: Metastatic dormancy in the brain remains a major clinical problem and a biological challenge to study, as disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) can persist undetectable in a non-proliferative state for years before metastatic relapse. Here, we described an integrated methodological workflow to identify, isolate, and functionally characterize dormant brain metastatic clones taking advantage of high-resolution microscopy including light-sheet and intravital two-photon microscopy. Here, we present a method to generate dormant brain metastatic clones combined with high-resolution imaging for characterization of their dormant state. Briefly, tumor cells are delivered to the brain via intracarotid injection, and light-sheet microscopy is performed for whole-brain visualization of disseminated tumor cells. Individual clones are isolated and screened ex vivo by employing organotypic brain culture, where dormancy-associated phenotypes are assessed by multiphoton imaging. To validate their dormant behavior in vivo, clones exhibiting delayed outgrowth are then reintroduced via intracarotid injection, and brain tissue is analyzed ex vivo via multiphoton imaging. Finally, intracranial intravital imaging enables real-time visualization of dormant tumor cells and their interactions with the brain microenvironment. This pipeline provides a reproducible approach to isolate dormant clones and study brain metastatic dormancy, highlighting the versatility of multiphoton imaging for dynamic analysis of dormant DTCs in the brain.

title: Visualization of Disseminated Tumor Cells and Metastatic Outgrowth in the Lung at Single Cell Resolution via Intravital Imaging.
abstract: Most cancer-related deaths are due to metastases. These metastases originate from disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) that detach from the primary tumor and spread to distant organs, where they proliferate and lead to metastatic lesions. Across all cancer types, one of the most frequent sites of metastasis is the lung. Thus, targeting DTCs in the lung would represent a promising therapeutic strategy to prevent and block metastatic relapse. Despite many advances, the biology of DTCs is still largely unknown. This is because technologies able to detect single DTCs in preclinical animal models are lacking. High-resolution intravital imaging has become a powerful tool for understanding the biological process of cancer metastasis. Indeed, recent advances enable direct visualization of DTCs at single-cell resolution in an intact lung. We present here a method for intravital imaging DTCs in the lung through a surgically implanted optical imaging window, called Window for High-Resolution Imaging of the Lung (WHRIL). The WHRIL allows longitudinally tracking the fate of each individual DTC in living lungs for weeks, through all stages of metastatic seeding, including tumor cell arrival; extravasation; growth and progression to micrometastases. The WHRIL will allow us to elucidate the mechanisms of metastasis and other lung diseases, such as lung fibrosis.

title: Multiphoton Imaging of the Tibial Bone Marrow for In Vivo Spatial-Temporal Analysis of Myeloma Microenvironment and Treatment.
abstract: The bone marrow is a critical niche for multiple myeloma initiation, growth, and pathology. The biological and technical complexities of the bone marrow microenvironment make it challenging to study tumor physiology in situ. We have developed a thinned-bone surgical preparation for imaging the mouse tibial bone marrow. Using this approach, we have studied the spatial organization and temporal dynamics of myeloma cells, their interactions with the immune microenvironment, and the effects of acute drug treatments. In this chapter, we detail a protocol describing this procedure and present two use cases for intravital imaging to study dynamics tumors. In one study, we describe the use of photoactivation to capture live immune cells that are present within myeloma foci within the bone marrow for downstream analysis by flow cytometry or by other methods. In the second use case, we used imaging to capture effects of drug treatment in real-time in situ in the bone marrow to understand mechanisms of action and side effects.

title: Imaging and Analyzing the Macrophages that Regulate Pathological Hematopoietic Clones in the Mouse Calvarial Bone Marrow.
abstract: The bone marrow microenvironment has been shown to regulate the progression of myeloid neoplasms. Given that bone remodeling is a dynamic process that releases bone particles as danger molecules into the bone marrow space, different stages of bone turnover across marrow cavities can impose spatial heterogeneity of inflammatory responses that impact both healthy and mutant hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Specifically, macrophages, serving as critical members in the HSC niche, can adopt either pro-inflammatory (M1) or anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotypes based on these local signals, which results in distinct surface receptor expression and cytokine secretion. Using intravital microscopy, a murine model of Tet2 deficiency (a prevalent mutation across the spectrum of myeloid disorders), and labeling strategies to track marrow macrophages, our recent work identified compartmentalized inflammatory landscapes in the bone marrow that differentially support expansion of mutant cells. In this chapter, we describe detailed protocols to track pathological clones with respect to marrow macrophage in live mouse calvaria, and protocols of image-guided bone button isolation to analyze pro-inflammatory cytokines from the marrow cavities of interest. These protocols can also be integrated with cell isolation for single-cell transcriptomic profiling or downstream functional assessments. The labeling strategies may be applied to image macrophages in other tissue types.

title: Intravital Imaging of Early AML Expansion in the Mouse Calvarial Bone Marrow.
abstract: Normal hematopoiesis and leukemia growth are profoundly influenced by the bone marrow microenvironment. Given that bone formation precedes hematopoiesis, and the endosteal surface is constantly undergoing remodeling, different stages of bone turnover can impose heterogeneity on the bone marrow microenvironment that can impact both healthy and malignant hematopoiesis. To visualize bone remodeling in vivo, we have developed an intravital labeling technique and identified distinct bone marrow cavities based on the features of local bone deposition and resorption. By combining intravital tracking of a HoxA9-Meis1 acute myeloid leukemia (AML) mouse model with these labeling strategies, we observed that HoaxA9-Meis1 leukemic cells expanded almost exclusively in a subset of cavities that underwent active bone remodeling. In this chapter, we describe step-by-step protocols to track early proliferation of AML blasts with respect to local bone remodeling in live mouse calvaria. We summarize labeling strategies and image parameters to allow simultaneous visualization of leukemic cell expansion, vascular organization, and bone remodeling status, as well as give examples of image analysis and quantification workflows. The protocols can be readily applied to study hematopoietic disorders that manifest as clonal expansion in the bone marrow. The findings from intravital imaging can also be integrated with spatially resolved tissue isolation and next-generation sequencing techniques to better understand the regulatory machineries supporting AML progression.

title: Intravital Multiphoton Microscopy of Schwann Cells in Mouse Models of Pancreatic Disease.
abstract: Over the past decade, the important role of nerves in the growth and progression of pancreatic cancer has been increasingly recognized. The most abundant cell type present in the nerves, Schwann cells (SCs), can be reprogrammed by cancer cells and fibrotic extracellular matrix (ECM), facilitating perineural invasion of cancer cells in the pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Activated SCs form tracks, which are then populated and used by cancer cells for invasion. Intravital microscopy of the pancreas under the pathological conditions holds the potential to visualize and decipher real-time interactions of SCs with the cancer cells, ECM, and host cells in the tumor microenvironment and to delineate SC activation dynamics and the responses to targeted therapies. Here, we describe a protocol for high-resolution intravital microscopy of Schwann cells, ECM, and cancer cells using mouse models of PDAC or pancreatitis.

title: Intravital Imaging of the In Situ-to-Invasive Transition of Breast Cancer.
abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the precursor of infiltrating ductal carcinoma (IDC); however, mechanisms underlying the invasive program of breast tumor epithelial cells remain largely unknown. Different assays and cell models have been developed to evaluate the invasive capacities of breast tumor cells (spheroids, organoids, tumor explants…). These models recapitulate basic interactions between the neoplastic cells and their microenvironment in a simplified setup. Whenever possible, hypotheses and mechanisms should be validated based on the observation of tumor cells in their native environment in the mammary gland using animal models. Here, we describe specific tools to study early breast tumor progression, taking into consideration reducing the number of xenografted animals and having the capacity to follow tumor progression over time. Combinations of these approaches have revealed new and exciting insights as to explain how DCIS progresses into a more aggressive invasive lesion. This chapter details technical procedures to generating in situ tumors after intraductal inoculation, visualizing the tumor xenograft directly in the mammary gland of the injected mouse using a mammary window for intravital multi-photon imaging of tumor cells in their environment. Finally, we illustrate how this procedure can be useful to analyze morphological changes in the matrix microenvironment during early breast cancer progression.

title: FLIM-FRET Intravital Imaging of Tumors.
abstract: Cancer progression is driven by the dynamic interactions between cancer cells and their surrounding environment. Intravital imaging is a powerful technology to assess dynamic cellular processes in real-time within live tissues in the context of their native physiological environment. In particular, Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) of Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) biosensors enables robust quantification of changes in signaling pathways that drive cancer progression and can also offer insights into how best to target these dynamic processes. Here, we provide a protocol for intravital FLIM-FRET imaging in tumors, including the delivery of FRET biosensors into cells, cancer cell inoculation into mice, surgical exposure of the tumor tissue and intravital FLIM-FRET imaging coupled with image stabilization and image analysis.

title: Intravital FLIM Pharmacodynamic Imaging Using FRET Biosensors.
abstract: When studying the effectiveness of targeted anti-tumor therapy, measuring in vivo protein activity within the cancer cells in real-time is vital. This however presents challenges as post-translational modifications or binding of cofactors, and their dynamics, cannot be captured at the single cell level with traditional methods. The work of the last two decades led to the development of a broad range of genetically encoded FLIM-FRET biosensors that can be used to study protein activity, pharmacodynamics and -kinetics in real-time at the single cell level in the in vitro or in vivo setting. In this chapter, we will introduce FLIM-FRET biosensors for RAC1 and AKT activity, two key modulators of carcinogenesis. We will discuss their application in studying the effectiveness of anti-tumor therapy in vivo using intravital microscopy. Furthermore, we describe how to visualize RAC1 and AKT activity in vivo using these FLIM-FRET biosensors in combination with intravital imaging through imaging windows. Finally, we included a detailed description of the subsequent quantitative analysis of the readout of these biosensors in the in vivo context to dynamically evaluate the effectiveness of targeted anti-cancer therapies.

title: RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction in Therapeutics and Drug Discovery.
abstract: RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as a transformative modality in modern medicine, enabling precise modulation of gene expression and offering new treatment strategies for previously intractable diseases. Central to the success and safety of many RNA therapeutics is a detailed understanding of RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs), including both intended target binding and unintended off-target effects. Computational prediction of RRIs plays a critical role in the design, optimization, and validation of therapeutic RNAs such as antisense oligonucleotides, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, and CRISPR-associated RNAs. This chapter examines the role of RRI prediction in therapeutic and drug discovery pipelines, highlighting computational strategies, deep learning models, and validation frameworks. Examples of applications in oncology, infectious diseases, and genetic disorders illustrate how accurate RRI modeling supports efficacy, safety assessment and contribute to evidence generation for therapeutic development. Challenges and future directions for clinically deployable RRI prediction systems are also discussed.

title: Multi-Omics Integration for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are central regulators of gene expression, governing processes such as microRNA-mediated silencing, lncRNA scaffolding, and viral RNA modulation. Traditional computational approaches, relying mainly on sequence or secondary structure, often fail to capture condition- and tissue-specific interactions. Multi-omics integration has emerged as a powerful strategy to overcome these limitations. By combining transcriptomics, RNA-protein interactions, and epitranscriptomic modifications, predictive models gain both accuracy and mechanistic insight. Transcriptomic data provide expression profiles across tissues and conditions, RNA-protein interaction maps (e.g., CLIP-seq from ENCODE) reveal protein-mediated modulation, and epitranscriptomic marks (m6A, m5C, pseudouridylation) influence RNA stability, localization, and interaction propensity. This chapter reviews key datasets, including TCGA for cancer transcriptomes, ENCODE for RNA-binding proteins, and epitranscriptome maps, and discusses strategies for multi-omics integration. Early fusion approaches combine features before modeling, while late fusion integrates predictions from modality-specific models. Applications in cancer and viral infection demonstrate the value of integrated RRI prediction. Finally, we address ongoing challenges such as data sparsity, context-dependency, and computational scalability, and highlight future directions for large-scale multi-omics RRI studies.

title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)-Based Review of RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction Methods.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) play a vital role in cellular processes including gene regulation, RNA editing, and translational control. Aberrant RRIs are increasingly recognized as contributors to cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis. Accurate computational prediction of RRIs therefore offers significant opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, understanding tumor biology, and therapeutic target identification. Among machine learning approaches, support vector machines (SVMs) have been applied in RRI prediction due to their robustness in handling high-dimensional, nonlinear data and relatively small training datasets. This chapter reviews SVM-based methods for RRI prediction, highlights representative tools and strategies, and discusses current challenges and relevance to cancer application. Emerging trends that integrate SVMs with deep learning and experimental data augmentation are also outlined, pointing toward pathways for clinical translation.

title: Wash-Free Live-Cell Imaging Using Homogeneous Immunosensors.
abstract: Imaging membrane proteins on the cell surface is crucial for studying cellular functions involving their mobility, localization, and clustering. Conventional antibody-based fluorescence imaging requires multiple washing steps to reduce background signals from unbound fluorescent antibodies. These steps stress living cells and potentially alter their characteristics and behavior. To address this, we propose a protocol for wash-free fluorescence imaging using an immunosensor, the Quenchbody (Q-body), which emits fluorescence upon antigen binding, eliminating the need for washing steps. In this chapter, we introduce the preparation of a Q-body against a cancer biomarker, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), and its application in live-cell imaging by simply adding to the culture medium without washing. This tool offers a minimally invasive and efficient approach to real-time membrane protein analysis. Importantly, because the antibody component is exchangeable with other target-specific antibodies, Q-bodies are adaptable for detecting a wide range of membrane proteins in live-cell imaging.

title: Generating and Evaluating New Chemigenetic Fluorescent Biosensors for Protein Kinase A Based on Synthetic Organic Fluorophores.
abstract: Intracellular signaling is often defined by rapid, localized biochemical events. Chemigenetic fluorescent biosensors are hybrid high-sensitivity imaging tools that allow the study of intracellular signaling in real time. They combine genetically encoded self-labeling protein tags with synthetic organic fluorophores and a protein-based sensing domain, allowing for functional fluorescence microscopy experiments with high spatial and temporal resolution. This chapter provides a practical workflow for the implementation of intensity-based chemigenetic biosensors, centered around the HaloAKAR2.1 scaffold, a biosensor for protein kinase A activity. We provide a step-by-step guide to performing functional microscopy experiments and their analysis with the viewpoint for it to be generalized to the biological system and infrastructure available. We additionally provide exemplary data on modifying the existing HaloAKAR2.1 biosensor by varying the composition of one of its linkers. By detailing both the practical application of established tools and the principles for engineering next-generation variants, this chapter serves as a comprehensive resource for deploying high-sensitivity chemigenetic biosensors in live-cell imaging.

title: Effects of Participation in a Community-Based Food Cooperative on Food Security and Dietary Behaviours: A Pre-Post Study.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Community-based food cooperatives have shown potential in addressing food insecurity, but longitudinal evidence assessing their impact is limited. This study evaluated the effects of participating in a community-based food cooperative on food insecurity, dietary behaviours, and physical health outcomes among Australian adults. METHODS: A pre-post survey of new cooperative members measured demographics, household food insecurity status (United States Department of Agriculture 6-item Household Food Security Survey Module (HFSSM)), dietary behaviours (servings/day of core food groups), and objective physical health indicators (weight, waist circumference, and blood pressure). Participants were classified as secure (HFSSM score = 0) or insecure (HFSSM score ≥ 1). A McNemar's test assessed the change in proportion of participants classified as food insecure from baseline to follow-up, and paired t-tests or non-parametric equivalents compared other outcomes. RESULTS: At baseline, 58 participants completed surveys, and 25 completed physical data collection. Participants were primarily female (93.1%), 18-33 or 35-44 years old (37.9% each), and of European background (81.0%). The proportion of participants reporting food security improved from baseline (54.2%) to follow-up (66.7%) (p = 0.041). Importantly, participants who were food secure remained so at follow-up. Those who were food insecure also reported more favourable improvements in dietary behaviours and meal preparation habits, though many of these did not reach statistical significance. CONCLUSION: Participation in a community-based food cooperative was associated with improved food security among Australian adults. SO WHAT?: These findings highlight the potential of community-based food cooperatives to reduce food insecurity and support their integration into broader health promotion and food security strategies.

title: Model-Based Normal Tissue Complication Probability Comparison Between Proton and Photon Therapies for Brain Tumors Complying With Planning Study Guidelines.
abstract: PURPOSE: The benefit of proton beam therapy (PBT) for primary brain tumors compared with x-ray therapy has not been demonstrated by randomized controlled trials. We performed a model-based approach study to evaluate the potential benefit of PBT for brain tumors using the normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models complying with the Radiotherapy Treatment plannINg study Guidelines (RATING). METHODS AND MATERIALS: Sixty-six patients with primary brain tumors treated with PBT were registered. We used 11 NTCP models, calculated NTCP for each adverse event, and estimated the PBT and intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) plans for the entire patient population and for groups classified by pathology. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed for statistically significant differences between the 2 modalities, and a 2-tailed test was considered significant when <.05. A reduction was considered clinically meaningful when the difference in NTCP between the 2 modalities (ΔNTCP) exceeded the prespecified threshold. RESULTS: Overall, PBT reduced NTCP from the cataracts, delayed recall, memory impairment, contralateral hearing impairment, and tinnitus. Patients with meningiomas and low-grade gliomas had similar tendencies. PBT was associated with a lower excess absolute risk of secondary cancer of the central nervous system in all patients. However, NTCPs for alopecia, blindness, and brain necrosis were higher in the PBT cohort, highlighting important clinical trade-offs. Thirty-one patients (47.0%) had at least 1 ΔNTCP above the specified threshold. CONCLUSIONS: In this model-based planning comparison, PBT was associated with lower estimated NTCPs for selected endpoints compared with virtual IMRT, whereas IMRT showed advantages for alopecia, blindness, and brain necrosis. PBT may offer meaningful clinical benefits, particularly in reducing the excess absolute risk of secondary cancer for patients with long-term survival. In addition, the comparison based on Radiotherapy Treatment plannINg study Guidelines made the study more objective than similar previous studies.

title: Rapid Response Palliative Radiation Therapy Program: Feasibility and Experience of Implementing a Nonclassical Model.
abstract: PURPOSE: Classical rapid access palliative radiation therapy (RAPRT) programs are typically organized as dedicated clinics designed to enable same-day consultation, simulation, treatment planning, and delivery of palliative radiation therapy. At our institution, urgent and expedited palliative radiation therapy is delivered through an integrated, nonclassical RAPRT model embedded in routine departmental practice. This study describes the implementation and performance of this model. METHODS AND MATERIALS: We retrospectively reviewed patients treated by our RAPRT workflow between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2024. Demographic, clinical, treatment-related, and workflow data were collected from the institutional oncology information system and clinical records. Workflow intervals were calculated using electronic timestamps. RESULTS: A total of 775 patients received 848 treatment courses; 37% were hospitalized at the time of treatment. Fifty-six patients (7.2%) received >1 treatment course, and 15 required reirradiation. The median time from referral to radiation oncology consultation was 1 day (Q1, 1; Q3, 3). Median age was 63 years (Q1, 54; Q3, 73), and the most common primary tumors were lung (25%) and gastrointestinal cancers (17%). Poor performance status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 3-4) was observed in 40% of cases. The most common treatment sites were bone (47%) and thorax (19%). A single fraction was prescribed in 797 extracranial courses, representing 94% of all courses. Median total treatment process time was 109 minutes (Q1, 102; Q3, 165), and median time spent in the radiation therapy center was 207 minutes (Q1, 111; Q3, 250). Time to simulation and dosimetry time were the most time-consuming workflow steps, accounting for 24% and 31% of the total workflow duration, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: An integrated, nonclassical RAPRT model using existing departmental resources is feasible and can achieve rapid palliative radiation therapy timelines comparable to those reported by dedicated RAPRT programs. Robust information systems and coordinated electronic workflows are central to the efficient implementation of this model.

title: Sequencing of Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy and Chemotherapy in Stage I Small Cell Lung Cancer: Practice Patterns and Outcomes.
abstract: PURPOSE: We evaluated practice patterns and survival outcomes associated with the sequencing of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and chemotherapy in patients with clinical stage I small cell lung cancer (SCLC) in the United States. METHODS AND MATERIALS: Using a large national database, we identified patients with clinical stage I (cT1-2N0M0) SCLC treated with SBRT and chemotherapy between 2004 and 2020. To assess practice patterns in relation to survival outcomes, patients were categorized into 2 cohorts: "SBRT before chemotherapy" and "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy." χ RESULTS: Among 631 patients with clinical stage I SCLC who were treated with SBRT and chemotherapy, 416 (65.9%) were categorized in "SBRT before chemotherapy" and 215 (34.1%) in "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy." Patients diagnosed after 2018 were less likely to receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy (odds ratio, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.32-0.66; CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that there is no statistically significant difference in survival outcomes for patients who receive SBRT before chemotherapy compared with those who receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy. Therefore, flexibility in treatment sequencing may be appropriate in this population.

title: Early and late CTCAE and patient-reported outcomes following breast radiotherapy in the REQUITE cohort.
abstract: PURPOSE: The international REQUITE study and its follow-up studies (RADprecise/REQUITEplus) prospectively collected longitudinal data from patients undergoing radiotherapy for breast, prostate, or lung cancer. We present data from 2057 women with breast cancer, describing patient-reported outcomes and acute and late adverse effects. METHODS: Patients were recruited between April 2014 and October 2016. Eligible patients received external-beam photon radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery, had no metastasis at inclusion, no other malignancy within the previous five years, and no prior breast irradiation. Blood samples were collected before radiotherapy for genotyping, molecular analysis, and biobanking. Standardised assessments included CTCAE v4, EORTC QLQ-C30 and BR23, MFI, GPAQ, and DICOM/DVH data. Follow-up continued annually for two years, extending to eight years at eligible sites. RESULTS: Acute side effects peaked at end of radiotherapy, with erythema in 83-89% of patients. Grade ≥ 2 acute effects, including pain (11% versus 4.3%) and skin ulceration (4.8% versus 0.8%), were more frequent with normofractionation than hypofractionation. Grade ≥ 2 late effects affected between 0.6% and 16.8% of patients; skin induration was the most frequent late effect. Patient-reported outcome scores varied over time, with functional scale scores at two years similar to or higher than at baseline. CONCLUSION: REQUITE provides real-world evidence of acute and late outcomes following normo- and hypofractionation, broadly consistent with published randomised trials. The dataset, combining clinical adverse effects, quality of life, dosimetric, and genetic data, is a resource for personalised radiotherapy research (www.requite.eu).

title: Optimized Low-Input ATAC-Seq Protocol for Freshly Sorted Muscle Stem Cells.
abstract: Skeletal muscle stem cells (MuSCs) are essential for tissue regeneration and repair, yet their scarcity has historically limited routine application of chromatin-level assays. Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) provides a powerful means to define the chromatin state and study cellular regulatory landscapes, but standard protocols require cell numbers far exceeding those that can be freshly sorted from muscle, particularly under conditions such as aging, disease, and various genetic models. Here, we present an optimized, low-input ATAC-seq workflow specifically tailored for analysis of MuSCs freshly isolated from skeletal muscle. This method integrates high-purity isolation of MuSCs by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), refined nuclei purification, and a high-efficiency transposition assay that can be applied to the analysis of chromatin using as few as 5000 cells. We describe critical steps for minimizing technical noise, including optimized mitochondrial depletion, micro-volume tagmentation, low-cycle ATAC-seq library amplification, and quantitative quality-control metrics. The workflow is compatible with FACS-purified MuSCs from young and aged mice, injury models, and genetic knockout models, enabling direct comparison of chromatin accessibility across biological conditions where cell numbers are limiting.

BACKGROUND: HPV-associated cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related death in women worldwide. The role of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and miR-129 in tumor progression remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: To investigate miR-129 expression and its clinical significance in HPV-associated cervical cancer and to explore whether BMSCs regulate malignant phenotypes through miR-129. METHODS: miR-129 expression was measured by qRT-PCR in 77 cervical cancer and 30 normal cervical tissues. Associations with clinicopathological features and overall survival (OS) were analyzed. Diagnostic value was assessed by ROC curve. Rat BMSCs were co-cultured with SiHa and HeLa cells. Following miR-129 overexpression or knockdown, cell proliferation (CCK-8, colony formation), invasion (Transwell) and expression of E-cadherin, N-cadherin and MRP1 (Western blot) were examined. RESULTS: miR-129 expression was significantly higher in cervical cancer tissues than in normal controls (3.24±0.56 vs. 1.00±0.32, P<0.05). High miR-129 expression correlated with tumor size ≥3 cm (P=0.009), FIGO stage III-IV (P=0.0034) and lymph node metastasis (P=0.038). High expression was associated with shorter OS (median: 28.4 vs. 46.2 months; HR=2.944, 95%CI:1.484-5.842, P=0.002). The AUC was 0.788 (95%CI:0.693-0.884), with a cut-off of 1.85 (sensitivity:76.9%, specificity:70.4%). BMSC co-culture upregulated miR-129 expression (SiHa: 3.52±0.42 vs. 1.00±0.08, P<0.01). miR-129 overexpression promoted proliferation, colony formation and invasion, while knockdown suppressed these phenotypes. Overexpression of miR-129 reduced E-cadherin (0.42±0.05 vs. 1.00±0.08, P<0.01) and increased N-cadherin (2.85±0.22 vs. 1.00±0.10, P<0.01) and MRP1 (2.46±0.18 vs. 1.00±0.09, P<0.01). Knockdown of miR-129 partially reversed BMSC-induced changes in these proteins. CONCLUSION: miR-129 is significantly upregulated in HPV-associated cervical cancer and shows potential as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker. BMSCs upregulate miR-129 in cervical cancer cells and miR-129 modulates proliferation, invasion, EMT marker expression and MRP1 expression. These findings suggest that the BMSCs/miR-129 axis may contribute to cervical cancer progression, but further in-vivo and mechanistic studies are needed.

title: Outcomes for Patients With Vestibular Schwannomas Treated With Gamma Knife Versus Linear Accelerator-Based Radiosurgery: A Retrospective Review.
abstract: PURPOSE: Prior studies have reported favorable local control for patients with vestibular schwannomas (VS) treated with Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) or linear accelerator (LINAC)-based radiosurgery; however, direct comparisons of quality-of-life outcomes with each approach are lacking. We assessed differences in quality-of-life outcomes and local control after radiation therapy for patients with VS treated with GKRS versus LINAC. METHODS AND MATERIALS: In this multicenter analysis, we retrospectively reviewed VS cases treated with either GKRS or LINAC and compared posttreatment clinical outcomes, including tumor control and new development of vertigo, gait disturbance, facial palsy, and tinnitus. Descriptive statistics were performed, and χ2 was used to assess intergroup differences. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to assess associations with the development of clinical outcomes. RESULTS: Thirty-six patients treated with GKRS and 49 patients treated with LINAC were included in our analysis. All patients were treated with single-fraction radiosurgery. There was no statistically significant difference between LINAC and GKRS in the development of vertigo, gait disturbance, or facial palsy after treatment, and no clinically significant difference in the development of tinnitus. Local control was 98.8% across all patients, with no statistically significant difference in tumor control between groups. CONCLUSIONS: This analysis showed comparable rates of new vertigo, gait disturbance, tinnitus, and facial palsy with GKRS and LINAC-based radiosurgery for VS, supporting the interchangeability of these treatment approaches. Prospective data are needed to further compare these treatment approaches.

title: Timing of cranial radiotherapy in HER2-positive breast Cancer brain metastases treated with Pyrotinib: a multicentre real-world cohort study.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Cranial radiotherapy (RT) and pyrotinib both demonstrate efficacy in HER2-positive breast cancer brain metastases (BCBM); however, the optimal sequencing of these modalities remains to be established. We evaluated survival across treatment sequences within a real-world cohort. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, two-centre study included 101 patients with HER2-positive BCBM treated with cranial RT plus pyrotinib (June 2018-July 2025). Based on treatment sequence, patients were categorized into: concurrent RT and pyrotinib (Group A, RESULTS: At a median follow-up of 43.3 months, 63 patients (62.4%) had died and 70 (69.3%) experienced CNS-PFS events. Median CNS-PFS was 14.8 months (95% CI 10.68-19.92) overall, and 14.3, 15.0, and 21.4 months in groups A, B, and C, respectively ( CONCLUSIONS: Treatment sequence did not significantly affect OS or CNS-PFS. Focal cranial RT was independently associated with longer survival, and toxicity was manageable. The proposed timing threshold is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective validation.

title: Metformin Use Is Associated With Reduced Rates of Primary Nerve Decompression Surgery and Revision in Type 2 Diabetes: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: PURPOSE: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for compressive neuropathy. The purpose of this study was to determine whether metformin use is associated with reduced rates of compressive neuropathy, primary nerve decompression surgery, and revision after carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release, while controlling for concurrent diabetes medications. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX federated research network. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus were stratified by metformin exposure, defined as at least 10 prescriptions over 5 years. The primary outcomes were incident compressive neuropathy and nerve decompression surgery. In a unilateral revision cohort, the outcome was ipsilateral revision between 30 days and 5 years after the index procedure. One-to-one propensity score matching balanced cohorts on demographics, comorbidities, and concurrent diabetes medications. Four prespecified medication-stratified sensitivity analyses addressed insulin, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. Carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release revision results were pooled via fixed-effect meta-analysis. RESULTS: After matching, the primary analysis included 260,823 pairs. Metformin users had lower rates of nerve decompression surgery (0.60% vs 0.72%; odds ratio, OR, 0.831 [0.776-0.889]) and compressive neuropathy diagnosis (2.78% vs 3.05%; OR, 0.909 [0.879-0.941]). The surgery-level association was stronger without concurrent insulin (OR, 0.727 [0.662-0.799]) and attenuated to nonsignificance with concurrent insulin (OR, 0.948 [0.836-1.076]), though the diagnosis-level association persisted. Among patients with unilateral carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome, ipsilateral revision was less frequent in metformin users (pooled OR, 0.711 [0.533-0.950]). Metformin users also had lower vitamin B12 levels (mean, 646.4 vs 707.4 pg/mL), consistent with sustained metformin exposure. CONCLUSIONS: Metformin use was associated with reduced incidence of nerve decompression surgery and ipsilateral revision after carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, with directionally consistent effects across sensitivity analyses. These findings suggest that maintaining metformin therapy may carry benefit beyond glycemic control. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings. TYPE OF STUDY/LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic II.

title: Radiotherapy dose escalation for the non-operative management of patients with unresectable locally recurrent rectal cancer (STEP-UP): Study protocol for a multicentre, prospective, open-label feasibility study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Curative-intent management of locally recurrent rectal cancer (LRRC) generally comprises neoadjuvant therapy and surgery. In patients with unresectable LRRC, where surgical intervention is not feasible, management is limited to non-operative bimodality therapy with systemic therapy and radiotherapy. Evidence guiding the optimisation of non-operative management remains limited. In this context, the therapeutic goal is to achieve prolonged local control while minimising treatment-related adverse events and preserving quality of life. Radiotherapy dose escalation has been proposed as a potential strategy to achieve this balance. However, its feasibility and safety in the non-operative management of unresectable LRRC have not yet been established. As such, this study aims to evaluate the feasibility and safety of this radiotherapeutic approach, and to determine its impact on both symptom control and oncological outcomes. METHODS: This prospective, multicentre, single-arm feasibility study will enrol 30 patients with unresectable or inoperable LRRC without distant metastases, or with (oligo)metastatic disease not requiring immediate systemic therapy. Previously irradiated patients will undergo reirradiation with stereotactic body radiotherapy (re-SBRT; 5 × 9 Gy) when feasible, or, alternatively hyperfractionated chemo-reirradiation (50.4 Gy in 1.2 Gy twice-daily fractions with concurrent capecitabine). Radiotherapy-naïve patients will receive chemoradiotherapy with a simultaneous integrated boost (25 × 2.6 Gy, EQD2Gy DISCUSSION: This protocol describes the STEP-UP study, which will determine the feasibility of radiotherapy dose escalation in unresectable LRRC. If feasible and safe, this approach could provide an effective treatment intensification strategy to improve local control and symptom burden in patients with unresectable LRRC, addressing a major unmet clinical need. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07721181Overview of Medical-Scientific Research in the Netherlands (OMON) Registry: NL-011150.International Clinical Trial Registry Platform (ICTRP): NL-OMON61161.

title: A Simple Clinical Index for Pretriage of Elevated Liver Stiffness in National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2017-2023.
abstract: BACKGROUND/AIMS: Simple pre-elastography tools may help prioritize adults for liver stiffness assessment. We evaluated the Simple Clinical Objective Predictor for fibrosis Evaluation (SCOPE) in two National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cycles. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective secondary analysis of NHANES 2017 to March 2020 as the development cohort and NHANES 2021-2023 as the temporal validation cohort. SCOPE combines age, diabetes status, gamma-glutamyl transferase, and weight-to-height ratio. Adults aged ≥20 yr with valid liver stiffness measurements and complete predictor data were included after excluding major competing chronic liver disease etiologies. Elevated liver stiffness was defined as liver stiffness measurement (LSM) ≥9.7 kPa. Discrimination was assessed using survey-weighted area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Two evaluation-cohort cutpoints approximating 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity were applied unchanged in temporal validation. Decision utility was assessed using survey-weighted decision-curve analysis, with secondary probability calibration. RESULTS: The analytic sample included 5488 adults in development and 3994 in temporal validation; weighted prevalence was 5.31% and 6.11%, respectively. SCOPE showed higher discrimination than Fibrosis-4, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease Fibrosis Score, and steatosis-associated fibrosis estimator in both cohorts. SCOPE area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.866 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.837-0.899) in development and 0.823 (95% CI, 0.790-0.859) in temporal validation. Sensitivity at the lower boundary decreased from 89.8% to 80.6%, whereas upper-boundary specificity remained near 90%; temporal validation positive predictive value was 27.5%. Fixed SCOPE referral strategies provided greater net benefit than comparator strategies across prespecified threshold probability ranges. The temporal validation Brier score was 0.0492, with calibration intercept 0.242 and slope 0.893. CONCLUSION: SCOPE showed higher discrimination than comparator scores for identifying adults with LSM ≥9.7 kPa who may warrant confirmatory assessment. Its modest positive predictive value precludes diagnostic use. Neither threshold is diagnostic, and the lower boundary should not be used to withhold guideline-indicated testing without external validation.

title: Retroviral Transduction of Human T Cells with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor Targeting PD-1 Ligands for Melanoma Immunotherapy.
abstract: T cells are able to target melanoma-associated antigens in an MHC-independent manner through the expression of chimeric antigen receptors. Using retroviral transduction, these receptor constructs can be efficiently delivered into human CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells. In this protocol, we describe the production of retroviral supernatants along with the activation, transduction, expansion, and selection of human T cells engineered to express a chimeric PD-1 receptor. This method can be readily adapted for any human chimeric antigen receptor construct.

title: Generation of Murine Chimeric Antigen Receptor T Cells for Adoptive T Cell Therapy for Melanoma.
abstract: Expression of chimeric antigen receptors enables T cells to be redirected toward melanoma-associated antigens in an MHC-independent manner. Retroviral transduction can be used to introduce these receptor constructs into murine CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells. Here, we outline the generation of retroviral supernatants and the activation, transduction, expansion, and selection of murine T cells expressing the chimeric-PD1 receptor. This protocol can be adapted for any murine chimeric antigen receptor construct.

title: Assessing the Antitumor Immune Effects of Gut Microbiota in a Preclinical Melanoma Model.
abstract: Antitumor immune responses are regulated by a multitude of factors, including the gut microbiota. Specific bacterial taxa and metabolites have been correlated with improved responses to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in melanoma patients. Gut microbiota and microbiota-derived metabolites can modulate antitumor immune responses by increasing antigen presentation capabilities and enhancing cytotoxic T-cell effector functions. To assess the effects of gut microbiota on antitumor immune responses, we optimized the following protocols focused on immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in a preclinical melanoma model. Analysis of tumor-infiltrating and circulating lymphocytes, bacterial translocation and growth, and immune cell activation provides a foundation for microbiota/cancer immunology research.

title: Lipoplex Nanoparticle-Based RNA Delivery to 3D Melanoma Spheroids.
abstract: Lipoplex nanoparticle-based vaccination technologies have shown tremendous efficiency for in vivo transfection during the COVID-19 pandemic and also hold promise for treating melanoma. While pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics need careful in vivo and clinical testing, other parameters of drug performance can be assessed with in vitro systems as well. Spheroids composed of more than one cell type can serve to assess drug penetration, cell-type specificity, and transfection efficiency at an early stage of drug development.

title: In Vivo Reversible Electroporation for Melanoma Therapy.
abstract: Reversible Electroporation (rEP) has been a venerable in vitro lab technique for the transfection of cells. Recent in vivo applications of rEP for manipulating tumors and forcing tumor cell expression of proteins of interest are being explored in clinical trials. The ability to perform in vivo rEP in the lab can create translational opportunities and study mechanisms for optimal outcomes in patients. A general protocol is described and may serve as a template for melanoma researchers.

title: Characterization of an Anti-Tryptophan 2,3-Dioxygenase Monoclonal Antibody and Use in a Melanoma Model.
abstract: Monoclonal antibodies have served as research tools to characterize specific proteins and biomolecules to understand their role in biological processes and disease. However, because of nonspecific reactivity with other components in samples, specific reactivity can be difficult to interpret. Using web-based tools, standard hybridoma technology, and standard immunostaining methods, we describe the development of a tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase 2 (TDO2)-targeted antibody with high specificity. In addition to providing a unique reagent needed as a research tool to investigate the role of TDO2 in preclinical models and human tissue samples, herein we provide methods to characterize TDO2 expression in human tissue samples and murine disease models. We note also that the general protocol described in this chapter will be useful to investigators interested in developing monoclonal antibodies against other targets of interest as well.

title: High-Throughput Identification of miRNA-Target Interactions in Melanoma Using miR-CATCHv2.0.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have the potential to regulate the expression of nearly every transcript in the cell, making the identification of miRNA-mRNA target interactions crucial for understanding their role in diverse biological processes. However, the identification of the miRNAs that regulate a given mRNA remains a challenge. Here, we describe miR-CATCHv2.0, an innovative method for the high-throughput identification of the miRNAs physically interacting with an mRNA of interest. We further highlight how miR-CATCHv2.0 overcomes key limitations of both current computational predictions and existing experimental strategies, enabling a more accurate and comprehensive characterization of physiologically relevant miRNA-mRNA interactions.

title: Assessment of Cell-Free MicroRNA by NGS Whole Transcriptome Analysis in Cutaneous Melanoma Patients' Blood.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRs) are small RNA molecules (18-22 nucleotides) that regulate the transcriptome at a post-transcriptional level by affecting the expression of specific genes. This regulatory mechanism is critical to maintain cell homeostasis and specific functions. Aberrant expression of miRs has been associated with pathobiological processes, including cancer. There are few technologies available that are able to profile whole-genome miR expression using minimal amounts of blood samples and without the need for time-consuming extraction steps. Here, we describe the HTG EdgeSeq miR Whole Transcriptome Assay (WTA) in serum and plasma samples. To identify specific cell-free miR (cfmiR) patterns, we have first focused on the analysis of normal donor samples and have then compared these to patients with cutaneous melanoma. The identification of specific cfmiR for melanoma patients will allow for better patient surveillance during targeted and/or checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy (CII) treatment.

title: Unbiased Microbiome and Metabolomic Profiling of Fecal Samples from Patients with Melanoma.
abstract: Gut microbiota influence and modulate host immune responses. In preclinical cancer models, mice lacking gut microbiota have a markedly diminished response to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Further, in melanoma patients, specific commensal gut microbiota have been associated with a positive clinical response to immunotherapy. In order to study the gut microbiome and metabolome, we have developed methods for fecal sample collection and processing, microbiome and metabolome profiling, and bioinformatic analysis. This protocol will be a useful tool for interrogating the taxonomic composition and functional output of a melanoma patient's gut microbiome.

title: Discovery of Salivary Metabolomic Biomarkers for Canine Oral Melanoma and Squamous Cell Carcinoma via CIL LC-MS Analysis.
abstract: In this case-control cross-sectional study, we examined the diagnostic potential of salivary metabolomics to differentiate canine oral melanoma (OM) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) from benign oral tumors (BN). Using high-performance chemical isotope labeling liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (CIL LC-MS) targeting at the amine/phenol submetabolome, we analyzed saliva from 65 dogs across malignant, benign, and healthy groups. Our results revealed distinct metabolic clustering among the groups, identifying 154 significantly altered metabolites in OM and 66 in OSCC compared to BN (P

title: Serum Peptidomic Profiling for Biomarker Discovery in Canine Oral Melanoma and Squamous Cell Carcinoma via MALDI-TOF and LC-MS/MS.
abstract: Canine oral malignancies, particularly oral melanoma (OM) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), present significant diagnostic hurdles due to their aggressive metastasis and the difficulty of early-stage detection. This study establishes a robust methodological workflow for identifying systemic biomarkers by analyzing the serum peptidome, a minimally invasive alternative to traditional tissue biopsies. Using a high-throughput approach that combines matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) for rapid screening with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for precise peptide identification, we successfully differentiated early and late-stage malignancies from benign and healthy controls. Principal component analysis confirmed distinct peptidomic clusters, leading to the identification of four key proteins: FKBP4, ESRRA, IGSF10, and ABCB5. Notably, FKBP4, ESRRA, and ABCB5 were overexpressed in both late-stage OM and late-stage OSCC, while IGSF10 showed specificity for late-stage OSCC. These markers are integral to metastatic pathways and correlate with chemotherapeutic sensitivity, providing a foundation for precision diagnostic and prognostic protocols in veterinary oncology.

title: Integrated Functional and Metabolomic Profiling of Melanoma Cells Treated with Redox-Active Compounds.
abstract: Metabolic plasticity is a hallmark of melanoma progression and therapy resistance. This chapter describes a reproducible protocol for comprehensive metabolic profiling of melanoma cells exposed to redox-active compounds such as emodin and aloe-emodin. The method integrates cell proliferation assays, mitochondrial functional analysis using Seahorse extracellular flux measurements, reactive oxygen species (ROS) quantification, LC-MS-based metabolomics, stable-isotope tracing, and

title: Methods for Analyzing Immune Infiltrates and Spatial Organization Within the Melanoma Microenvironment Using Multiplex Immunofluorescence.
abstract: Immunotherapies improve survival in patients with melanoma by enhancing the immune system's ability to recognize and eliminate tumor cells. Understanding the immunological effects of these therapies requires evaluation of both changes in lymphocyte composition and activation within the tumor microenvironment (TME) as well as the spatial organization of these cells. Increased lymphocyte infiltration and distinct patterns of immune cell distribution within the TME have been associated with improved survival and enhanced response to immunotherapy in melanoma. However, relatively few methodologies currently enable detailed characterization of both the structural organization and immunological features of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. In this chapter, we describe multiplex immunofluorescence staining approaches for the identification, characterization, and quantification of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in melanoma.

title: A Method for Quantifying Immune Infiltrates and Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Murine Melanoma Tumors by Multiplex Immunofluorescence.
abstract: The presence of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) and elevated levels of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes have been linked to improved survival outcomes in several solid cancers, including melanoma. Despite this association, the precise function and immunological impact of TLS remain incompletely understood, as do factors that drive their formation and which might potentially be leveraged to enhance patient outcomes. Functional studies using murine models may help clarify the biological roles of TLS; however, relatively few methodologies currently exist that allow for detailed assessment of the structural organization and functional characteristics of TLS within solid tumors. To advance understanding of the biology underlying TLS, this chapter describes multiplex immunohistochemistry panels designed for the identification, characterization, and quantification of TLS and intratumoral immune infiltrates in melanoma. Although these methods are presented in the context of melanoma, they are broadly applicable and can be used to investigate TLS across a wide range of human cancers.

title: Preparation of Melanoma Tissue for Multiplex Immunofluorescence Histology Analysis of Immune Infiltration and Spatial Organization.
abstract: Immunotherapies extend survival in melanoma patients by increasing the immune system's capacity to detect tumors and mediate tumor cell death. Understanding mechanisms of antitumor immunity requires evaluating changes in immune infiltrate composition, activation, and spatial distribution within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Despite this need, relatively few methods allow for detailed analysis of both the structural organization and immunological characteristics of tumor-infiltrating immune cells in preclinical cancer models. In this chapter, we present a multiplex immunofluorescence staining approach for identifying, characterizing, and quantifying tumor-infiltrating immune cells in murine melanoma, allowing evaluation of how therapies influence immune infiltration in preclinical models.

title: PET Imaging of Melanoma Using a Melanocortin 1 Receptor-Targeted Probe.
abstract: The melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) is overexpressed in more than 80% of melanoma cells but is expressed at low levels in normal tissues, making it an important target for melanoma imaging and therapy. Recently, MC1R has attracted the interest of numerous researchers as a target for melanoma. Radiolabeled alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) peptides bind specifically to MC1R and internalize into tumor cells, enabling melanoma diagnosis and therapy. Several radiolabeled α-MSH peptides have been developed. Among those, a cyclized α-MSH peptide produced via an alternative click chemistry cyclization strategy offers faster and more specific bindings to MC1R. It could be labeled with ²0³Pb/²¹²Pb (VMT01) for melanoma single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging and therapy and also could be labeled with

title: SPECT Imaging of Melanoma Using a
abstract: Melanoma is a highly aggressive cutaneous malignancy characterized by a poor clinical prognosis, making early and accurate detection paramount for patient survival. Melanin, abundantly expressed in most melanoma lesions, serves as an ideal and highly specific biomarker for targeted molecular imaging. While various imaging modalities exist, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) provides a highly accessible and cost-effective strategy for widespread clinical translation. From our recent studies,

title: PET Imaging of Melanoma Using a Melanin-Targeted Probe.
abstract: Melanin exists in most melanoma lesions. Melanin plays an important role in melanoma progression, metastasis, therapy response, and the overall survival of patients. Therefore, melanin is a critical target for melanoma diagnosis and therapy. Many melanin-targeting probes, such as radioisotope-labeled benzamide analogs, have been developed for melanoma diagnosis using positron emission tomography (PET). The N-(2-(diethylamino)-ethyl)-

title: Radiopharmaceuticals for Melanoma Theranostics.
abstract: Malignant melanoma (MM) remains a formidable clinical challenge due to its high metastatic potential and the eventual emergence of resistance to current BRAF/MEK and immune checkpoint inhibitors. To address these limitations, the theranostic strategy integrating diagnostic imaging with targeted radionuclide therapy to enable personalized treatment has gained significant traction. Current research primarily exploits the overexpression of the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R), very late antigen-4 (VLA-4), and melanin as primary molecular targets for radiopharmaceutical development. For MC1R, α-MSH peptide analogs have been engineered with β-emitters such as

title: Multi-Analyte Responsive Fluorescent Sensing of Pathological Cellular States in Melanoma.
abstract: Melanoma progression involves multiple biomarkers and signaling pathways, and relying on a single marker can lead to incomplete or inaccurate diagnoses. Multi-analyte sensors allow simultaneous monitoring of several biomarkers, providing a more comprehensive picture of the tumor microenvironment, identifying distinct cellular states, and improving diagnostic accuracy.
