This chapter presents protocols that can be used for fluorescence sensing of the melanoma marker enzyme tyrosinase in conjunction with different In Vitro microenvironmental signals, including hypoxia and reactive oxygen species.

title: Design Strategies for Melanoma-Targeting Fluorescent Probes.
abstract: Melanoma is responsible for most skin cancer-related mortalities, and clinical urgency drives the development of novel diagnostic tools. Precision diagnostics relying on fluorescence output provide many advantages, including easy and noninvasive readout and a high signal-to-noise ratio that is enabled through a change in the intensity or the wavelength of fluorescence in response to disease-associated parameters. This chapter explores the chemical design strategies for fluorescent probes, focusing on the exploitation of melanogenic enzymes, protein biomarkers, and the targeting of the dysregulated tumor microenvironment to achieve unprecedented diagnostic precision.

title: Imaging and Isolation of Extravasation-Participating Endothelial and Melanoma Cells During Angiopellosis.
abstract: Cancer mortality is driven largely by metastatic progression rather than by primary tumor burden. The ability of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) to exit the vasculature and invade surrounding tissues-known as extravasation-is a critical and rate-limiting step in metastasis. Recent advances in high-resolution intravital microscopy have made it possible to directly visualize this process in vivo, enabling real-time imaging of individual CTCs as they interact with, transmigrate through, and recruit components of the endothelium. In this chapter, we describe intravital microscopy approaches that allow for both visualization and isolation of extravasating CTCs, as well as the endothelial cells that actively participate in their transendothelial migration. These methods provide a powerful platform for dissecting the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying metastatic spread. Beyond mechanistic insights, the approach can also serve as a functional screening system for evaluating anticancer therapeutics that target CTC behavior, endothelial interactions, or early metastatic niche formation.

title: Detection of Biomarkers for EMT-Associated Phenotype Switching in Melanoma-Derived Extracellular Vesicles.
abstract: Melanoma cells exhibit epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-like phenotype switching during targeted therapy, which contributes to the development of drug resistance. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by melanoma cells carry surface proteins reflective of this EMT-associated transition, providing an accessible window to track therapeutic response. This chapter presents a step-by-step protocol for profiling EMT-related melanoma EV protein signatures directly from unpurified sera using a microfluidic surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) biosensing platform. The method integrates melanoma-specific EV capture, alternating current-electrohydrodynamic nanomixing-enhanced binding, and multiplex SERS nanotag labeling to enable sensitive quantification of EMT surface markers in a streamlined assay. Detailed instructions for reagent preparation, SERS nanotag synthesis, biosensor fabrication and operation, spectral acquisition, and data processing are provided to support implementation in melanoma translational research laboratories. This protocol enables reproducible monitoring of EMT-like phenotypic evolution in melanoma models and patient samples and may assist future studies aiming to predict or mechanistically dissect resistance to targeted therapy.

title: Imaging and Analysis of Melanoma-Secreted Extracellular Vesicles in Tumor-Draining Lymph Nodes.
abstract: Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are key mediators of intercellular communication and play important roles in both physiological and pathological processes. In cancer, sEVs mediate communication between the tumor and its microenvironment but also contribute to metastatic organotropism and the formation of pre-metastatic niches in regional and distant organs. Lymph nodes (LNs) are central regulators of immune responses and primary sites of early metastasis, and, as such, they are critical targets for understanding cancer progression and improving immunotherapy. sEVs contribute to the conditioning of lymph nodes during pre-metastatic niche formation by altering lymphatic endothelial cell function and modulating immune cell populations, thereby promoting tumor progression. Because these interactions are complex and dynamic, their study requires in vivo models and specifically tailored sEVs-based techniques. In this chapter, we describe several approaches for studying sEVs in the LN context, including biodistribution analysis in the lymphatic system, imaging by immunofluorescence, and uptake measurement by flow cytometry.

title: Post-Lymphadenectomy Analysis of Small Extracellular Vesicles from Lymphatic Drainage/Exudative Seroma of Melanoma Patients.
abstract: Circulating extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as a promising source of disease biomarkers in biofluids. Although multiple isolation methods are available, differential ultracentrifugation remains a gold standard for small EV purification. Small EVs purified using this approach retain functional activity both in vitro and in vivo and are suitable for downstream applications, including proteomics, electron microscopy, mass spectrometry, and nucleic acid analysis. An additional purification step, either by density gradient centrifugation or size-exclusion chromatography, allows for the isolation of highly pure EV fractions for subsequent biomarker analysis. Here, we describe a protocol based on differential ultracentrifugation followed by a density gradient centrifugation or size exclusion chromatography step for the recovery of highly pure small extracellular vesicles (EVs) from lymphatic exudate (seroma) collected following lymphadenectomy, with the aim of supporting biomarker discovery and liquid biopsy applications.

title: A Rapid Exosome Isolation Using Ultrafiltration and Size Exclusion Chromatography (REIUS) Method for Exosome Isolation from Melanoma Cell Lines.
abstract: Cells release extracellular vesicles (EVs) that can be detected both in vivo and in cell culture medium. Among EVs, exosomes are 50-150 nm vesicles that are systematically packaged into multivesicular bodies for release into the external environment. In cancer, these intentionally packaged exosomes carry a payload of molecules such as protein, RNA, and surface receptors that facilitate the reprogramming of proximal cells to assemble a pro-tumor microenvironment. Exosomes have been implicated as an important intermediary extracellular communication pathway between cells, including in melanoma. Human melanoma-derived exosomes (HMEX) have been demonstrated to modulate the extracellular environment and inhibit immune cell activation. There are many methods to isolate and enrich for exosomes, and the method applied can impact yield and purity of the isolates. In this chapter, we describe the REIUS (Rapid Exosome Isolation Using Size exclusion chromatography) method to isolate HMEX from melanoma cell cultures and then demonstrate their enrichment using molecular and microscopic approaches.

title: Capture and Isolation of Circulating Melanoma Cells Using Photoacoustic Flowmetry.
abstract: Early detection of cancer has been a goal of cancer research in general and melanoma research in particular. Early detection of metastasis has been targeted as pivotal to increasing survival rates. Melanoma, though curable in its early stages, has a dramatic decrease in survival rates once metastasis has occurred. The transition to metastasis is not well understood and is an area of increasing interest. Metastasis is always premeditated by the shedding of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) from the primary tumor. The ability to isolate rare CTCs from the bloodstream has led to a host of new targets and therapies for cancer. Detection of CTCs also allows for disease progression to be tracked in real time while eliminating the need to wait for additional tumors to grow. Using a photoacoustic flow cytometer, in which we induce ultrasonic responses from circulating melanoma cells (CMCs), we identify and quantify these cells in order to track disease progression. Additionally, these CMCs are captured and isolated, allowing for future analysis such as RNA-Seq or microarray analysis. Finally, anticipating the need to streamline clinical workflow, a method for testing in whole blood is offered.

title: Modeling Proliferative Versus Migratory Melanoma Cell Phenotypes Using Biofabricated Matrices.
abstract: Biofabrication enables the controlled generation of three-dimensional cell cultures that can be highly useful to study different cellular phenotypes. As melanoma cells reveal high plasticity, and the "phenotype switching model" defining the cells as either proliferative or migratory active has been described, we recently developed a 3D bioprinted model mimicking these phenotypes. Here, we describe the generation of these bioprinted models based on either Matrigel or Cellink Bioink, which can be used with various cell lines and which allows for the analysis of cell response on microscopic and molecular levels. This model system offers novel opportunities for fundamental research and drug testing on heterogeneous tumors like melanoma.

title: Skin Organ Constructs for In Vitro Modeling of Melanoma Invasion.
abstract: Melanoma progression from an in situ lesion to an invasive dermal tumor is strongly associated with poor patient prognosis, with depth of invasion serving as a predictor of survival. Increasing evidence indicates that remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM) plays a central role in this transition by altering both mechanical and biochemical cues within the tumor microenvironment. To facilitate mechanistic studies of ECM-mediated melanoma invasion, we developed a reproducible in vitro skin organ construct (SOC) model that recapitulates key structural and cellular features of human skin. The SOC system is assembled using a two-layer collagen-based dermal equivalent containing primary human dermal fibroblasts, overlaid with normal human epidermal keratinocytes to generate a stratified epidermis. Melanoma cells are subsequently seeded onto the reconstructed epidermal surface and cultured under defined conditions, including staged modulation of epidermal growth factor and exposure to an air-liquid interface to promote keratinization. The model permits incorporation of defined ECM components or genetically modified melanoma cells to evaluate their impact on tumor invasion. Melanoma progression is assessed by measuring radial growth and quantifying invasion depth and patterns in paraffin-embedded sections using histological and immunohistochemical analyses. This SOC platform provides a physiologically relevant and customizable system to investigate ECM-driven mechanisms of melanoma invasion and to evaluate candidate therapeutic targets that modulate tumor-microenvironment interactions.

title: Evaluating Melanoma Cell Migration/Invasion in Transwell Assays by Flow Cytometry.
abstract: Cell migration and invasion are vital aspects of melanoma biology that are critical to the progression of this aggressive cancer. Numerous in vitro assays are available to study these hallmark properties of cancer, including two-dimensional wound healing ("scratch") and transwell (Boyden chamber) assays, as well as three-dimensional microfluidic-based video microscopy assays and matrix/skin organ construct-based assays. Though each of these assays has unique advantages depending on the experimental question at hand, transwell assays are highly adaptable and thus particularly well-suited for investigating the role of specific stimulators/inhibitors of cancer cell migration and invasion. Traditionally, quantification of migrating/invading cells that are capable of transiting the Boyden chamber utilized in these assays is achieved by manual counting of cells that have reached the bottom chamber or by colorimetric/fluorometric detection of transited cells that were preloaded with specific dyes prior to assay initiation. These approaches, while commonly used, have inherent limitations in their design, including the introduction of quantification artifacts that arise from human error during direct cell counting or uneven/inconsistent cell labeling within/across experiments. To overcome these limitations, we have optimized a non-fluorescent flow cytometry-based assay for quantifying melanoma transwell migration and invasion, and we present herein an application of this assay to assess the role of the FOXC2 transcription factor in these processes.

title: Wound Healing Assay for Melanoma Cell Migration.
abstract: Cell migration is a critical process involved in morphogenesis, inflammation, and cancer metastasis. The wound healing assay is a simple, nonexpensive, and highly reproducible method to study cancer cell migration in vitro. It is based on the observation that cells growing in a monolayer migrate to re-establish cell contacts after the development of an artificial wound. The assay involves creation of a wound in a monolayer, image acquisition during wound closure, and comparison of migrated area at initial and final time points.

title: A Flow Cytometric Assay for Investigating Melanoma Cell Adhesion to Lymphatic Endothelial Cells.
abstract: Lymph node invasion by tumor cells is an important process in the progression of melanoma and is a poor prognostic factor for patients with this cancer. Before they are able to spread to regional lymph nodes, though, melanoma cells must first adhere to lymphatic endothelium and transmigrate into the lymphatic vasculature. In order to study melanoma cell adhesion to lymphatic endothelial cells and the factors that regulate this process, we have developed an in vitro flow cytometry-based assay to measure melanoma cell attachment to lymphatic endothelial cells. This assay will be a useful tool for investigating the interactions that take place between melanoma cells and lymphatic endothelial cells during the adhesion process.

title: Indirect Coculture of Melanoma Cells with Stromal Cells Present in Their Microenvironment as a Method for Evaluation of Their Mutual Interactions.
abstract: A tumor tissue consists not only of cancer cells but also of stromal cells, which often support cancer cell progression. Therefore, oncology research utilizes models that enable the study of cancer cell characteristics in the presence of noncancereous cells that, in vivo, also form the tumor. The following protocol describes the culturing of cancer cells with stromal cells (such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and adipocytes) in an indirect coculture model, in which both cell types exchange secretory factors in the culture medium but do not interact directly. This system allows for the assessment of the influence of one cell type on the other without the need to separate them through sorting to conduct further experiments based on only one selected cell type.

title: Generation of Functional Gene Knockout Melanoma Cell Lines by CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing.
abstract: Recent advances in the treatment of metastatic melanoma have emerged only from advances in our understanding of melanoma development and progression at the cellular and molecular level. Despite the impact that such advances have made on the clinical management of this cancer over the last decade, additional insights into factors that promote melanoma progression and therapeutic resistance are needed to combat this disease. CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology is a powerful tool for studying gene function in a timely and cost-effective manner, enabling the manipulation of specific DNA sequences via a targeted approach. Herein, we describe a protocol for generating functional gene knockouts in melanoma cell lines by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, and we present an example application of this protocol for the successful knockout of the Foxc2 transcription factor-encoding gene in the B16-F1 murine melanoma cell line.

title: Model Systems for the Study of Malignant Melanoma.
abstract: Since the first resection of melanoma by Hunter in 1787, efforts to treat patients with this deadly malignancy have been ongoing. Initial work to understand melanoma biology for therapeutics development began with the employment of isolated cancer cells grown in culture. However, these models lack in vivo interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Melanoma cell line transplantation into suitable animals, such as mice, has been informative and useful for testing therapeutics as a pre-clinical model. Injection of freshly isolated patient melanomas into immunodeficient animals has shown the capacity to retain the genetic heterogeneity of the tumors, which is lost during long-term culture of melanoma cells. Upon the advancement of technology, genetically engineered animals have been generated to study the spontaneous development of melanomas in light of newly discovered genetic aberrations associated with melanoma formation. Culturing melanoma cells in a matrix generates tumor spheroids, providing an in vitro environment that promotes the heterogeneity commonplace with human melanoma and displaces the need for animal care facilities. Advanced 3D cultures have been created simulating the structure and cellularity of human skin to permit in vitro testing of therapeutics on melanomas expressing the same phenotype as demonstrated in vivo. This review discusses these models and their relevance to the study of melanomagenesis, growth, metastasis, and therapy.

title: Curcumin carried by polystyrene nanoparticles inhibits phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B signaling pathway through miR-186 and down-regulates Twist to inhibit the epithelial-mesenchymal transition in colorectal cancer in mice.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is involved in colorectal cancer (CRC) pathogenesis. Curcumin (CUR) is widely used in the treatment of CRC. Polystyrene nanoparticles (PS-NPS) have a high specific affinity and have an inhibitory effect on cell proliferation. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to investigate the mechanism of inhibition of EMT in colorectal cancer mice by preparing curcumin polystyrene nanoparticles (CUR-PS-NPS). OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to construct CUR-PS-NPS and investigate their mechanism in inhibiting CRC EMT via the miR-186/PI3K/AKT/Twist axis. METHOD: CUR-PS-NPS were prepared and characterized. RESULTS: In CRC mice intervened with CUR-PS-NPS, the tumor volume was reduced by 50%, the expression of mir-186 was up-regulated by 2.5 times, the phosphorylation level of PI3K/AKT was decreased by 40%, the expression of Twist protein was down-regulated by 35% and the expression of the EMT marker E-cadherin was increased. The expressions of N-cadherin, Vimentin and Snail decreased significantly. CONCLUSION: CUR-PS-NPS can effectively delay the EMT process of CRC by up-regulating mir-186, inhibiting the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway and the expression of Twist. This discovery provides a new strategy for targeted therapy based on nanocarriers and its application potential in clinical practice can be further explored in the future.

title: Evaluation of a four-herb Chinese medicine formula at different concentrations on muscle damage and inflammation in a rat model of DOMS.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) impairs exercise recovery, while current treatments remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) formulas may provide safe, multi-target interventions. OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the dose-dependent protective effects of a four-herb Chinese medicine formulation (safflower, Chinese Angelica, peach kernel and myrrh) against DOMS in a rat model. METHODS: Thirty-two male SPF SD rats were randomly allocated to control or low- (1696 mg/kg), medium- (3392 mg/kg), or high-dose (6784 mg/kg) groups. The formulation was administered orally for 11 days, with DOMS induced by exhaustive swimming on day 8. Serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-exercise. RESULTS: The medium- and high-dose groups exhibited significantly lower serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 levels than controls, with the high-dose group showing the largest reductions. The low-dose group showed limited or no significant reductions in most markers, demonstrating a clear dose-dependent protective effect. CONCLUSIONS: The formulation dose-dependently attenuates muscle damage and inflammation in a rat DOMS model, with high-dose treatment achieving the fastest recovery. Clinical trials are warranted to confirm the efficacy and safety in humans.

title: Randomized controlled trials of radiation therapy for cutaneous malignancies: a systematic review.
abstract: PURPOSE: In cutaneous oncology, radiotherapy use is largely based on retrospective studies, institutional experience, and expert consensus, with limited high-level evidence to guide practice. We summarize randomized controlled trials in cutaneous radiation oncology and identify gaps in contemporary treatment warranting additional study. METHODS AND MATERIALS: We searched Ovid MEDLINE ALL, Embase.com, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for randomized controlled trials of radiotherapy for cutaneous malignancies: basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), melanoma, and Merkel cell carcinoma. Outcomes of interest included recurrence, survival, toxicity and cosmesis. Study inclusion required approval by three authors, with discrepancies resolved by an additional author. RESULTS: Thirteen trials entailing fewer than 2500 patients were identified, with only four studies published in the last decade. Three BCC studies compared radiotherapy with other treatments, while two additional BCC studies and one mixed BCC/SCC study compared dose-fractionation regimens. One SCC study evaluated adjuvant radiotherapy versus chemoradiotherapy. Among five melanoma trials, four evaluated adjuvant radiotherapy, including one for the primary tumor site and three for the regional nodal basin, and one compared definitive radiotherapy with topical imiquimod for unresectable melanoma in situ. One Merkel cell carcinoma trial evaluated lymph node basin radiotherapy. CONCLUSIONS: Randomized trials of radiotherapy for cutaneous malignancies are limited, small and heterogeneous, relative to the frequency of these diseases and clinical trials of other therapeutic interventions. Modern randomized trials are needed to bridge these gaps.

title: The value of breast brachytherapy boost in the current era: a narrative literature review from the GEC-ESTRO breast cancer working group.
abstract: PURPOSE: To identify patients who may benefit from an interstitial brachytherapy boost in the era of hypofractionation and widespread use of simultaneous integrated boost. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Between 1984 and 2025, 112 articles were identified through a narrative search of the PubMed, MEDLINE, and Cochrane databases using the keywords "breast cancer", "boost", "interstitial brachytherapy", and "interventional radiotherapy". Two main areas were addressed: an update on risk factors and patient selection, and a review of boost techniques, with an emphasis on interstitial brachytherapy and comparisons with other techniques. Based on this evidence, we formulated recommendations on the role of brachytherapy boost in contemporary breast cancer (BC) treatment. RESULTS: Based on the available literature, the addition of a boost should be strongly recommended for patients aged <40 years, patients with positive margins, and patients aged <50 years with at least one of the following features: high-grade disease, extensive intraductal carcinoma, and/or a triple-negative phenotype. In other scenarios, including residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, a balanced shared decision should be made. Interstitial brachytherapy allows delivery of a high radiation dose to the target volume while significantly reducing the dose received by adjacent organs at risk. CONCLUSION: The use of brachytherapy as a boost has declined, particularly since the introduction of integrated and ultra-hypofractionated regimens. In the current era of breast cancer treatment, we suggest that brachytherapy remains a valuable option for selected high-risk patients because it enables dose escalation tailored to the risk volume while sparing surrounding organs at risk.

title: Liver fibrosis risk, missed follow-up, and inequitable specialist referral in the All of Us Research Program: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is highly prevalent and frequently undiagnosed, despite liver fibrosis being the strongest predictor of liver-related morbidity and mortality. We aimed to quantify Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index-based fibrosis risk and to evaluate guideline-recommended follow-up-FIB-4 documentation, confirmatory testing, and specialist referral-in a large US cohort. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of electronic health record data from the US All of Us Research Program. Among adults aged 35 years or older with sufficient laboratory data, FIB-4 scores were calculated from routinely captured biomarkers, classified as low (<1.3), indeterminate (1.3-2.67; 2.0-2.67 if aged ≥65 years), or high risk (>2.67), and described across sociodemographic and metabolic subgroups; associations with incident major adverse liver outcomes (MALO) were assessed with Cox proportional-hazards regression. We examined FIB-4 documentation, confirmatory testing, and specialty referrals within 365 days of the index FIB-4 date. FINDINGS: Among 136,004 participants (mean age 60.8 years [SD 13.5]; 79,365 [58.4%] female; 81,420 [59.9%] White, 21,779 [16.0%] Hispanic or Latino, 20,076 [14.8%] Black), 26,971 (19.8%, 95% CI 19.6-20.0) had indeterminate and 11,217 (8.2%, 8.1-8.4) high FIB-4-based fibrosis risk. Elevated risk was more frequent with cardiovascular disease (41.7% vs 25.6%), hypertension (30.7% vs 23.4%), and type 2 diabetes (29.7% vs 27.4%), rising from 25.6% with no metabolic comorbidities to 36.6% with four. FIB-4 documentation was rare, and fewer than 1% of high-risk participants underwent confirmatory testing or referral; referral was low across risk categories (0.19% high, 0.19% indeterminate, 0.25% low risk). MALO occurred in 1308 (11.7%) high-risk vs 830 (0.8%) low-risk participants (adjusted hazard ratio 19.68, 95% CI 17.88-21.67). INTERPRETATION: Routinely collected laboratory data identify substantial liver fibrosis risk in this volunteer US cohort, yet guideline-recommended follow-up is uncommon. Implementation strategies such as automated risk calculation and reflex-based testing pathways could reduce missed opportunities for earlier diagnosis and intervention. FUNDING: No specific funding was received for this study.

title: Analysis of Metabolomics Response to Tick Saliva in Human Cells.
abstract: This chapter describes a workflow for the analysis of the metabolomic response of the human basophilic cell line KU812 exposed to Ixodes ricinus tick saliva using ¹H-nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The protocol includes procedures for cell culture, harvesting, washing, and metabolite extraction, followed by the separation of aqueous and lipid fractions. Detailed instructions for sample preparation and NMR data acquisition are provided for both fractions. Spectral processing and metabolite quantification are performed using targeted profiling approaches based on constrained line-shape fitting, enabling accurate analysis of complex biological samples. Metabolite identification is supported by spectral databases and literature references, and absolute concentrations are obtained using internal standard-based quantification methods. Finally, data normalization based on cell number ensures comparability across samples. Overall, this protocol provides a robust and reproducible strategy for investigating metabolic alterations induced by tick saliva in human cells.

title: In Vivo LncRNA Inhibition in Human Tumor Xenografts Using Antisense Locked Nucleic Acid GapmeRs.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as significant regulators of many physiological and pathological processes and play a key role in the onset and progression of a variety of diseases, including cancer. Currently, the functions of the majority of lncRNAs in carcinogenesis are still unclear. Functional characterization of specific lncRNAs is often challenging using the conventional RNA interference method, due to their specific and restricted subcellular localization. Antisense locked nucleic acid (LNA) GapmeRs, which induce RNase H1-mediated RNA cleavage, provide a promising strategy to knock down lncRNAs regardless of their intracellular localization. Here, we describe a protocol for suppressing the lncRNA BIN3 Intronic Transcript 1 (BIN3-IT1) in human breast cancer xenografts using Antisense LNA GapmeRs.

title: A Bioinformatic Framework for Enhancer RNAs Identification in Cancer Based on RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq.
abstract: Enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) are noncoding RNAs transcribed from the genomic regions of enhancers. eRNAs are increasingly recognized to play an important role in gene regulation, and they can associate with various traits in humans. Here, we provide a bioinformatic pipeline to identify eRNA expression profiles using either an in-house dataset or public datasets from large-scale samples. We also summarized approaches for the identification of eRNAs' putative regulatory network, and eRNA-correlated traits and clinical features. This workflow provides guidance for readers to use bioinformatic tools for analyzing eRNA expression and eRNA-associated traits.

title: In Vitro RNA Pulldown and Validation of lncRNA-Protein Interactions.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) play important roles in gene regulation and cancer progression through interactions with proteins, DNA, and other RNA molecules. Identification of lncRNA-protein interactions is therefore essential for understanding the molecular mechanisms by which lncRNAs regulate cellular processes. Among the available approaches, in vitro RNA pulldown coupled with mass spectrometry has become a widely used strategy for identifying proteins that associate with specific lncRNAs. In this chapter, we describe a detailed protocol for in vitro RNA pulldown using biotin-labeled RNA transcripts and magnetic bead capture to isolate lncRNA-binding proteins from cell lysates. We further outline complementary validation approaches, including western blot analysis, modified dot-blot assays, and RNA electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), which can be used to confirm candidate RNA-protein interactions and to map RNA-binding regions. Together, these methods provide a practical workflow for identifying and validating lncRNA-protein interactions in cancer research.

title: Using BruUV-Seq to Identify Enhancer RNA Expression in Live Cells.
abstract: BruUV-seq is a nascent RNA sequencing technique that uses bromouridine to label RNA and UV light to suppress both transcription elongation and RNA degradation, enabling the enrichment and study of labile RNA species, such as enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), in live-cell culture models. Here, we describe both the BruUV-seq experimental method and the next-generation sequencing data analysis, which allow for the identification of eRNAs produced at active enhancer elements.

title: Role of Chromatin-Associated RNAs in Eye Physiology and Pathology.
abstract: Noncoding RNAs, including long noncoding RNAs, enhancer RNAs, circular RNAs, and small nuclear and nucleolar RNAs, represent a major, yet still largely uncharacterized, regulatory layer in the eye. A subset of these molecules, chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs), physically interacts with DNA and nuclear protein complexes to influence genome organization, transcriptional output, and stress responses. Although caRNAs have emerged as essential regulators of chromatin topology and gene expression in diverse tissues, their identity, dynamics, and mechanisms in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remain elusive. Recent high-resolution genomic studies, disease transcriptomes, and mechanistic studies implicate dysregulated caRNAs in age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy, yet causal chromatin-level functions have rarely been demonstrated. In this review, we summarize current understanding of ncRNA-mediated regulation in vision, highlight emerging evidence for caRNA involvement in retinal development, photoreceptor and RPE specialization, and disease-associated epigenetic remodeling, and outline major mechanistic gaps that must be addressed. We then survey the rapidly expanding CRISPR toolbox, including base and prime editors, CRISPRi/a, Cas13 knockdown and editing platforms, and RNA-recruitment and spatial repositioning systems, that now enable targeted perturbation of both caRNA genomic loci and transcripts. These technologies provide the first practical route to move beyond correlative RNA-chromatin maps toward the mechanistic dissection of how caRNAs organize regulatory hubs, modulate enhancer-promoter communication, and shape long-range genome interactions in the eye. As the catalog of pathogenic noncoding variants grows, the ability to decode and engineer caRNA networks will be central to future precision therapeutic strategies for ocular disorders.

title: Methodological Approaches for the Preservation of Akkermansia muciniphila as Microbial Genetic Resource.
abstract: Akkermansia muciniphila is part of the intestinal microbiota and uses mucin as its primary source of carbon and nitrogen. It is considered a promising next-generation probiotic, with numerous beneficial functions. It regulates metabolic functions and immune response and improves the intestinal barrier, to name a few. This translates into the prevention of diseases such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, among others. However, despite its diverse benefits, A. muciniphila presents technical challenges in its cultivation and application, such as the need for a medium with a specific composition, the bacteria's high sensitivity to oxygen, a slow growth rate and stability, as well as differences between strains. In this sense, this protocol reflects the conditions for the preservation and maintenance of A. muciniphila.

title: Study protocol for the TROG 21.08 VITaL trial: a randomized controlled trial investigating ventilation imaging to improve the quality of life for patients with lung cancer treated with radiation therapy.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Radiation therapy (RT) is indicated for 77% of patients with lung cancer. Over 20% of patients are affected by radiation-induced lung injury. Computed tomography ventilation imaging (CTVI) estimates high and low functioning lung regions. During RT planning, CTVI can guide preferential avoidance of higher ventilated regions by redirecting dose to less well ventilated regions, sparing healthy lung tissue. The double-masked randomized Trans-Tasman Radiation Oncology Group (TROG) 21.08 VITaL trial will investigate if sparing healthy lung can improve the quality of life (QoL) for patients with stage 3 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with RT. METHODS: 165 patients will be recruited to test the hypothesis that patients receiving healthy lung-sparing RT have better QoL than patients receiving standard RT. CTVI will be generated from exhale and inhale breath-hold CT scan pairs. A healthy lung-sparing plan and a standard treatment plan will be created for each patient and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio for the patient's treatment. QoL will be assessed with the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Lung questionnaire before and after treatment. Secondary hypotheses include that patients in the healthy lung-sparing arm will have fewer treatment side effects, better lung function, be more likely to receive and complete adjuvant immunotherapy, and healthy lung-sparing treatment will be cost-effective. Patient follow-up will continue for three years. DISCUSSION: This prospective randomized trial will determine whether the incorporation of healthy lung-sparing RT based on CTVI improves QoL, reduces pulmonary toxicity, and increases eligibility to receive curative immunotherapy for patients with stage 3 NSCLC. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06127654).

title: Application of Low-Dose Radiotherapy Combined with Immunotherapy for Drug-Resistant Hepatic Metastasis: a Case Series Analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: There is no established standard regimen for end-stage patients suffering from multi-line refractory diffuse hepatic metastases. This case series intended to assess the antitumor activity, treatment tolerance and palliative value of whole-liver low-dose radiotherapy combined with PD-1 immunotherapy, with special attention paid to the occurrence of systemic abscopal effect. PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective case series aimed to evaluate the clinical efficacy and safety of low-dose whole-liver radiotherapy (LDRT) combined with PD-1 inhibitor immunotherapy in patients with refractory diffuse hepatic metastases from solid tumors. Six patients who developed progressive diffuse hepatic metastases after one or more lines of prior systemic therapy and subsequently received LDRT plus immunotherapy were enrolled. All patients were followed up until the predefined cutoff date of July 2026. The primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR) and the incidence of treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). The secondary endpoints included symptomatic improvement and changes in quality of life. Tumor response was assessed according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1, and adverse events were graded based on the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. All enrolled patients presented with extensive diffuse intrahepatic metastasis at baseline. RESULTS: With a median follow-up of 7.5 months, tumor regression or radiological remission was observed in several patients,yielding an objective response rate (ORR) of 66.7%. Clinical symptomatic relief and improved quality of life were achieved in four patients after combination treatment. In terms of safety, No grade 3 or higher TRAEs definitively attributable to this combined regimen were observed during treatment.The combined regimen appeared to be generally tolerable for the liver. Collectively, these preliminary findings suggest a potential clinical benefit and acceptable safety of this LDRT plus immunotherapy combination in one or more lines pretreated patients with diffuse hepatic metastases. CONCLUSION: This exploratory case-series generates the hypothesis that low-dose radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy may yield clinical benefits for selected patients with diffuse treatment-refractory hepatic metastases. Further prospective clinical trials and translational research are warranted to elucidate the underlying immunomodulatory mechanisms and define patient subsets most likely to derive clinical benefit from this approach.

title: Burden of cardiovascular disease in Brazil, 1996-2023: a retrospective descriptive study of the epidemiology and impact on public healthcare.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are the leading cause of death worldwide, and their epidemiology is correlated with genetic predisposition and exposure to risk. Brazil is a developing country with a vast territory, which leads to structural inequalities. We aimed to comprehensively characterise the epidemiology and burden of CVD in Brazil between 1996 and 2023, examining temporal trends, regional disparities, demographic patterns, healthcare costs, and heart transplantation. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective descriptive ecological study using aggregated administrative data from the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), Brazil's publicly funded national health system. Mortality, hospitalization, and heart transplantation data from 1996 to 2023 were analysed according to sex, race/ethnicity, age, and geographic region. We estimated mortality rates for the major CVD, hospital length of stay, healthcare expenditures, and heart transplantation activity. FINDINGS: Acute myocardial infarction remained the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality throughout the study period, while hypertensive diseases overtook heart failure after 2016 as the second leading cause of death. The overall CVD mortality rate-calculated as the number of CVD-related deaths divided by the total population and expressed as a percentage-increased from 7.3% in 1998 to 8.3% in 2023, peaking at 10.1% in 2021. Marked regional, age-, sex-, and race/ethnicity-related disparities were observed, including the complete absence of heart transplantation in the North region throughout the study period. Although hospitalization rates remained relatively stable, CVD-related healthcare expenditures and heart transplantation activity increased over time. INTERPRETATION: CVD remains a major and growing public health challenge in Brazil, with substantial regional and demographic inequalities in disease burden and access to specialised care. These findings highlight the need for targeted public health strategies and more equitable allocation of healthcare resources to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. FUNDING: This study was funded by CNPq, CAPES, FAPEMIG, INCT.

title: Left atrial and left ventricular radiation exposure predict long-term cardiovascular events after breast cancer radiotherapy.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adjuvant breast cancer (BC) radiotherapy (RT) improves survival and local control, but cardiovascular (CV) toxicity remains a concern. AIM: This retrospective study investigated the association between RT doses to cardiac substructures and CV toxicity 15 years after BC RT. METHODS: Women with unilateral BC diagnosed between 2007 and 2008, treated with RT at [Anonymous] were retrospectively included. Patients with major adverse cardiac events (MACE) were matched to controls by CV risk factors, anthracycline and anti-HER2 therapy. Cardiac substructures were delineated on simulation scans, and multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess associations between RT doses to these substructures and MACE or other CV events. RESULTS: After a median follow-up of 16.5 years (IQR 16.1-17.1), and inclusion of 878 patients, 173 patients experienced MACE and were matched to 167 controls. All patients underwent adjuvant RT using 3-dimensional conformal RT to a total dose of 50 Gy in 25 fractions, with or without a boost to the tumor bed. New individual cardiac toxicities included: atrial fibrillation (AF) 98/878 (11.16%), heart failure (HF) 82/878 (9.34%), coronary artery disease (CAD) 46/878 (5.24%) and valvular disease 180/878 (20.50%). Mean heart doses were 6.62 ± 5.20Gy (MACE) and 5.76 ± 4.96Gy (controls) ( CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that patients treated with RT for BC may experience diverse CV toxicities during long-term follow-up. Higher doses to left-sided cardiac substructures, particularly the LA and LV, were associated with specific CV endpoints, while MHD was not associated with toxicity.

title: Efficacy and safety of single-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for the curative treatment of extracranial primary Tumors: A collaborative systematic review on behalf of the SBRT Focus Group of the European Society for Radiotherapy & Oncology (ESTRO).
abstract: Single-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SF-SBRT) represents one of the most advanced frontiers in modern radiation oncology. While ultra-hypofractionation has entered everyday clinical practice in different fields of the oncological care, curative treatments in one session are increasingly attractive for the potential favorable combination of logistic advantages with safety and clinical outcomes. This collaborative systematic review promoted by the ESTRO SBRT Focus Group in participation with members of different disease-site Focus Groups collects the available data in support of SF-SBRT for the curative treatment of the main extracranial primary tumors. The findings highlight that, for specific anatomical sites, SF-SBRT is both safe and effective though the results emphasize the critical importance of careful patient selection and mandatory technological requirements for treatment planning and delivery. This collaborative work provides a comprehensive overview of current evidence and identifies key knowledge gaps for future investigation and upcoming clinical trials.

title: Intervention Strategies of Nonanastomotic Biliary Strictures: From Mechanical Repair to Biological Reconstruction.
abstract: Nonanastomotic strictures (NAS) are the most troublesome biliary complications following liver transplantation. This narrative review systematically summarizes the interventions of NAS, such as prevention methods (eg, machine perfusion) and conventional treatments (eg, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography). Magnetic compression anastomosis is an alternative to endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography in complex anatomical sites. Additionally, taking into consideration the current therapeutic strategy shift from mechanical repair to biological reconstruction, applications of mesenchymal stem cells and organoids are also discussed. However, the clinical application of organoids requires further investigation. Additionally, retransplantation is the definitive treatment of NAS and has efficacy on ischemic biliary lesions. Current intervention for NAS remains palliative, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is regarded as the main therapeutic strategy. Future investigations need to focus on powered studies investigating prevention, the combination of different interventions, and the translation of regenerative medicine. Effective interventions for NAS are important for improving the prognosis and long-term graft function of recipients.

title: Current role of boron neutron capture therapy in head and neck cancer: insights from 4 years of clinical experience.
abstract: PURPOSE: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) was approved in Japan in June 2020 as a curative option for unresectable, locally advanced, or recurrent head and neck cancers. Relevantly, its efficacy and safety in clinical practice should be regularly monitored, particularly regarding its optimal positioning. Therefore, to advance its clinical application, we assessed clinical data on BNCT for head and neck cancers. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 285 patients who received initial BNCT between June 2020 and May 2024 with available ≥1 month follow-up data. The primary endpoint was local control (LC); secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), treatment response, and grade ≥ 3 adverse events. RESULTS: The 2-year LC, PFS, and OS rates were 41.5%, 26.4%, and 59.2%, respectively. The complete response (CR), partial response (PR), and objective response (CR + PR) rates were 47.0%, 33.3%, and 80.4%, respectively. The cumulative incidence of grade ≥ 3 late adverse events was 14.0% at 2 years, with grade 5 adverse events occurring in 2.1% of patients. No significant differences were observed in LC or PFS among histological type subgroups; however, OS was significantly worse in patients with squamous cell carcinoma (SqCC) than in patients with non-SqCC. Regarding TNM stage at irradiation, radiation therapy at an early disease stage was significantly associated with improved LC. CONCLUSIONS: BNCT should be administered during the early disease stages when no other effective treatment options are available. Further studies should determine the factors contributing to treatment efficacy and safety, thereby optimizing multimodal treatment strategies involving BNCT.

title: Dose-related cardiac side effects and its impact on survival following thoracic radiotherapy: A scoping review.
abstract: Radiation dose to the heart is associated with various cardiac side effects. However, the specific cardiac and pulmonary structures that contribute to these toxicities remain incompletely understood. Moreover, although multiple factors contribute to reduced survival after radiotherapy, the role of radiation-induced cardiac toxicity remains underrecognized. This scoping review aimed to evaluate the associations between radiation dose to specific cardiac and pulmonary structures, cardiac side effects, and survival. A total of 137 clinical studies were analysed in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Associations between radiation dose and cardiac side effects were identified not only for the whole heart but also for specific cardiac substructures, including myocardial segments, coronary arteries, and the pericardium. Notably, radiation dose to the lungs was also associated with decline in cardiac function, suggesting that minimizing cardiac toxicity may require consideration of both local cardiac irradiation and non-local irradiation of adjacent organs, particularly the lungs. Direct evidence linking cardiac side effects to survival was limited. Nevertheless, the observed associations between higher radiation doses, increased cardiac toxicity, and poorer survival suggest a potential relationship that warrants further investigation. These findings support the hypothesis that reducing specific cardiac side effects may benefit from targeted sparing of the relevant cardiac and pulmonary substructures. While many radiation-related cardiac side effects are now recognized, further research is needed to identify and characterize previously unrecognized manifestations and to clarify their contribution to long-term survival.

title: Association of adverse pregnancy outcomes with coronary microvascular dysfunction: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs) are recognized cardiovascular risk enhancers, yet their association with coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) has not been systematically quantified. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between APOs and CMD and to provide pooled estimates of CMD prevalence and severity in women with APO history. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched through December 2025. Observational studies evaluating coronary microvascular function using PET, Doppler echocardiography, stress CMR, or invasive physiology in women with APOs versus controls were included. Multivariate random-effects meta-analysis was performed to account for non-independent effect estimates arising from shared control groups. Risk of bias was assessed using NOS; certainty of evidence using GRADE. RESULTS: Five studies (1,183 participants; 583 APO, 600 controls) were included. Women with APO history demonstrated significantly reduced CFR (SMD -0.94; 95% CI, -1.43 to -0.45; p<0.0001; I²=88.2%) and elevated CMD prevalence (OR 6.74; 95% CI, 1.55-29.42; p0.011; I²=92.2%). An exploratory graded pattern was observed, with combined preeclampsia and gestational diabetes associated with the largest CFR reduction (SMD -1.27); however, this was driven primarily by a single study with shared controls. Publication bias assessment was non-significant for CFR (p0.312) but borderline for CMD prevalence (p0.078). CONCLUSIONS: APOs are associated with reduced CFR and elevated CMD prevalence, suggesting CMD may represent a plausible intermediate phenotype linking pregnancy complications to long-term cardiovascular disease. Given low to very low certainty evidence and substantial heterogeneity, these findings are hypothesis-generating and support further prospective research.

title: Carotid atherosclerosis and aortic stiffness in masters athletes: Multimodality vascular phenotyping from the Master@Heart study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Middle-aged male Masters athletes exhibit a higher burden of coronary atherosclerosis on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) compared with healthy controls. Whether this is accompanied by differences in carotid atherosclerosis or aortic stiffness remains uncertain. We assessed carotid atherosclerosis and aortic stiffness across groups, association between carotid atherosclerosis and coronary disease, and the incremental value of carotid plaque beyond traditional risk factors. METHODS: In this cross-sectional analysis of the Master@Heart study, 549 low cardiovascular risk men (median age 55 [50-60] years), including lifelong athletes, late-onset athletes, and healthy controls, underwent vascular phenotyping. Carotid plaque was assessed by ultrasound, aortic stiffness by carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (PWV), and coronary atherosclerosis by CCTA. Group differences were assessed using chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Association between carotid and coronary atherosclerosis was evaluated using regression models. Incremental discriminatory value was assessed using ROC curve analysis. RESULTS: Prevalence of ≥1 carotid plaque did not differ between lifelong athletes, late-onset athletes, and controls (29.5%vs. 33.2% vs. 27.9%; p = 0.54). Carotid stenosis ≥50% was rare (1.2%-2.7%) and similar across groups (p = 0.54). Median PWV did not differ between groups (p = 0.29). Carotid plaque was associated with coronary atherosclerosis on CCTA. However, adding carotid plaque to traditional risk factors did not improve discrimination of coronary atherosclerosis. CONCLUSION: In middle-aged male Masters athletes, excess subclinical coronary atherosclerosis is observed without corresponding differences in carotid plaque or aortic stiffness. Although carotid plaque is associated with coronary atherosclerosis, it does not meaningfully improve risk discrimination beyond traditional risk factors.

title: Epicardial adipose tissue radiomics complement calcium scoring in black adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Conventional markers of risk such as coronary artery calcium (CAC) scores are lower and less predictive in Black adults, despite a high prevalence of Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and Metabolic Syndrome We evaluated whether incorporation of epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) features capture prognostic signal beyond CAC and social deprivation index, in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events. METHODS: Adults with T2DM undergoing non-contrast CT calcium scoring from the CLARIFY registry (NCT04075162), including 1024 non-Hispanic Black participants and 3072 propensity-matched non-Hispanic White participants were included. EAT was automatically segmented and radiomic features were extracted and selected using survival-based machine learning. Cox proportional hazards models were constructed using CAC, Social Deprivation Index (SDI), and EAT features alone and in combination. The primary endpoint was 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE-3P), defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal stroke. Model discrimination, reclassification, and calibration were assessed. RESULTS: During a median follow-up of approximately 5 years, 206 (20%) Black participants and 422 (14%) matched White participants experienced MACE-3P In Black participants, the SDI+CAC+EAT model demonstrated the highest discrimination (C-index 0.62) and significantly improved reclassification compared with CAC alone (NRI) of 0.29 (95% CI 0.15-0.56; p < 0.0007). In contrast, the SDI+CAC+EAT model showed no improvement in discrimination when compared to CAC alone (C-index 0.67 v. 0.67) in the White cohort. CONCLUSION: In adults with T2DM, EAT may serve as a complimentary imaging marker when combined with CAC scores to provide incremental prognostic information or refine risk characterization.

title: Heart failure and atrial fibrillation prediction from non-gated chest CT scans using AI-based cardiac chamber volumetry: an AI-CVD study within the multi-ethnic study of atherosclerosis (MESA).
abstract: BACKGROUND: We previously demonstrated that AI-derived cardiac chamber volumetry in ECG-gated CT scans predicts atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (HF). Since most chest CTs are non-gated, and the American Heart Association recently highlighted their value for opportunistic cardiovascular risk assessment using AI-based coronary artery calcium scoring, we extended this concept to evaluate whether AI-derived chamber volumetry from non-gated CTs can reliably predict HF and AF.s. METHODS: We compared AI-derived chamber volumetry from non-gated and ECG-gated chest CTs in 2053 Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) Exam 5 participants using mean and standard-deviation of absolute differences, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), and Cohen's κ. Variability between paired ECG-gated scans was determined by analyzing scans acquired 2 min apart in 5749 MESA Exam 1 participants. Predictive performance for incident HF and AF was compared using cumulative incidence curves, age- and sex-adjusted C-indices, and non-inferiority testing (δ=0.05). RESULTS: Non-gated scans demonstrated excellent overall agreement with ECG-gated scans, with comparable performance for detecting cardiac chamber enlargement (98.8-99.2%, κ=0.76-0.84), relative to agreement observed between paired ECG-gated scans (98.6-98.9%, κ=0.72-0.77). Cumulative incidence curves for HF and AF stratified by quartiles showed substantial overlap. Age- and sex-adjusted C-indices were comparable for left atrial volume (0.75 vs 0.74, CONCLUSION: AI-based evaluation of non-gated chest CT may provide reliable cardiac chamber volumetry and cardiovascular outcome prediction, enabling opportunistic screening for HF and AF risk.

title: Absence of significant coronary artery disease does not eliminate smoking-related cardiovascular risk: insights from the PROMISE trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although the relationship between smoking and cardiovascular events is well established, it remains uncertain whether the outcomes of noninvasive testing (NIT) influence this relationship and how systemic biomarkers may aid risk stratification in patients presenting with chest pain. METHODS: This study included PROMISE participants with stable chest pain and available smoking status (current, ever, or never) and NIT results (Positive NIT: ≥70% coronary stenosis on CT angiography or inducible ischemia on stress testing). Smoking was associated with systemic biomarkers (e.g., hsCRP, IL-6, MMP-9), NIT results, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina), using regression and mediation models adjusted for traditional cardiovascular risk factors (median follow-up 24.4 months). RESULTS: Among 9100 individuals (mean age 61±8 years; 53% female), 51% were ever-smokers, including 18% current smokers. Smoking was independently associated with MACE, with positive NIT mediating this relationship (current: 16%; ever: 12%, CONCLUSIONS: Negative NIT does not reduce smoking-associated MACE risk in patients with stable chest pain. Particularly, current smoking confers substantial residual cardiovascular risk, potentially mediated by MMP-9-related matrix remodeling not captured by standard testing, supporting aggressive smoking cessation irrespective of NIT results.

title: External validation of artificial intelligence-guided electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) in detecting asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: AIM: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (LVD) represents a key and frequently under-recognized stage in the heart failure (HF) continuum. Early identification enables targeted prevention and timely initiation of evidence-based therapies. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) may provide a scalable alternative to imaging for LVD detection. This systematic review synthesized evidence from exclusively externally validated AI-ECG studies evaluating the detection of asymptomatic LVD, with symptomatic HF cohorts included to contextualize the evidence base across the HF continuum. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted on 8th September 2025. The main output was the pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). RESULTS: From 3,587 records, 12 asymptomatic and 30 symptomatic studies were identified (538,735 participants). In asymptomatic cohorts evaluating left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD), AI-ECG demonstrated promising but heterogeneous discriminatory performance (I²>85%) with pooled AUROCs of 0.87 (95% CI 0.75-0.99) for LVEF ≤35%, 0.93 (95% CI 0.88-0.97) for LVEF ≤40%, and 0.89 (95% CI 0.85-0.97) for LVEF ≤50%. Symptomatic cohorts showed AUROCs of 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.92), 0.90 (95% CI 0.88-0.92), and 0.85 (95% CI 0.83-0.86) respectively. Asymptomatic left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (LVDD) demonstrated moderate performance (AUROC 0.76, 95% CI 0.66-0.86) with no externally validated symptomatic LVDD studies identified. Small-study effects were detected exclusively in asymptomatic cohorts. CONCLUSIONS: Discriminatory performance of AI-ECG in asymptomatic LVSD is broadly comparable to symptomatic populations. High risk of bias driven by prolonged ECG-to-echocardiogram intervals reflecting real-world logistical constraints necessitate cautious interpretation of results and further prospective validation.

title: Utility of a coronary artery disease polygenic risk score in a low-risk primary prevention cohort.
abstract: AIMS: To evaluate whether a coronary artery disease (CAD) polygenic risk score (PRS) identifies clinically low-risk individuals at elevated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk. METHODS: We conducted a longitudinal cohort study within the UK Biobank including adults aged 40-74 years, free of ASCVD and diabetes, not on lipid-lowering therapy, and with baseline LDL <190 mg/dL. Participants were enrolled from 2006 to 2010 and followed through 2021. Ten-year ASCVD risk was estimated using pooled cohort equations. A CAD PRS derived from 2.3 million genome-wide variants was categorized as top 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and bottom 50%. Lipoprotein(a) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were similarly stratified. The primary endpoint was a composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or cardiovascular death. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for 10-year ASCVD events, and net reclassification improvement (NRI) was assessed at 5% and 7.5% risk thresholds. RESULTS: Among 266,917 low-risk individuals (median age 54; 38% male), ASCVD risk increased substantially across higher PRS strata. Compared with the bottom 50%, individuals in the top 50% had more than double the risk (aHR 2.48), the top 20% had over triple the risk (aHR 3.71), and the top 5% and 1% had 6-fold (aHR 6.31) and 9-fold (aHR 9.73) higher risks, respectively (all p < 0.0001). Adding PRS improved model discrimination (AUC 0.76 vs 0.72) and reclassified 12% of low-risk individuals upward-over tenfold more than Lp(a) or hs-CRP. CONCLUSION: In primary prevention, a CAD PRS identifies individuals with markedly higher ASCVD risk despite low clinical risk estimates and may merit consideration among ASCVD risk enhancers.

title: Genetically determined very low lipoprotein(a) is not associated with type 2 diabetes and glycemic traits.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)] is an independent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factor, with levels largely determined by variation in the OBJECTIVES: Estimate associations between very low Lp(a), inferred by METHODS: A multi-population study of European, Hispanic/Latino, and South Asian populations from five cohort studies was assembled. Effects of the null allele rs41272114 (CC, wild-type; T, null allele) on type 2 diabetes and glycemic biomarkers (fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c), triglyceride-to-high-density lipoprotein ratio, and HOMA-IR) were estimated using multivariable-adjusted and cohort-specific linear or logistic regression models that were combined using inverse variance meta-analysis. RESULTS: Of n=519,892 participants, the T null allele was common (n=49,841 CT and n=2,039 TT) and n=38,320 participants had type 2 diabetes (prevalence range: 4.7, 29.5%). Participants with the TT genotype had a median Lp(a) ranging 1.5-1.9 nmol/L compared to median Lp(a) ranging 15.8-30.0 nmol/L in participants with the CC genotype. We did not observe increased odds of type 2 diabetes by rs412722114 genotype (OR CONCLUSIONS: In a large multi-population study with high burdens of type 2 diabetes, life-long very low Lp(a) did not increase type 2 diabetes risk.

title: Whole heart atherosclerosis volume and risk for major adverse cardiovascular events across the clinical likelihood for obstructive CAD; the CONFIRM2 study.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The totality of atherosclerosis from the coronary tree can be measured with quantitative coronary CT and is increasingly being recognized as important marker for future cardiovascular events. We evaluated the risk and absolute event rates of plaque volume staging systems and provided analyses according to the clinical likelihood of obstructive CAD. METHODS: CONFIRM2 is an ongoing, global, multicenter, observational registry that included patients with clinically indicated coronary CT angiography and follow-up for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Patients without cardiac symptoms and prior CAD were excluded. Atherosclerosis was quantified across all coronary segments by AI-QCT. Total plaque volume (TPV) was categorized into non-calcified plaque (NCPV, HU <350) and calcified (HU>350). The primary end point was the incidence rate of MACE over at 4 years and included all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, congestive heart failure, late revascularizations (occurring >90 days post index CCTA), and hospitalization for unstable angina. Secondary endpoint included Death, MI, and stroke. The prognostic value of TPV and NCPV was evaluated across the pretest likelihood according to the ESC Risk Factor Weighted Likelihood (ESC RF-CL). RESULTS: A total of 6061 patients (mean age 58.6 ± 12.1 years, 48.6% male) were included and the mean follow-up duration was: 4.4 ± 1.8 years. According to the ESC RF-CL for obstructive CAD, patients were classified as very-low, low, and moderate risk in 36.0%, 43.0%, and 22.0%, and obstructive CAD rates were 6.8%, 15.7%. and 28.2, respectively. Within the total cohort, TPV >0-250, 250-750, and >750 mm CONCLUSION: Among a large cohort of symptomatic patients evaluated by coronary CT angiography, the burden of atherosclerosis by AI-QCT was the main driver for cardiovascular events. Absolute event rates were consistently higher by each plaque volume stage, and consistent across the clinical likelihood subgroups for obstructive CAD. While quantitative atherosclerosis was present in the majority of patients, risk increased significantly from 250 mm

title: Association of reproductive factors with acute myocardial infarction in young women: A VIRGO and NHANES case-control study.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Young women with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) often present with distinct risk profiles compared with older women and men, but the role of reproductive factors remains poorly understood. This study examines associations of reproductive factors with AMI in young women. METHODS: We conducted a case-control study of 1561 women aged 18-55 years with AMI from VIRGO and age-matched controls from NHANES. A wide range of reproductive factors were evaluated. Conditional logistic regression estimated odds ratios for AMI, sequentially adjusted for race/ethnicity, socioeconomic variables, and traditional risk factors. Stratified analyses were performed by menopausal status. RESULTS: Early menarche (<11 years; OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56-2.73), menopause (OR 1.82, 95% CI 1.50-2.22), gestational diabetes (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.23-2.19), birth control pills use for 1-5 years (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.36-2.05), and ever use of female hormones (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.62-2.46) were associated with higher odds of AMI, while first live birth at ≥30 years (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.36-0.69), breastfeeding ≥1 month (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.38-0.56), and current contraceptive use (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32-0.76) were associated with lower odds. After adjustment for traditional risk factors, birth control pills use for 1-5 years (OR 1.71, 95% CI 1.25-2.34) and female hormone use (OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.28-2.38) remained significantly associated. Associations varied by menopausal status. CONCLUSION: Reproductive factors are associated with early-onset AMI in young women. Recognition of reproductive history may inform prevention strategies in young women.

title: Heterogeneity in proteomic risk factors for coronary heart disease by sex and menopause status.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet current prediction tools do not fully capture sex differences in risk. Menopause further modifies women's risk of CHD, but underlying molecular mechanisms are not well understood. Proteomic profiling may provide new insights into these mechanisms. METHODS: We analyzed 4,877 SomaScan™-based plasma proteins in 10,034 Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) participants. Using linear regression, we identified sex- and menopause-related differences in circulating protein concentrations. We performed pathway enrichment analyses to capture underlying biological mechanisms. To evaluate the associations between proteins and incident CHD and differences by sex or menopause status, we applied Cox regression. Finally, we used LASSO regression to identify proteins that improve CHD risk prediction beyond an established clinical model. RESULTS: We observed significant differences in circulating proteins by sex and menopausal status, including early changes during the menopausal transition. We found protein associations with incident CHD differed markedly by sex and menopausal stage: eight proteins were associated with CHD in men, compared with 54 in women, and six and 17 proteins in peri‑ and postmenopausal women, respectively. In risk prediction analyses, adding sex-specific protein panels improved CHD prediction (ΔC-statistic=0.05 in men and 0.03 in women), with similar improvement across menopausal stages. CONCLUSIONS: Proteomic profiles underlying CHD risk differ substantially by sex and menopausal stage. These findings suggest potential biological heterogeneity in CHD and support the study of sex- and menopause-related differences in underlying mechanisms.

title: Use of an AI metabolomics score to predict cardiovascular risk among patients with Psoriasis in the MGB and UK Biobanks.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Systemic inflammation in psoriasis accelerates atherosclerosis and confers excess cardiovascular risk that is not fully captured by traditional clinical predictors. Metabolomic profiling may identify disease-specific metabolic signatures associated with cardiovascular events and enhance risk prediction beyond conventional factors. OBJECTIVES: To determine whether plasma metabolomic profiling improves cardiovascular risk prediction in patients with psoriasis and to develop and externally validate an artificial intelligence-driven metabolomic risk score (MetaPsoAI) for incident cardiovascular events. METHODS: We analyzed 1086 individuals with psoriasis and no prior coronary artery disease from the Mass General Brigham (MGB) Biobank who underwent nuclear magnetic resonance-based quantification of 168 circulating metabolites. Associations between metabolites and incident all-cause death or myocardial infarction were assessed. An extreme gradient boosting algorithm was used to develop MetaPsoAI for prediction of myocardial infarction or stroke. External validation was performed in the UK Biobank ( RESULTS: Multiple metabolites, particularly HDL subfractions and amino acid metabolites, were associated with cardiovascular outcomes. MetaPsoAI stratified risk across quartiles, with individuals in the highest quartile demonstrating a 3.6-fold higher risk of myocardial infarction or stroke in the MGB cohort. In the UK Biobank, the highest quartile was associated with a 1.9-fold increased risk among psoriasis patients, with stronger effect sizes compared with non-psoriasis controls. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the potential of AI-driven metabolomics to refine cardiovascular risk prediction in immune-mediated diseases and enable precision prevention strategies for patients with psoriasis.

title: Delayed elective nodal irradiation in head-and-neck cancer radiotherapy reduces acute lymphocyte damage, lymphopenia, and modulates immune signatures.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Elective nodal irradiation (ENI) for locally advanced head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-HNSCC) contributes to hematotoxicity and may impair radiotherapy-immunotherapy synergy. We investigated whether delayed ENI, using an upfront boost to gross disease and involved nodes followed by standard ENI, reduces radiation-induced lymphocyte DNA damage and lymphopenia (RIL) while modulating peripheral immune signaling compared with standard ENI. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty-eight LA-HNSCC patients assigned for adjuvant ( RESULTS: Delayed ENI reduced initial planning target volume and whole-body dose by 9.9- and 4.4-fold (both CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that delaying elective nodal irradiation may help preserve circulating immune cells during radiotherapy and provide a mechanistic rationale for future prospective studies evaluating whether this strategy can enhance radiotherapy-immunotherapy synergy in LA-HNSCC.

title: HeatRisk and air quality risk recommendations: A narrative review and action algorithm for the care of people at risk for and living with cardiovascular disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide and is influenced by climate change-related exposures. Non-optimal temperature and poor air quality exposure worsens cardiovascular outcomes, particularly for individuals with preexisting cardiovascular disease. While the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Environmental Protection Agency recommend tools like HeatRisk and Air Quality Index, there is limited guidance for implementation in those with preexisting cardiovascular disease. This narrative review addresses this gap. METHODS: A literature review was conducted using PubMed, supplemented by snowballing to identify studies published between 2000 and 2025 related to the cardiovascular effects of temperature extremes and poor air quality. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were prioritized, particularly those that addressed risk factors such as pregnancy, obesity, geography, and socioeconomic status. Additional context was obtained from public health agencies including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Environmental Protection Agency, and National Weather Service. The pathophysiology and risk factors were then applied to the existing guidance, recommendations, and algorithms of these agencies. RESULTS: Non-optimal temperature and poor air quality are associated with an increased mortality and morbidity in patients with heart failure, ischemic heart disease, stroke, and myocardial infarction. These exposures also worsen cardiometabolic risk factors such as hypertension, insulin resistance, and atherosclerosis. High-risk subgroups included women, older adults, residents of temperate climates, individuals taking certain medications, pregnant individuals, and those with socioeconomic or occupational exposure risk. CONCLUSIONS: Patients with cardiovascular disease should be counseled on the risks associated with non-optimal temperature and poor air quality. It is recommended that high risk individuals (risk score greater than or equal to three) should take precautions at HeatRisk Level 1 (Yellow) and/or the AQI ≥ 50, while moderate risk individuals (score less than two) should consider precautions at HeatRisk Level 2 (Orange) and/or AQI ≥ 100 (Central Illustration).

title: Feasibility and potential benefits of daily online adaptive radiotherapy for head and neck cancer without margin reduction using an RTT-only workflow.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Online adaptive radiotherapy (oART) may improve head and neck cancer (HNC) treatment, where anatomical changes during radiotherapy (RT) are common. However, oART is resource-intensive and clinical data are limited. We conducted a prospective feasibility trial implementating an RT technologist (RTT)-led workflow to evaluate dosimetric outcomes, workflow strategies, and intrafractional motion in daily oART. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Ten patients receiving curatively intended oART (33-34 fractions) using standard PTV margins were included (NCT: 07506902). For each fraction, a scheduled plan (original plan recalculated on daily anatomy) and an adapted plan (reoptimized to daily anatomy) were generated, and the preferred plan was delivered. Target coverage (PTV1 V95%), mean dose (D RESULTS: A total of 322 adaptive session were completed. The median treatment time was 29.9 min. The adapted plan was selected in 78% of fractions. oART improved target coverage in 76% of fractions. D CONCLUSION: Daily oART for HNC is feasible with improvements in target coverage but modest and inconsistent OAR sparing.

title: Evaluation of the nutritional and digestive impact of irradiation in nasopharyngeal cancers: the French multicenter retrospective DRAKAR study.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Radiotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancers is associated with frequent digestive and nutritional toxicities, weight loss (WL), and malnutrition, criteria of poor tolerance and poor prognosis. The primary objective of DRAKAR was to evaluate the effect of prophylactic enteral nutrition (EN) on weight change (WC) during, at the end of, and after radiotherapy in patients with nasopharyngeal cancer from a non-endemic French population. MATERIALS AND METHODS: DRAKAR is a retrospective, multicenter study conducted in five French centers. Patients received radiotherapy with curative intent, with or without concurrent chemotherapy, for primary nasopharyngeal cancer between 2015 and 2024. The primary endpoint was WC according to nutritional support modality at the end of radiotherapy. Secondary endpoints included rates of moderate and severe malnutrition (5% or 10% WL in one month for moderate and severe malnutrition), grade ≥ 3 toxicities, dosimetry parameters (volumes, particles), use and duration of EN and parenteral nutrition, prolonged radiotherapy due to treatment interruption, hospitalizations, and overall survival. RESULTS: Among the 124 patients analyzed (59.7% UCNT, 40.3% squamous cell carcinoma), mean WC was -6.45% at the end of radiotherapy. At one month, 35.5% were malnourished, compared with 8% before treatment. EN was used in 55.6% of patients, including 16.1% prophylactically. Prophylactic EN was associated with stabilization of WC after treatment. Regarding malnutrition, age < 55 years was the only significant clinical factor associated with its occurrence, with no association found with toxicity, dosimetric, or therapeutic characteristics.
