CONCLUSION: In patients treated for nasopharyngeal cancer, prophylactic EN was associated with post-treatment WC stabilization but not with hospitalization or improved survival. Given potential confounding by indication, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, and prospective studies are needed to confirm the benefit and optimal indications for prophylactic EN.

title: Advancing brachytherapy: The GEC-ESTRO strategic vision.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Brachytherapy (BT) is an established and highly effective component of modern radiotherapy, offering a favourable therapeutic ratio for several tumor sites. Despite technological advances and strong clinical evidence, its use has declined in some countries. The GEC-ESTRO Committee of ESTRO therefore initiated a strategic process to promote and strengthen BT within European radiation oncology. METHODS: The BT Think Tank (B3T), established in September 2024, comprised eight European BT specialists supported by ESTRO staff. Through structured discussions, topic prioritisation and feedback from the GEC-ESTRO Committee, key barriers to the wider implementation and promotion of BT were identified and strategic actions developed. RESULTS: Five major areas were identified: communication, scientific research, training, reimbursement and technical development. Communication was ranked as the highest priority. Particular emphasis was placed on improving communication with patients, referring and non-BT specialists, other scientific societies, industry and healthcare stakeholders. To implement this strategy, five communication work packages were established addressing patients, other scientific societies, social media, industry, and healthcare administration/insurance. Specific milestones and activities were defined through 2028. In parallel, ongoing initiatives address clinical research, including prospective trials and real-world evidence, structured training programmes such as the EuroBT Fellowship, reimbursement analyses, and evaluation of technical developments. CONCLUSION: The GEC-ESTRO strategic vision aims to reposition BT as an integral component of personalised, value-based radiotherapy within the overarching strategy of ESTRO. Strengthening communication and interdisciplinary collaboration, alongside continued investment in research, training and advocacy, is essential to ensure that BT is considered as a treatment option for appropriate patients and remains accessible in the future.

title: Association of mitochondrial copy number and heteroplasmy with cognitive function in the ACCORD trial.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in cognitive decline and dementia, but the relationship between mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy and copy number with cognitive function remains poorly understood. We aimed to study these associations among individuals with diabetes who face elevated risk for mitochondrial dysfunction and cognitive impairment. We analyzed data from 954 participants (mean age 62.8 years, 52.1% female) in the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes Blood Pressure trial. Mitochondrial heteroplasmy burden was quantified using the modified mitochondrial local constraint score sum (mMSS) from whole mitochondrial genome sequencing. Mitochondrial copy number was measured using quantitative PCR. Cognitive function was assessed using the Digit Symbol Substitution Test for processing speed and the Mini-Mental State Examination for global cognition at baseline, 20 months, and 40 months. Our primary regression models adjusted for demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and mitochondrial haplogroup. Participants with mMSS > 0.5 had significantly worse processing speed at baseline compared to those with mMSS= 0 (β=-4.94 points, 95% CI: -9.44, -0.43) after adjustment. Higher mitochondrial copy number was associated with better processing speed at baseline among men (β=1.67 per SD, 95% CI: 0.31, 3.03). Neither heteroplasmy nor copy number was significantly associated with global cognition or with longitudinal cognitive decline. Higher mitochondrial heteroplasmy burden and lower copy number (in men) were associated with worse processing speed but not global cognition or cognitive decline. Mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to domain-specific cognitive impairment in diabetes, with potential sex differences. Further research is needed to elucidate mechanisms and evaluate mitochondrial measures in brain tissue.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis of Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is a collection of methods to quantify gene expression in situ. In cancer research, these technologies offer researchers new avenues for studying intra-tumoral heterogeneity and interactions between tumor cells and their tumor microenvironment (TME) in a spatially resolved fashion. In Ewing sarcoma research, a few pioneering spatial transcriptomics studies have begun to characterize the spatial landscape of tumors in unprecedented detail. In this chapter, we provide a series of tutorials on tissue selection, sample preparation, panel design and analysis pipeline for Ewing sarcoma spatial transcriptomic data.

title: Leveraging Single-Cell RNA Sequencing to Characterize Murine Ewing Sarcoma Xenografts.
abstract: High-quality single-cell analyses critically depend on standardized tissue processing workflows that preserve cellular integrity and minimize dissociation-induced artifacts. Here, we describe a robust and reproducible protocol for the isolation, cryopreservation, and downstream processing of single-cell suspensions from Ewing sarcoma (EwS) tumors, including the bioinformatic analyses and tools to interrogate the resulting data. The workflow is optimized for strict cold-chain handling and employs a cold-active Bacillus licheniformis protease-based digestion strategy coupled with gentle mechanical dissociation to reduce cellular stress and transcriptional perturbations. Tumor tissue is processed under controlled low-temperature conditions, followed by filtration, cryopreservation, and storage compatible with single-cell RNA sequencing and multi-omics applications. This protocol supports high cell viability, preserves physiologically relevant transcriptional states, and provides a reproducible framework for downstream computational single-cell analyses of EwS tumor samples. The computational pipeline performs ambient RNA correction, barcode calling, doublet detection, SCTransform normalization, PCA/UMAP and clustering, and cell type annotation via the AUCell module scoring combined with multi-reference Azimuth label transfer. Cluster labels are validated by differential expression-based marker enrichment, and integrated embeddings are used for visualization. This end-to-end workflow ensures high cell viability, preserves physiologically relevant transcriptional states, and provides a reproducible framework for downstream computational single-cell analyses of EwS tumor samples.

title: Epigenetic Analysis in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant tumor of bone and soft tissue, primarily driven by the EWSR1::FLI1 fusion oncogene. This chimeric transcription factor reprograms gene regulatory networks by aberrantly activating enhancers and binding to GGAA microsatellite repeats, thereby reshaping the epigenetic landscape of tumor cells. Given that chromatin accessibility governs transcription factor binding and downstream gene expression, high-resolution mapping of protein-DNA interactions is critical for elucidating the epigenetic mechanisms underlying Ewing sarcoma pathogenesis. This chapter presents a comprehensive, end-to-end framework for the analysis of Cleavage Under Targets and Release Using Nuclease (CUT&RUN) data, with a focus on profiling EWSR1::FLI1 binding sites and their associated chromatin features. We detail each step of the analytical pipeline, including raw FASTQ processing, alignment, quality control, peak calling, and downstream analyses. To demonstrate the workflow, both publicly available data and data generated in our laboratory are used. Overall, this chapter serves as a practical and detailed methodological guide for researchers aiming to dissect the epigenetic architecture of Ewing sarcoma using CUT&RUN technology.

title: Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Followed by Next-Generation Sequencing in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) is a widely used technique to study the distribution of transcription factors, histones, posttranslational modifications, or other DNA-associated proteins across the genome. This methodology is based on the isolation of DNA fragments bound by the protein of interest using specific antibodies. Computational analysis of sequencing libraries derived from the isolated DNA fragments will delineate genome-wide maps of protein-DNA interactions. ChIP-seq profiling of EWSR1::FLI1 oncogene has enormously contributed to the understanding of gene reprogramming in Ewing Sarcoma (EwS) defining EWSR1::FLI1 bound sites, the GGAA microsatellites, and the direct targets regulated by the translocation. ChIP-seq methodology has also provided novel biological insight into the proteins contributing to chromatin remodeling as well as the histone modification patterns associated with EWSR1::FLI1 genome-wide. This protocol provides detailed steps on how to conduct quantitative ChIP-seq experiments in EwS cell lines incorporating spike-in controls along with the core of a bioinformatic framework to analyze the results and infer novel biological knowledge.

title: A Practical Compass to Biological Digital Resources and Omics Integration in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a paradigmatic fusion-driven cancer in which oncogenic FET::ETS transcription factor fusions orchestrate complex regulatory, epigenomic, transcriptional, and proteomic programs. Despite extensive molecular profiling, biological insight, and translational progress, EwS are strongly shaped by how data are generated, structured, and shared across heterogeneous initiatives. Fragmented cohorts, uneven molecular depth, and limited longitudinal sampling influence both integrative analyses and systems-level interpretation. This chapter is organized around this structural reality. It first maps the current EwS data landscape, including patient-derived and preclinical omics datasets, profiling initiatives, repositories, and annotation resources, highlighting how their design and governance define the biological questions that can be addressed. It then synthesizes key biological insights derived from genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and single-cell studies, with an emphasis on regulatory logic, transcriptional plasticity, and context-dependent vulnerabilities revealed through integrative analyses. Particular attention is given to the predominance of preclinical approaches in systems-level EwS biology, reflecting the experimental resolution required to interrogate regulatory mechanisms that remain largely inaccessible in most patient cohorts. Finally, the chapter examines how these observations motivate a shift from opportunistic data aggregation toward intentionally designed EwS-specific data ecosystems. It discusses the technical, ethical, and organizational requirements for longitudinal, multilayer profiling and federated data access, and argues that such infrastructures are necessary to support reproducible systems biology and therapeutic translation in EwS.

title: A Drosophila Study Model for EWS::FLI1-Induced Molecular Pathways.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is an aggressive, human-exclusive tumor typically driven by the EWS::FLI1 fusion protein. The paucity of genetically modified animal models hinders in vivo functional studies of this oncogene. Here, we describe the generation of transgenic Drosophila lines expressing different levels of human EWS::FLI1 and fluorescent reporters of conversion of quiescent GGAA-repeat microsatellites (GGAAμSats) into neoenhancers. We also describe experimental setups to test EWS::FLI1 activity, and to carry out genetic and chemical screens. Altogether, the collection of transgenic Drosophila lines described here permits quantifiable, spatial, and temporal control of EWS::FLI1 expression in vivo, thus offering new experimental tools to investigate the molecular pathways affected by varying levels of EWS::FLI1 in different cell lineages within a living organism. This platform is a versatile resource for hypothesis-driven research, as well as high-content genetic and chemical screening that may facilitate the identification of potential therapeutic targets and lead compounds.

title: Chorioallantoic Membrane Assay to Assess Primary and Metastatic Tumor Growth in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: The chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) assay provides a rapid, cost-effective, and ethically advantageous in vivo model to investigate tumor growth, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis. The CAM of the developing chicken embryo forms a highly vascularized and naturally immunodeficient environment that supports the implantation and proliferation of human or murine cells without the need for immunosuppression. This chapter presents a detailed and standardized protocol for performing tumor xenografts and metastasis analyses on the CAM, including optimized conditions for egg handling, embryo viability, and aseptic manipulation. The described workflow covers the complete experimental timeline-from preincubation of fertilized eggs, windowing and antimicrobial treatment, cell inoculation and drug administration, to harvesting and molecular downstream analysis of Ewing sarcoma samples. The method allows for quantitative assessment of tumor size, vascularization, and metastatic spread through the extra-embryonal membrane and can be combined with histological-, molecular-, or imaging-based readouts. The CAM assay serves as a valuable intermediate system between in vitro culture and mammalian xenografts, enabling reproducible, fast, and physiologically relevant studies on cancer cell behavior and therapeutic response.

title: Using Zebrafish Larvae as a Xenotransplantation Model to Study Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Tumor models allowing for the in vivo investigation of molecular mechanisms driving tumor progression and metastasis are important to develop novel strategies for cancer treatment. Unfortunately, for Ewing sarcoma, no adequate genetic animal models are currently available, although there is progress in zebrafish. Nevertheless, mouse xenotransplantation models are the state-of-the-art to model Ewing sarcoma in vivo. Here, we describe an alternative Ewing sarcoma xenotransplantation model in embryonic and larval zebrafish. This zebrafish model offers live imaging and easy compound testing opportunities, thereby complementing mouse xenotransplantation models. In this chapter, we provide a detailed protocol for how to xenograft Ewing sarcoma cells into 2-day-old zebrafish and how xenografted zebrafish can be imaged and analyzed over consecutive days to study tumor proliferation and response to small compound treatment.

title: Ewing Sarcoma PDX Models.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EWS) is a rare malignant pediatric tumor, and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) could represent a possibility to increase the number of available models to study this disease. Compared to cell-derived xenografts (CDX), PDXs are reported to recapitulate better tumor microenvironment, heterogeneity, genetic, and epigenetic features. They are considered reliable models due to their superior predictive value when comparing preclinical efficacy and treatment response in patients. In this chapter, we extensively describe a method for generating EWS PDX models, along with their validation and molecular characterization.

title: Orthotopic Implants in Mice.
abstract: By directly implanting patient tumor cells into mice in a relevant location, we can mimic both the biology and tumor microenvironment of the original tumor. Here, we describe the process of generating an orthotopic patient-derived xenograft model by injecting a single cell suspension of Ewing sarcoma cells into the femur of a recipient mouse.

title: Metastasis Assessment in Ewing Sarcoma Using Orthotopic Xenografts.
abstract: Orthotopic models are based on the implantation of tumor cells directly into the organ of origin, which allows interaction between the cells and the surrounding host tissues. Here, we describe a modified version of an orthotopic model that closely recapitulates the steps required for metastasis development in Ewing sarcoma: tumor cells are injected into the calf muscles of the mouse, and once the tumor reaches a certain volume, the muscles containing the tumor are surgically resected. This procedure involves a nonaggressive surgery of the muscle, which allows for the survival of the mouse during a period of time that is long enough to enable the development of distant metastases. This spreading of tumor cells to metastatic sites in other organs takes place by a physiological mechanism similar to what occurs in human Ewing sarcoma. We have adapted this protocol for the implantation of tumor fragments derived from human patients into the calf muscle of mice. This method enables the analysis of human tumor growth of human tumors in mice and the evaluation of potential therapies in a highly specific manner.

title: Tumor Growth Analysis of Ewing Sarcoma Cell Lines Using Subcutaneous Xenografts in Mice.
abstract: Subcutaneous murine xenograft models are one of the most commonly used in vivo experimental methods in the cancer research field. Due to the lack of syngenic animal models for Ewing sarcoma, subcutaneous murine xenograft models currently offer the simplest way to investigate antineoplastic effects of therapeutics or biological functions of target genes in vivo. In this chapter, we describe in detail a widely used procedure for subcutaneous injection in mice, focusing on the specific characteristics of Ewing sarcoma cell lines.

title: Genetically Engineered Mouse Model in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Modeling Ewing sarcoma is challenging, since overexpression of EWSR1::FLI1 induces apoptosis and is not sufficient for tumor induction. It is therefore important to obtain the cell-of-origin of Ewing sarcoma that is tolerant of EWSR1::FLI1 expression. Here we describe the generation of the EWSR1::FLI1-expressing mouse model for Ewing sarcoma by selecting embryonic chondrogenic progenitor, eSZ cells that contain Ewing sarcoma precursors.

title: 3D Ewing Sarcoma Modeling for Metabolic Studies.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) in vitro models provide a physiologically relevant platform that more accurately recapitulates tissue architecture, cell-cell and cell-extracellular matrix interactions, and the physical microenvironment than traditional two-dimensional (2D) cultures. In particular, these models reproduce metabolic gradients, including oxygen and nutrient availability, enabling more precise investigations of cellular metabolism. This chapter describes two methods to grow Ewing sarcoma cell lines as 3D spheroids using physiological media, as well as the collection of spheroids in bulk or individually for different downstream analyses, particularly those related to metabolic studies.

title: Post-Translational Regulation Using Degrons in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: The EWSR1::FLI1 (EF1) chimeric transcription factor is pathognomonic in Ewing Sarcoma (EwS) and is often the sole oncogenic mutation harbored by EwS tumors. Disrupting the function of EF1 to study its role in tumor biology using small molecules has proven challenging. Here, we describe complementary strategies to incorporate inducible protein degrons into the endogenous EWSR1::FLI1 locus in patient-derived EwS cells. These systems enable precise control over the timing and level of EF1 protein abundance as well as downstream functional analyses.

title: Genetic and Epigenetic Manipulation Using CRISPR Techniques in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: CRISPR-based technologies have transformed experimental biology by enabling precise, efficient, and programmable manipulation of the genome and epigenome. This chapter provides a comprehensive and practical guide to genetic and epigenetic editing using CRISPR technology, with a particular focus on applications in Ewing sarcoma cell models. We describe strategies for CRISPR-mediated gene knockout (CRISPR KO) via nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), precise gene knock-in (CRISPR KI) through homology-directed repair (HDR), and reversible transcriptional modulation using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and CRISPR activation (CRISPRa). We emphasize the use of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery of Cas9 and single guide RNAs, which offers improved editing efficiency, reduced off-target activity, and enhanced safety compared to plasmid-based approaches. Detailed protocols are provided for guide RNA design, RNP assembly, electroporation-based delivery, single-cell cloning, and molecular validation of edited clones. In addition, we outline best practices for HDR template design, discuss strategies to improve KI efficiency, and address common challenges such as polyploidy, variable editing rates, and DNA-mediated cytotoxicity. For CRISPRi and CRISPRa applications, we describe plasmid-based systems employing catalytically inactive Cas9 fused to transcriptional repressors or activators, enabling potentially tunable and reversible control of endogenous gene expression. Throughout the chapter, practical advice, troubleshooting tips, and critical considerations are included to facilitate successful implementation across diverse experimental settings. Collectively, this chapter serves as a detailed methodological resource for researchers aiming to employ CRISPR-based engineering for functional studies.

title: Analysis of Colony Formation Capacity in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Colony formation assays enable an assessment of the cells' ability to grow in colonies under in vitro conditions. Following the seeding and an incubation period, the cell colonies are stained using a crystal violet staining solution, and the resulting colonies are imaged and assessed. This method can be leveraged to investigate the effect of genetic modifications or the application of different drug compounds on colony growth. Here, we describe a protocol applied to Ewing sarcoma cell lines, as well as possible modifications.

title: Analysis of Migration and Invasion in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Metastasis is a complex, well-orchestrated process, which includes migration from the primary tumor and invasion into secondary locations as main features. In Ewing sarcoma, metastasis is the main determinant of malignancy, with ~30% of patients presenting with metastatic disease at diagnosis. Therefore, analyzing migration and invasion in different experimental settings in vitro is key to understanding this disease. Among the variety of possible techniques to study migration, this chapter describes the methods of wound healing (migration in 2D) and transwell (migration through a porous membrane in response to a given stimulus). Additionally, this chapter includes a variation of the transwell protocol that allows the analysis of cell invasion through a gel matrix in response to a stimulus.

title: Application of Resazurin and ATP Detection Cell Viability Assays for Drug Sensitivity Screening in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Developing new effective therapies for Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is crucial to improving patient outcomes, especially in cases of metastatic or recurrent disease. In various stages of drug discovery and especially early preclinical development, cell viability assays are often used to assess the antitumor efficacy of compounds of interest. Here, we review and provide guidelines for the application of resazurin- and ATP-based cell viability assays for drug sensitivity screening in EwS. This includes dose-response drug screening to identify metrics such as potency and to compare sensitivity across multiple cell lines, as well as high-throughput drug screening to identify hit compounds that inhibit EwS cells.

title: Proliferation Assessment by Trypan Blue Exclusion in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Cell proliferation is broadly defined as the process that increases cell number, essentially depending on a balance among cell cycle progression, cell division, cell death, and cellular senescence. Deregulation of cell proliferation is a key feature of cancer cells, making assessment of proliferation a central methodological issue in cancer research. Especially in Ewing sarcoma (EwS), which exhibits a high proliferative capacity, experimental assessment of proliferation in preclinical research plays an important role. Among the available methods, Trypan blue exclusion is described here as a robust, easy-to-perform, and cost-effective method for assessing cell proliferation in an experimental setting.

title: Analysis of Regulatory DNA Sequences by Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assays in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Reporter gene assays allow for examining the influence of regulatory DNA sequences on the transcription of target genes. In Ewing sarcoma, the study of these DNA sequences is paramount because the disease's main driver mutation is a fusion transcription factor that binds distinct motifs compared with its wild-type constituents. Here, we describe a workflow for analyzing the enhancer activity of regulatory DNA sequences using transfection-based dual-luciferase reporter assays in Ewing sarcoma cell lines. To this end, we provide a protocol for cloning genomic sequences into a firefly luciferase-containing plasmid, co-transfecting Ewing sarcoma cells with firefly reporter and Renilla control plasmids and measuring luciferase expression by luminescence. The entire procedure can be completed in 14 days.

title: Ewing Sarcoma-Specific (Re)Expression Models.
abstract: Gene expression and knockdown systems are powerful tools for studying the function of single genes and their interactions within pathways. Plasmid transfection and viral transduction have revolutionized the field of molecular biology and paved the way for various gene-editing strategies such as TALEN, Zink finger nucleases, and ultimately CRISPR. In Ewing sarcoma (EwS), almost as many genes are repressed by the expression of EWSR1-FLI1 as are upregulated by the fusion oncogene. Here, we present a useful point-by-point protocol for generating transgene expression systems in EwS that allow (conditional) re-expression of a gene of interest. We provide an extensive instruction on molecular cloning, plasmid generation, viral transduction, and expression validation. Finally, we address common problems and highlight potential pitfalls that can be easily avoided with thoughtful guidance.

title: Molecular Approaches to Diagnosis in Ewing Sarcoma: Targeted RNA Sequencing.
abstract: Molecular testing for pathognomonic gene fusions is mandatory for the diagnosis of small round cell tumors. In particular, in Ewing sarcoma, the identification of specific chimeric fusion genes is critical to distinguish it from other histologically similar subtypes. As the clinical relevance of gene fusion detection continues to grow, many laboratories have adopted targeted next-generation sequencing approaches to overcome the limitations of conventional singleplex assays. We were among the early adopters of targeted RNA sequencing using anchored multiplex PCR, a technique that enables the simultaneous detection of multiple fusion transcripts with prior knowledge of only one fusion partner. In this chapter, we provide a detailed description of our workflow, including recommendations for nucleic acid extraction, library preparation, sequencing, and interpretation of gene fusion results.

title: Molecular Approaches to Diagnosis in Ewing Sarcoma: RT-PCR.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive, poorly differentiated solid tumor that most commonly arises in the bone and soft tissues of adolescents and young adults. It is defined by recurrent chromosomal translocations generating oncogenic fusions between a FET family gene-most frequently EWSR1-and ETS family transcription factors, most commonly FLI1 or ERG. The EWSR1::FLI1 fusion represents the predominant oncogenic event, occurring in approximately 85% of cases, while EWSR1::ERG is identified in about 10% of tumors; the remaining cases harbor rarer fusion variants. Although additional recurrent genetic alterations have been described, they occur at a lower frequency. Consequently, the identification of gene fusions remains central to the diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma. This chapter describes an RT-PCR-based assay that allows for sensitive and specific detection of known fusion genes, enabling rapid and accurate genetic confirmation of Ewing sarcoma diagnosis.

title: Molecular Approaches to Diagnosis in Ewing Sarcoma: Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH).
abstract: The differential diagnosis of small round cell tumors of bone and soft tissue (SRCT) crucially relies on the synoptic evaluation of morphology, immunohistochemical patterns, and molecular features. Although the implementation of broad RNA sequencing in diagnostic molecular pathology routines has substantially changed the standards for molecular confirmation of diagnoses, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections remains an essential tool for rapid molecular corroboration of diagnoses, which is essentially required for therapeutic decisions. We discuss the major FISH approaches currently employed in diagnostic molecular pathology, addressing classic Ewing sarcoma and differential diagnoses among SRCT, which often cannot be sufficiently ruled out by immunohistochemistry. This chapter will address technical issues, particularly strategies and pitfalls in interpreting FISH patterns.

title: (Immuno-)Histological Analysis of Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: The diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma requires integrating information from numerous techniques, some of which are very sophisticated. However, the first steps of the diagnostic process are crucial to achieve the maximum possible diagnostic performance. In this chapter, we will review how to handle the diagnostic specimen from its collection, how to prepare it for diagnosis, how to make a complete pathology report, and provide guidance for the reasonable use of immunohistochemical techniques in this malignancy.

title: Untargeted Metabolite Screening of Ewing Sarcoma Cells and Tissues with Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).
abstract: Altered metabolism is a hallmark of cancer, where rewiring of cellular metabolic pathways is essential for tumor initiation, support of rapid proliferation, and adaptation to new metastatic sites. Metabolomics has emerged as a powerful tool to comprehensively characterize the metabolome of cancers and holds promise to transform understanding of how oncogenes can drive tumorigenesis and metastasis, identify cancer-specific metabolic dependencies, and provide novel therapeutic opportunities. This chapter describes methods to extract metabolites from Ewing sarcoma (EwS) cells grown in 2D or 3D cultures and from EwS mouse xenograft tissues, and to broadly analyze these compounds using an untargeted metabolite profiling approach. This methodology is likely applicable to a wide range of cultured cell and tissue types.

title: Tissue Preservation and FFPE Samples: Optimized Nucleic Acids Isolation in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Different methods have been described for the preservation of biopsy or resection samples. In routine pathology, the cheapest and most used method is fixation of samples in formalin and embedding in paraffin (FFPE samples). This method preserves tissue samples for a very long time and is suitable for several specialized techniques, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and immunohistochemistry, the latter being the most frequent and often the only additional method used for the establishment of the final diagnosis. However, in light of the growing need for next-generation sequencing and microarray technologies that are often very helpful to establish and/or confirm diagnoses in the field of pediatric sarcoma (including Ewing sarcoma), preservation of high-quality and quantity of nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) is desirable. Herein, we describe how to ideally preserve samples, as well as how to proceed to isolate nucleic acids for successful subsequent molecular assays with a special focus on Ewing sarcoma samples.

title: Western Blot Analysis in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: A Western blot is an experimental method used to analyze protein expression. In Ewing sarcoma, as in many other diseases, Western blot provides information about the level of protein expression in different cell conditions, in comparison with other tissues or upon induced molecular changes. Based on the specific pattern of protein expression of the tissue, as well as on the characteristics of the protein of interest, the antibodies and protocol of Western blot may be modified according to different specifications. Here, we describe some of these peculiarities in the framework of the Ewing sarcoma field.

title: Germline Variation and Somatic Alterations in Ewing Sarcoma.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a rare bone or soft tissue tumor that occurs early in life, suggesting genetic variation is likely a major contributor to EwS risk. To date, genetic investigations have identified key somatic mutations and germline variants of importance for EwS risk. While substantial progress has been made in uncovering the genetic etiology of EwS, considerable gaps in knowledge remain. Herein, we provide a summary of methodological approaches for future genomic investigations of EwS. We anticipate that this recommended analytical framework for germline and somatic investigations, along with genomic data from growing EwS case series, will aid in accelerating new genomic discoveries in EwS and expand knowledge of the genetic architecture of this aggressive sarcoma.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics and Metabolomics.
abstract: Analytical chemistry, and particularly mass spectrometry (MS), plays a central role in the molecular characterization of biological and environmental samples. These data are essential for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying healthy aging, disease onset and progression, and the complex chemical composition of environmental systems. Over the past decades, MS has undergone unprecedented technological advancements. Current state-of-the-art instruments enable the thorough characterization of deep proteomes at the single-cell level and achieve comprehensive coverage of metabolites and proteins. Innovations such as new mass analyzers (e.g., the Astral mass analyzer) and the integration of multidimensional separation techniques (e.g., trapped/cyclic ion mobility) have significantly expanded the analytical capabilities of the instrumentation. However, the volume and complexity of the data produced by these advanced platforms pose major challenges for interpretation and integration. To address these challenges, machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) methods are emerging as indispensable tools in analytical chemistry. These approaches, particularly deep learning, generative AI, and large language models, offer powerful solutions for analyzing, integrating, and interpreting the high-dimensional, heterogeneous datasets generated in proteomics and metabolomics research. This chapter first introduces the fundamental principles and operational mechanisms of commonly used AI/ML methods in analytical chemistry. These include regression models, decision trees, k-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, neural networks, deep learning architectures, and generative AI. The first part of the chapter also discusses key requirements for model training, including the need for sufficient sample and molecular coverage, and evaluates how data noise affects model performance and reliability. In the second part, a series of representative applications are presented, demonstrating the use of AI/ML for peptide and metabolite observability prediction, retention time and ion mobility prediction, fragment ion spectrum generation, de novo compound identification, and improvements in compound quantification and scoring of identifications. The chapter concludes with practical recommendations for applying AI/ML approaches in proteomics and metabolomics studies, and for their integration into bioinformatics pipelines to enhance data interpretation, reproducibility, and scientific discovery.

title: Pathway and Kinase Analysis in Proteomics and Phosphoproteomics with rROMA.
abstract: Advances in data acquisition tools, particularly mass spectrometry-based techniques, have made high-throughput methods like proteomics and phosphoproteomics increasingly accessible. However, the volume and complexity of the data require specialized computational tools for analysis and interpretation to extract meaningful insights. Here, we describe the use of rROMA software to analyze pathway and kinase activity in proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets. rROMA is an open-source package available on Github at: www.github.com/sysbio-curie/rROMA . As a case study, we applied rROMA to breast cancer samples from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC), which provides precise relative quantification of proteins and phosphorylation sites of a large cohort of breast cancer samples through Tandem mass tag (TMT)-based mass spectrometry. These analyses illustrate how to identify active pathways and kinase-driven mechanisms potentially involved in disease subtypes, along with their associated proteins and phosphosites.

title: Integrated Analysis of Posttranslational Modifications and Total Proteome: Methods for Distinguishing Abundance from Usage Changes.
abstract: Posttranslational modifications (PTMs), particularly phosphorylation, regulate protein function at substoichiometric levels, making their quantitative analysis technically challenging. A critical limitation in PTM studies is distinguishing between changes in modification abundance due to altered protein expression versus genuine changes in modification stoichiometry (the fraction of protein molecules that are modified). This chapter presents a comprehensive workflow integrating Tandem-Mass-Tag (TMT)-based quantitative proteomics with specialized computational analysis to distinguish differential PTM abundance (DPA) from differential PTM usage (DPU) using the prolfqua, prolfquapp, and prophosqua R packages. The workflow introduces a robust statistical framework for integrated PTM-protein analysis; comprehensive visualization tools, including N-terminus to C-terminus (N-to-C) plots for protein-centric PTM mapping and sequence motif analysis for kinase prediction. This integrated approach enables researchers to identify actual signaling changes in PTM studies, prioritize functionally relevant modification sites, understand pathway-level regulation in disease contexts, and generate robust datasets suitable for publication in high-impact journals.

title: Benchmarking deep learning-based reconstruction methods for photoacoustic computed tomography with clinically relevant synthetic datasets.
abstract: SIGNIFICANCE: Deep learning (DL)-based image reconstruction methods for photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) have developed rapidly in recent years. However, most existing methods have not employed standardized datasets, and their evaluations rely on traditional image quality (IQ) metrics that may lack clinical relevance. The absence of a standardized framework for clinically meaningful IQ assessment hinders fair comparison and raises concerns about the reproducibility and reliability of reported advancements in PACT. AIM: A benchmarking framework is proposed that provides open-source, anatomically plausible synthetic datasets and evaluation strategies for DL-based acoustic inversion methods in PACT. APPROACH: The datasets each include over 10,000 two-dimensional (2D) stochastic breast objects with clinically relevant lesions and paired measurements at varying modeling complexity. The evaluation strategies incorporate both traditional and task-based IQ measures to assess fidelity and clinical utility. A preliminary benchmarking study is conducted to demonstrate the framework's utility by comparing DL-based and physics-based reconstruction methods. RESULTS: The benchmarking study demonstrated that the proposed framework enabled comprehensive, quantitative comparisons of reconstruction performance and revealed important limitations in certain DL-based methods. Although they performed well according to traditional IQ measures, they often failed to accurately recover lesions. This highlights the inadequacy of traditional metrics and motivates the need for task-based assessments. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed benchmarking framework enables systematic comparisons of DL-based acoustic inversion methods for 2D PACT. By integrating clinically relevant synthetic datasets with rigorous evaluation protocols, it enables reproducible, objective assessments and facilitates method development and system optimization in PACT.

title: A unified and domain-robust framework enables controllable multimodal brain MRI synthesis.
abstract: Multimodal magnetic resonance image (MRI) synthesis can shorten examinations, reduce cost, and furnish contrasts that are difficult or impossible to acquire, but current models remain hard to control and brittle to shifts in scanner, protocol, and pathology. We present a unified, domain-robust synthesis framework that modulates spatial carriers with physically informed, domain-stable statistical guidance. A balanced soft-plus-hard conditioning scheme enables a single model to perform diverse contrast mapping, while allowing smooth user adjustment of contrast weighting. Evaluated on 991 test subjects from five public and three private datasets spanning cross-dataset, cross-protocol, and related cross-pathology scenarios, our approach matches or outperforms advanced baselines for both in-domain synthesis and inference under unseen domains without finetuning. Clinician Turing test and downstream glioma grading experiments further indicate realistic appearance, preservation of pathology-relevant information, and potential practical value under clinically heterogeneous conditions. By jointly delivering controllability, robustness to real-world variability, and physically informed, domain-stable guidance within one architecture, this work advances MRI synthesis toward deployment in heterogeneous clinical environments.

title: Streamline pathology foundation model by cross-magnification distillation.
abstract: Foundation models (FM) have transformed computational pathology but remain computationally prohibitive for clinical deployment due to their massive parameter counts and high-magnification processing requirements. Here, we introduce XMAG, a lightweight FM developed through cross-magnification distillation that transfers knowledge from a state-of-the-art 20x magnification teacher to an efficient 5x magnification student architecture. XMAG employs a compact backbone and operates entirely at 5x, requiring 11.3 times fewer patches per whole slide image (WSI) compared to existing approaches. Our novel distillation framework incorporates dual-level knowledge transfer, aligning both global image representations and local spatial features across magnification levels through carefully designed projection heads and spatial token mapping. We trained XMAG on 3.49 million images curated from publicly available datasets and evaluated performance across seven clinically relevant histopathology analysis tasks spanning multiple cancer types. Across four WSI-level classification tasks, XMAG achieved an average AUC within 1% of substantially larger foundation models while delivering up to 29.5-fold faster encoder-level processing, corresponding to an encoder throughput of 8.8 WSIs per minute in a controlled patch-encoding benchmark. We also found that performance differences remained task-dependent, with larger gaps observed for fine-grained tasks such as ISUP grading and patch-level phenotyping. We further explore end-to-end XMAG training as a direction for task-specific adaptation of the compact model. These results suggest that cross-magnification distillation is a promising strategy for developing efficient low-magnification pathology foundation models and may support more scalable WSI analysis in computationally constrained research and translational settings.

title: Effects of rectal retractor use on dosimetric parameters, treatment-related adverse events, and clinical outcomes of cervical cancer brachytherapy: A retrospective tertiary-centre study.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: We assessed whether rectal retractor use was associated with dose parameters, organ volumes, treatment-related adverse events, and oncological outcomes in patients who underwent cervical cancer brachytherapy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 148 patients treated with intracavitary brachytherapy between June 2020 and June 2025. Patients treated with and without a rectal retractor were compared regarding dosimetric, volumetric, adverse event, and survival outcomes. Adverse events were graded via RTOG criteria. Cumulative dose parameters were calculated using EQD2. ROC analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed to evaluate factors associated with grade ≥ 2 adverse events. RESULTS: Rectal retractor use occurred in 58 patients (39.2%). Baseline demographic characteristics and tumour size were comparable between groups, although rectal retractor use differed according to applicator type. Rectal retractor use was associated with lower rectal D2cc (no retractor vs. retractor: 65.70 Gy vs. 60.79 Gy, CONCLUSIONS: Rectal retractor use was associated with rectal dose sparing and lower odds of grade ≥ 2 vaginal adverse events without compromising target coverage. However, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because rectal retractor placement was not randomised and was influenced by applicator compatibility.

title: HyM
abstract: Survival prediction is a critical task in cancer prognosis assessment. In recent years, deep learning methods based on multimodal data have been widely applied to this task. However, existing studies primarily focus on the integration of whole slide images (WSIs) and genomic data, while the utilization of intratumoral microbiome information remains limited. Meanwhile, current approaches face two limitations: (i) they fail to fully exploit the multi-magnification information of WSIs, limiting the joint representation learning across different resolutions; and (ii) high-magnification pathological features tend to dominate, leading to modality imbalance between pathology and intratumoral microbiome data. In this study, we propose HyM

title: Mind the Gap: A survey of chronic wound datasets, methods, and clinical translation.
abstract: Chronic wounds, including diabetic foot ulcers, venous ulcers, arterial ulcers and pressure ulcers, represent a growing global health challenge with significant morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. Advancements in medical image analysis have shown promise in automating wound detection, segmentation, and measurement. However, translation of these research advances into clinical practice through mobile applications remains limited. This survey presents systematic analysis of the relationship between chronic wound datasets, deep learning methods, and mobile wound assessment applications. We analyse 20 datasets (14 public/partially public and 6 private), including iterative challenge datasets that extend image pool through synthetic augmentation. We review 50 deep learning methods spanning encoder-decoder architectures to self-supervised learning approaches, and evaluate 13 mobile applications (commercially deployed clinical tools and research prototypes). We examine the alignment between publicly available chronic wound datasets and the documented capabilities of mobile wound assessment mobile applications. Our analysis reveals critical misalignments between datasets, algorithms and mobile applications. Existing datasets are typically designed for algorithm benchmarking rather than clinical deployment, and therefore lack standardised acquisition protocols, scale calibration markers, depth information, detailed tissue composition annotations, and representation of diverse skin types. Conversely, reviewed mobile applications report capabilities, including automatic tissue classification, calibrated wound measurement and depth estimation, for which publicly available data is insufficient. We map documented dataset characteristics to capabilities reported among reviewed mobile applications, identify unresolved methodological challenges, and outline key priorities for the field. Based on these insights, we propose actionable recommendations for developing clinically translatable computer vision system for wound assessment. This survey is intended to serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to bridge the gap between medical imaging methodologies and practical demands of clinical wound care.

title: Lower Urinary Tract Complications After Radiotherapy for Prostate Cancer: An Organ-Based Clinical Framework.
abstract: PURPOSE: This study presents a structured narrative review of lower urinary tract (LUT) complications following prostate cancer (PCa) radiotherapy and proposes an organ-based clinical framework for their evaluation and management. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, including studies published between January 2000 and December 2025 and supplemented by seminal studies in radiation biology and reconstructive urology. Search terms included prostate cancer, radiotherapy, radiation cystitis, bladder dysfunction, urethral stricture, bladder neck contracture, urinary incontinence, urinary fistulae, ureteral stricture, and post-radiotherapy outlet surgery. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively and organized into organ-specific domains. RESULTS: Radiation-induced LUT complications include radiation cystitis, detrusor overactivity and impaired compliance associated with bladder fibrosis, urethral and bladder neck strictures, sphincteric insufficiency with urinary incontinence, urinary fistulae, and ureteral strictures. These conditions frequently coexist because of the multifocal and progressive nature of radiation injury. Management is challenging because tissue hypovascularity, fibrosis, and impaired healing increase the risks of recurrence, infection, erosion, and fistula formation. Evaluation requires integrated anatomical and functional assessment, including cystoscopy, urodynamics, and imaging when indicated. Conservative, endoscopic, and reconstructive treatments should be individualized according to bladder function, outlet status, tissue quality, and patient characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: LUT complications after prostate radiotherapy represent a complex and evolving spectrum of injury. An organ-based framework facilitates identification of the primary site of dysfunction, recognition of associated abnormalities, and appropriate staged management. As PCa survivorship increases, multidisciplinary care will be essential to optimize outcomes and reduce long-term morbidity.

title: Establishment of In Vivo Mouse Models to Study Salmonella-Induced Chronic Infection and Gastrointestinal Cancer.
abstract: Salmonella infection increases the risk of chronic diseases, e.g., inflammatory bowel diseases, colon cancer, and gallbladder cancer. However, the mechanisms leading to the development of these conditions are still not completely understood. Here, we describe the methods to establish in vivo mouse models to study Salmonella-induced chronic infection and colon cancer. These models will allow us to investigate the initiation and progression of diseases.

title: Esc2 and Rad57 contribute to RNA polymerase II distribution at highly transcribed genes.
abstract: Transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) must be tightly regulated to maintain gene expression homeostasis, yet how Pol II occupancy is shaped at highly active genes remains incompletely understood. Here, we examine the relationship between the homologous recombination-related factors Esc2 and Rad57 and Pol II distribution in budding yeast. Genome-wide analyses reveal that Esc2 and Rad57 preferentially associate with the gene bodies of highly transcribed housekeeping genes and are linked to a chromatin context that also includes the protein phosphatase Sit4 and its cofactor Rrd1. Loss of Esc2 and Rad57 is accompanied by increased Pol II occupancy within gene bodies, whereas the effect on steady-state RNA abundance is selective rather than uniform. title: Towards scalable cancer prognosis by aligning semi-supervised learning with survival modeling.
abstract: Prognostic assessment via whole-slide images (WSIs) is a key task in computational pathology. However, the development of robust predictive models is often bottlenecked by the scarcity of survival-annotated data, given the longitudinal nature of clinical follow-up. Despite its potential, semi-supervised learning (SSL) remains underexplored in this field. Existing SSL methods, primarily designed for natural image classification, rely on the assumption of marginally independent categories, which makes them difficult to adapt to the high-dimensional complexity of WSIs and the temporal continuity inherent in survival outcomes. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel semi-supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) framework tailored for WSI-based prognosis. Specifically, we first introduce a morphology-perceived MIL network (Morph-MIL) that jointly models tissue composition and global semantic representations. To maintain a stable reference, a dynamic memory bank is employed to encapsulate the multi-level representations of labeled samples (censored & uncensored). Furthermore, we develop a pseudo-labeling strategy that assigns discrete labels containing temporal relationships to annotation-free data by aligning their features with the memory bank through bin-wise aggregation. Comprehensive evaluation establishes the superiority of the proposed framework, while extensive ablation analyses and visualizations confirm its efficacy in prognostic prediction and biological interpretation. Consequently, this study offers a scalable solution for WSI survival modeling in scenarios with limited annotations. The code is available at: https://github.com/yihuangswust-alt/SSL-Morph_MIL.

title: Assays to Study SUMOylation of RNA Helicase DHX9.
abstract: RNA helicase DHX9 is a multi-functional protein governing transcriptional modulation, RNA processing, R-loop balance, and genome stability. SUMOylation is a post-translational modification that adds a critical regulatory layer to protein function by diversifying subcellular localization, stability, enzymatic activity, and protein-protein interactions. This protocol describes a basic but detailed approach for the analysis of DHX9 SUMOylation. We demonstrate that accurate site identification, specifically at Lysine 120 (K120), is the prerequisite for defining the molecular mechanism of this modification. Identifying the K120 acceptor site enables the generation of specific mutants to dissect how DHX9 SUMOylation orchestrates the protein interactions necessary to preserve genomic integrity. Furthermore, this protocol provides a versatile framework for characterizing the SUMOylation of other RNA helicases involved in RNA regulation.

title: Fast Analysis of RNA from Transcription and Rho-Dependent Termination Assays Using Automated Capillary Electrophoresis.
abstract: Conventional analysis of RNA products synthesized by bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in in vitro transcription assays relies on radioactive labeling, followed by separation of labeled RNAs by denaturing urea-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). This approach provides excellent resolution across a wide range of RNA lengths (from 2 nt to several hundred nucleotides), but the use of radioisotopes requires specialized facilities, strict waste-disposal procedures, and is often restricted. To circumvent these limitations, we adapted a standard in vitro transcription assay for use with the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer capillary electrophoresis system. Here, we describe the application of this method to analyze run-off transcription by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) RNAP and its transcription termination products generated by the Mtb Rho factor. We demonstrate that RNAs produced in in vitro transcription reactions can be detected and quantified without radioactive labeling, simplifying and accelerating the workflow. Although capillary electrophoresis lacks the single-nucleotide resolution of denaturing urea-PAGE, it provides a practical alternative that is compatible with any laboratory environment. This protocol is broadly applicable for analyzing RNA products generated by in vitro transcription with any bacterial RNAP, in the presence or absence of RNA remodeling factors such as the Rho protein.

title: Probing the Role of RNA Helicases in Modulating Stress Granules, RNA Localization, and P-Body Docking.
abstract: Stress granules (SGs) are cytoplasmic, membrane-less ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules that form in response to cellular stress following the inhibition of translation initiation. Their assembly, composition, and crosstalk with processing bodies (P-bodies) are mediated by protein-protein, RNA-protein, and RNA-RNA interactions. DEAD/DEAH-box RNA helicases are key regulators of stress granules. Here, we present standardized protocols for (i) immunofluorescence of stress granule and P-body scaffold proteins and helicases, (ii) single-molecule RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (smRNA FISH), and (iii) quantitative image analysis using Imaris software, including single-cell and nuclear segmentation, stress granule and P-body surface rendering, docking interaction analysis, and RNA spot detection.

title: In Vitro Assay of Bacterial RNA Helicases Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation.
abstract: DEAD-box RNA helicases are widespread ATP-driven enzymes that reshape RNA structures and RNA-protein complexes during many steps of RNA metabolism. In bacteria, DEAD-box RNA helicases support cellular growth and responses to stress by contributing to ribosome biogenesis, RNA degradation, and translation initiation. Growing evidence indicates that several DEAD-box RNA helicases can also form liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates that concentrate RNA and partner proteins. This behavior adds a new layer of control to RNA regulation, although the molecular factors that promote or tune liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) are still unclear. Here, we describe an in vitro microscopy-based assay to characterize the LLPS behavior of bacterial DEAD-box RNA helicases. The protocol includes step-by-step procedures to evaluate condensate formation, salt sensitivity and dissolution, RNA dependency and specificity, and ATP effects. We further provide detailed instructions for quantitative analysis of microscope images, including size and assessment of protein enrichment within condensates. Altogether, this workflow enables systematic dissection of key physicochemical parameters governing DEAD-box helicase LLPS and provides a standardised framework for comparative studies across bacterial DEAD-box proteins or variants.

title: Using Magnetic Tweezers to Unravel the Mechanism of the G-Quadruplex Binding and Unwinding Activities of DHX36 Helicase.
abstract: Single-molecule manipulation methods are useful techniques to probe the interactions of proteins and nucleic acid structures. Here, we describe magnetic tweezers-based single-molecule investigation of the binding of helicases to G-quadruplex structures and their ATP-dependent unwinding activity, using DHX36 (also known as RHAU and G4R1) helicase and both DNA and RNA G-quadruplex structures as examples. We specifically emphasize the principle and method to probe the interactions between DHX36 and the DNA G-quadruplex in different intermediate states during an ATPase cycle of DHX36, based on detecting the DHX36-induced changes in the lifetime of the DNA and RNA G-quadruplex under tension. The principle of the measurement can be broadly extended to the studies of other DNA or RNA G-quadruplex helicases.

title: Using Solution NMR to Study the RNA-Binding Properties and Molecular Mechanisms of the RNA Helicase DDX3X.
abstract: DEAD-box RNA helicases (DDXs) are a family of enzymes that participate in nearly all aspects of cellular RNA metabolism by remodeling RNA structures. Among them, DDX3X plays key roles in diverse physiological processes, including the translational regulation of gene expression, and its malfunction is frequently associated with the onset of disease. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms of DDX3X, solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy provides unique insights into its RNA-binding properties, dynamic behavior, and intermolecular interactions, complementing conventional structural approaches aimed at determining high-resolution atomic models. In this chapter, we present a detailed protocol for preparing isotopically labeled proteins for NMR analysis, using the minimal functional core region of DDX3X as an example. The presented protocol enables the production of large amounts of purified protein, which can also be adapted for other in vitro structural and biochemical experiments used to characterize helicase function.

title: Mapping of RNA Helicase Dynamics by HDX-MS.
abstract: RNA helicases are RNA-binding enzymes that remodel RNA structures and ribonucleoprotein complexes through regulated conformational changes. Their RecA-like catalytic cores cooperate with auxiliary domains, many of which contain flexible or partially disordered regions whose rearrangements are difficult to characterize using static structural methods. Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) overcomes this limitation by examining protein conformation in solution, providing peptide-resolved information on local stability, dynamics, and ligand-dependent structural changes. In this chapter, we describe a bottom-up HDX-MS workflow for mapping RNA helicase-RNA interactions and conformational dynamics, using the Pseudomonas aeruginosa DExH-box helicase HrpB as a model. The protocol covers sample preparation, deuterium labeling, quenching, protein digestion, peptide separation, MS acquisition, and data analysis. We outline practical guidelines for optimizing peptide coverage, preserving deuterium labeling throughout the workflow, and obtaining quantitative comparisons between the apo and RNA-bound states. The chapter provides a framework for using HDX-MS to identify where RNA, nucleotides, and small-molecule inhibitors bind, to characterize the conformational changes they induce, and to connect these dynamics to the RNA helicase mechanism of action.

title: Insights into the Activities of Helicases from Thermococcales: The Cases of the RNA Helicase ASH-Ski2, the DNA Helicase Hel308, and the RNA:DNA Helicase Lhr2.
abstract: Helicases are versatile enzymes. Superfamily 2 (SF2) is the largest and most diverse group of helicases. SF2 helicases are involved in fundamental processes dealing with nucleic acids in the three domains of life and can be specific to DNA, RNA, or DNA:RNA hybrids. They are known to catalyze unwinding reactions in vitro or disrupt duplexes in vivo. More recently, it has emerged that they can also anneal single strands to form duplexes. Here, we describe biochemical assays used to investigate the activities of the Ski2-like helicases ASH-Ski2 and Hel308, as well as the Lhr-like helicase Lhr2 from Thermococcales, an order of hyperthermophilic archaea. Unwinding and strand-annealing assays using a range of substrates revealed that they are RNA-, DNA-, or RNA:DNA-specific helicases, respectively.

title: Unwinding Quadruplex Structures with RNA Helicases.
abstract: The interaction of RNA helicases and non-canonical G-rich quadruplex (G4) structures in all aspects of RNA metabolism is a rapidly expanding field of study. Both cellular and viral RNA helicases dynamically maintain and disrupt G4 RNA structures in multiple compartments of the cell for efficient trafficking, transcription, splicing, translation, and, in the case of viral RNA genomes, replication. The conserved domains shared by diverse members of the helicase superfamilies for RNA binding and ATP-mediated duplex unwinding suggest that quadruplex disruption is a critical activity for many helicases. To probe the conditions and required energetics for quadruplex interaction and unwinding, robust in vitro assays are needed. To overcome the challenges of studying G4 unwinding under optimized conditions, we have adapted standard helicase unwinding assays to closely examine quadruplex dynamics. This chapter provides detailed protocols for describing the capacity for RNA helicases to remodel G4 structures.

title: Measuring the Affinity of the Bacterial Rho Helicase for RNA Using a Double-Membrane Slot-Blot Filtration Assay.
abstract: Quantitating the binding of oligomeric proteins to RNA is not always straightforward with standard biochemical approaches such as the Electrophoretic Mobility Shift Assay (EMSA). Here, we detail how we use a simple, alternative approach based on sample filtering through stacked nitrocellulose and positively charged nylon membranes to measure the affinity of the hexameric transcription termination factor Rho for RNA. The method is quick and easy to implement and should be useful to study the interaction of other RNA-binding proteins using RNA substrates bearing a

title: In Vitro RNA-Protein Binding Assays to Identify RNA Helicases for U snRNA Nuclear Export.
abstract: RNA helicases play a critical role in RNA biogenesis by modulating RNA-protein interactions in an ATP-dependent manner. Although many RNA helicases function by unwinding RNA secondary structures or displacing proteins from RNA, a subset of RNA helicases facilitates the loading of their interacting proteins onto RNA. Here, I present an in vitro method for analyzing the formation of the uridine-rich small nuclear RNA (U snRNA) export complex, for which the involvement of RNA helicases was previously unknown. This method can be used to determine whether complex formation is ATP-dependent and identify RNA helicases that facilitate the loading of the U snRNA export factor onto RNA. This approach can identify RNA helicases involved in protein loading onto various RNA-protein complexes.

title: Global Identification of RNA Helicase Substrates from Large Nucleic Acid Sequence Libraries Using Helicase-SELEX.
abstract: In many instances, the RNA sequences or motifs that constitute optimal or physiological substrates for a given RNA helicase are unknown or difficult to identify. In this chapter, we describe a recent methodology, Helicase-induced Selection of Ligands by Exponential enrichment (Helicase-SELEX), which allows the global identification of catalytically productive substrates for a RNA helicase from a large library of nucleic acid sequences. We explain how to use the methodology to identify Rut (Rho utilization) sequences in bacterial genomes, which likely encode the physiological RNA targets used by the transcription termination factor Rho helicase. We discuss the advantages and limitations of the Helicase-SELEX methodology, including which categories of helicases are, in principle, the most amenable to Helicase-SELEX analysis.

title: Using Cross-Linking and ImmunoPrecipitation (CLIP) to Identify Targets and Specificity Determinants of the YTHDC2 Helicase.
abstract: The 3'→5' RNA helicase YTHDC2 is a posttranscriptional regulator of gene expression in reproductive cells, where it is essential for the progression of meiosis. But a detailed understanding of its molecular mechanism is currently lacking. Cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) followed by high-throughput sequencing is a well-established method for transcriptome-wide identification of the positions of protein-RNA interactions and has played a critical role in studies of RNA-binding proteins. In this chapter, we present an optimized protocol for performing YTHDC2 CLIP in mouse testes to identify YTHDC2-RNA interactions, from harvesting testis tissue, through isolation of cross-linked YTHDC2-RNA complexes, to the preparation of sequencing libraries.

title: A Workflow for Identifying Helicase-Dependent RNA Structural Changes in Transcriptional Termination: From DMS Sequencing Analysis to Reporter Assay-Based Validation.
abstract: RNA helicases are essential in all aspects of RNA biology where they remodel RNA secondary structures and RNA-protein (RNP) complexes. DEAD-box RNA helicases represent the largest RNA helicase family in eukaryotes. However, identification of biological targets for such helicases has been challenging. Structural probing methods involving treatment of cells with reagents such as SHAPE or dimethyl sulfate (DMS) coupled with sequencing (seq) have now enabled identification of RNA targets for these enzymes. These methods require extensive bioinformatics to derive RNA secondary structure predictions from readouts. Predicted targets must then be experimentally validated to determine the biological relevance of a given RNA structural rearrangement. We have utilized DMS-seq to identify RNA secondary structure targets of the DEAD-box RNA helicase Dbp2 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and further linked their remodeling to transcription termination efficiency. This chapter outlines a data-analysis workflow for extracting DMS reactivity signals from short-read sequencing data and identifying regions of differential RNA structure between wild-type and dbp2Δ strains. It also describes a reporter assay-based method to assess if predicted structural rearrangements are linked to transcription termination efficiency. These approaches establish an integrated computational framework followed by experimental validation for elucidating helicase-dependent RNA structural dynamics and their functional interplay.

title: Tools for Experimental and Computational Genome-Wide Analysis of the Function of DDX5 and DDX17 Helicases in RNA Processing.
abstract: DEAD-box helicases DDX5 and DDX17 play a key role in regulating gene expression and RNA processing in mammalian cells. In particular, they are involved in alternative splicing and in the 3' end processing of nascent transcripts associated with the termination of transcription. In this chapter, we present experimental protocols and computational tools that altogether enable the prediction and validation of various types of changes in the neuroblastoma cell transcriptome upon the depletion of both helicases. This includes protocols for monitoring variations in alternative splicing, readthrough transcription resulting from defects in 3' end processing, and the production of fusion transcripts associated with readthrough.

title: Prolonging breath-hold duration in radiotherapy using cognitive engagement.
abstract: PURPOSE/OBJECTIVE: Deep inspiration breath-hold (DIBH) is commonly used in breast cancer radiotherapy to decrease cardiac radiation exposure. Using high-flow nasal oxygen and hyperventilation we achieved voluntary long deep inspiration breath-holds (L-DIBH) exceeding 3 min. Substantial variability in L-DIBH duration among subjects remains, not explained by physical factors. We investigated how cognitive engagement could impact the L-DIBH. MATERIALS/METHODS: Thirty-six subjects (20 volunteers and 16 patients) each performed 12 L-DIBHs over 4 sessions. During half of the sessions, they were instructed to focus on a mental exercise. Each L-DIBH was preceded by a validated hyperventilation and oxygenation protocol. The baseline DIBH time was calculated by taking the mean of 3 DIBHs. Linear Mixed Models were used to analyse the impact of this exercise on L-DIBH duration. RESULTS: All 36 subjects completed the four sessions, yielding 432 L-DIBHs, including 216 with mental exercises. The mean L-DIBH duration was 152 s overall and 126 s in the patient subgroup. Volunteers outperformed patients. L-DIBH duration increased both within and between sessions, demonstrating a learning effect. The mental exercise increased mean duration by 14,9 s in the full cohort and by 19,0 s among patients. Its relative benefit compared with the between-session learning effect was greatest in those with poorer baseline DIBH times. CONCLUSION: A simple mental exercise effectively increases voluntary L-DIBH duration, providing a particularly meaningful benefit for participants with lower baseline DIBH times.

title: Type 2 diabetes-associated gut microbial composition and short chain fatty acids differ across the epidemiologic transition in African origin populations.
abstract: The gut microbiota and microbially produced short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are increasingly linked to type 2 diabetes (T2D), particularly in the context of dietary transitions from fiber-rich to more ultra-processed foods. Data in African origin populations are lacking. We examined the cross-sectional relationships between the gut microbiota, SCFAs, and T2D by performing amplicon sequencing and targeted metabolomics from fecal samples and measuring fasting glucose, insulin, and C-peptide in 1505 African origin middle-aged adults from Ghana, South Africa, Jamaica, Seychelles, and the US. Microbial diversity and SCFAs were highest among Ghanaian and lowest among US participants. T2D was associated with lower microbial diversity, but not when stratifying by site. Differential abundance analysis (adjusted for site, sex, BMI, and age) identified microbes associated with T2D:

title: Influence of gut microbiota on chronic lymphocytic leukemia development and aggressiveness.
abstract: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is highly heterogeneous both clinically and biologically. Although genetic factors have been identified, several lines of evidence suggest a role for environmental factors in disease onset and progression. Diet is a recognized risk factor for various diseases, including cancer, with an established relationship to the composition of the gut microbiome. Taking advantage of the widely used Eμ-

title: Fabrication of AuNS and o-ABA mediated electrochemical immunosensor for voltammetric detection of osteocalcin.
abstract: A novel electrochemical immunosensor was designed for the ultrasensitive and selective detection of osteocalcin (OCN) normally overexpressed by osteosarcoma cells. The immunosensing was performed using anti-osteocalcin antibody (anti-OCN) modified probe along with a bio-conjugate, where the probe was fabricated by the covalent assembly of anti-OCN with conducting polymer poly-o-aminobenzoic acid (poly-o-ABA) formed over a layer of gold nanostar (AuNS). Bio-conjugates comprised of hydrazine (Hyd) along with anti-OCN was covalently immobilized on citrate capped AuNPs, reveals the immunoreaction at the sensor probe, where Hyd in bioconjugate was used to reduce hydrogen peroxide for direct signal amplification. The osteocalcin was quantitively analyzed using cyclic voltammetry. This technique exhibited an excellent diagnosis tool for the sensitive and selective detection of OCN, and shows broad dynamic range 2 to 64 ng mL

title: Mast cell degranulation damages glymphatic system via PKC/p38MAPK/AQP4 to exacerbate hydrocephalus post intraventricular hemorrhage.
abstract: Hydrocephalus following intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) remains a serious neurological condition with limited treatment options beyond invasive surgical interventions, underscoring the urgent need to elucidate its underlying mechanisms. Emerging evidence implicates impaired glymphatic system function in the pathogenesis of hydrocephalus, particularly through dysregulation of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) expression in astrocytes, which is essential for cerebral waste clearance and fluid homeostasis. Since mast cells are key mediators of neuroinflammation and can influence cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics, this study investigated their role and underlying mechanisms in hydrocephalus following IVH. An IVH model was established in male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats by injecting autologous blood into the lateral ventricle. Rats were divided into the following groups: sham operation, IVH, IVH treated with the mast cell stabilizer disodium cromoglycate (DSCG), and IVH treated with DSCG plus the protein kinase C (PKC) activator phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA). In a rat model of IVH, mast cell degranulation and the release of tryptase and chymase were observed, accompanied by significant impairment of glymphatic influx and efflux. This dysfunction was characterized by reduced penetration of CSF tracers into the brain parenchyma and diminished clearance of interstitial solutes. Pharmacological stabilization of mast cells with DSCG substantially improved glymphatic function, restored glymphatic structural integrity, reduced ventricular enlargement, and ameliorated neurological deficits. Mechanistically, mast cell-derived proteases activated the PKC/p38MAPK signaling pathway, leading to decreased AQP4 expression and altered AQP4 distribution at astrocytic endfeet, thereby disrupting the perivascular polarization critical for glymphatic flow. This mechanism was supported by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), which demonstrated an interaction between p38MAPK and AQP4, and by rescue experiments, which showed that PKC activation reversed DSCG's protective effects. In vitro experiments conducted under indirect co-culture conditions further demonstrated the interaction between mast cells and astrocytes. Our results reveal a novel mast cell-PKC/p38MAPK/AQP4 pathway in the development of hydrocephalus following IVH and identify mast cell stabilization as a promising therapeutic strategy for hydrocephalus post-IVH, offering a potential non-invasive approach to manage this devastating complication.

title: An optimized Matrigel-assisted orthotopic GL261 glioma model improves tumor engraftment and reproducibility.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Reliable and reproducible orthotopic GL261 glioma models are essential for preclinical glioblastoma research, particularly for evaluating therapeutic strategies in immunocompetent mice. However, conventional intracranial implantation of GL261 cells frequently results in variable tumor engraftment and heterogeneous tumor growth, limiting experimental reproducibility and increasing variability in therapeutic studies. NEW METHOD: We developed an optimized Matrigel-assisted orthotopic GL261 glioma model by incorporating Matrigel into the conventional intracranial implantation procedure. Tumor establishment and progression were evaluated using bioluminescence imaging and micro-computed tomography, followed by histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses. RESULTS: The optimized Matrigel-assisted approach achieved highly consistent tumor engraftment and significantly improved the reproducibility of intracranial tumor growth compared with the conventional implantation method. Histopathological analyses demonstrated intracranial GL261 tumors with characteristic histopathological features.
